0.title: Daniel: The Most High Rules
0.overview:
The message. Daniel tells God’s people, living far from home under rulers who do not know him, who is really on the throne. One sentence, spoken three times in chapter 4, carries the whole book: “the Most High rules the kingdom of men and gives it to whom he will” (4:17). Empires rise and fall at his word; “he removes kings and sets up kings” (2:21). So his people can serve faithfully in a hostile world, refuse to bow where bowing would betray him, and wait without despair, for every kingdom of this world will give way to “a kingdom that shall never be destroyed” (2:44).

Background: the writer. Daniel was a young man of Judah’s leading families, taken to Babylon with three friends better known by their Babylonian names, Shadrach, Meshach and Abednego (1:3–7). The stories of chapters 1–6 speak of him in the third person; from chapter 7 the visions are told in his own voice: “I, Daniel” (7:15; 8:1). Jewish and Christian tradition has always held that he wrote the book, and Jesus speaks of “the prophet Daniel” (Matthew 24:15).

When and where. In 605 BC Nebuchadnezzar of Babylon came to Jerusalem and took hostages from its leading families. Daniel, probably still a teenager, was among them. In 586 BC Jerusalem and its temple were destroyed, as Jeremiah had warned. Daniel spent his life serving the empire that had done it. He saw Babylon fall to the Medes and Persians in a single night in 539 BC, under Belshazzar (chapter 5). He was still there “until the first year of King Cyrus” (1:21), when the exiles were allowed home, and his last vision is dated two years later (10:1).

The kind of writing. Chapters 1–6 are court stories: true accounts of faithful exiles in a pagan court. Chapters 7–12 are apocalyptic visions, prophecy that “unveils” the unseen meaning of history in vivid symbols: beasts, horns, a heavenly court, angels at war. The angels interpret the main symbols; follow their lead and look for the main point rather than decoding every detail. It is also in two languages: from 2:4 to the end of chapter 7, the part about all the nations, it is in Aramaic, the empire’s common language; the rest, about God’s own people, is in Hebrew.

How the book makes its case. In the stories Daniel courteously declines the king’s food (chapter 1); Nebuchadnezzar dreams of a statue of four metals smashed by a stone “cut out by no human hand” that fills the whole earth (chapter 2); the three friends will not bow even if God does not rescue them, and he meets them in the fire (chapter 3); a proud king is humbled and restored (chapter 4), a prouder one weighed and found wanting (chapter 5); and God shuts the lions’ mouths (chapter 6). The Aramaic chapters are arranged in matching pairs around the centre: four kingdoms (2 and 7), rescue from death (3 and 6), a king judged (4 and 5). Chapter 7, the hinge, shows the same four kingdoms as heaven sees them, savage beasts, until the Ancient of Days takes his seat and gives the kingdom to the Son of Man and his saints. Chapter 8 narrows to a Greek persecutor who defiles the sanctuary; chapter 9 is Daniel’s prayer of confession, answered with the seventy weeks; chapters 10–12 show the unseen war behind history and end in the resurrection of the dead. The stories teach how to live in Babylon; the visions show why it is worth it.

When was it written? Many modern scholars date the finished book to about 165 BC, when the Greek king Antiochus IV was persecuting the Jews. Chapter 11 traces the wars of the third and second centuries BC closely but seems less exact about Antiochus’s end; three instruments in 3:5 have Greek names; and Darius the Mede is hard to match with other records. For many, a belief that detailed prediction cannot happen settles it, though some believing scholars hold the late date on literary grounds. This commentary holds the traditional answer, while granting that the date is debated: the visions came to Daniel himself in the sixth century BC, as the book says. Belshazzar, once thought never to have existed, is now known from Babylonian records as the son of King Nabonidus, ruling Babylon while his father was away; that is why the highest place he could offer was third in the kingdom (5:7). Instrument names travelled with trade long before Alexander, and the Dead Sea Scrolls show Daniel copied and treasured as Scripture within a few generations of 165 BC. And the visions reach beyond 165 BC, to a kingdom after Greece and an everlasting kingdom that came with Christ.

Reading the hard visions. Christians differ over details. This commentary takes the four kingdoms as Babylon, Medo-Persia, Greece and Rome, as the early church and the Reformers did; many modern scholars read them as Babylon, Media, Persia and Greece. It reads the stone as Christ’s kingdom, begun at his first coming, and the seventy weeks of 9:24–27 as fulfilled in his death and the fall of Jerusalem in AD 70, with no gap the text does not mention; dispensational interpreters place a final seven years at the end of history. Antiochus IV, the persecutor of chapter 8, foreshadows a final enemy (11:36–45), and “a time, times, and half a time” is a limited period God has fixed. Daniel himself sets the tone: “I heard, but I did not understand” (12:8). What matters most is plain: the persecutor’s time is short, and the saints receive the kingdom.

Where it leads: to Christ. Daniel leads to Christ chiefly by promise. In his vision Daniel sees “with the clouds of heaven there came one like a son of man”, and to him is given “dominion and glory and a kingdom, that all peoples, nations, and languages should serve him” (7:13–14). Son of Man was Jesus’ own favourite name for himself, and on trial he told the high priest, “you will see the Son of Man seated at the right hand of Power, and coming with the clouds of heaven” (Mark 14:62). The stone that smashes the kingdoms of the world is the kingdom Jesus came preaching; the anointed one who is “cut off” and has “nothing” (9:26), to “atone for iniquity” (9:24), is the crucified Messiah. Daniel leads to Christ by pattern too. The fourth man walking in the fire, whom this commentary takes as the Son of God before his birth, meets his servants in the furnace (3:25). Daniel is condemned under an unchangeable law, shut in by a sealed stone (6:17) and brought out alive at dawn; a greater Servant would go down into death itself and rise. When John saw the risen Jesus, he saw “one like a son of man” with hair “white, like white wool” (Revelation 1:13–14): Daniel’s Son of Man, with the Ancient of Days’ glory.

For us. Christians are “elect exiles” (1 Peter 1:1), in Babylon but not of it. Daniel shows how to serve such a world well and still say no where it matters, with courage that comes from knowing who rules. When we fail, there is Daniel’s own prayer, “we do not present our pleas before you because of our righteousness, but because of your great mercy” (9:18), answered in Christ, who stood firm for us. And the book ends with the hope that steadies every exile: “many of those who sleep in the dust of the earth shall awake, some to everlasting life” (12:2), and the old man is told, “you shall rest and shall stand in your allotted place at the end of the days” (12:13). The kingdoms of this world will pass, and “the people who know their God shall stand firm and take action” (11:32).

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God, not Babylon, is the one at work in Jerusalem’s fall. Nebuchadnezzar came against the city and besieged it (v. 1), but the narrator gives the real explanation in three words: “the Lord gave” Jehoiakim into his hand (v. 2). The temple vessels went to the land of Shinar, the old country of Babel, and were placed in the treasury of Babylon’s god as trophies. To every eye it looked as though Israel’s God had been beaten. In fact he was keeping the word his prophets had spoken for generations, judging his unfaithful people, and both the vessels and the pride that took them will meet him again later in the book.
verseByVerse.theology: Even the defeat of God's people happens under God's hand, not outside it.

verseByVerse.quote: In the third year of the reign of Jehoiakim king of Judah, Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon came to Jerusalem and besieged it. And the Lord gave Jehoiakim king of Judah into his hand, with some of the vessels of the house of God. And he brought them to the land of Shinar, to the house of his god, and placed the vessels in the treasury of his god.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jerusalem fell to Babylon because the Lord gave it, and what looked like the defeat of Israel’s God was in fact his judgment and the keeping of his word.

Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon came to Jerusalem. In 605 BC Nebuchadnezzar, crown prince and within months king, had just defeated Egypt and was master of the region. Jehoiakim submitted (2 Kings 24:1), the first of several blows: more captives were taken in 597 BC, and in 586 BC the city and temple were destroyed.

In the third year of the reign of Jehoiakim. Jeremiah dates Nebuchadnezzar’s first year to “the fourth year of Jehoiakim” (Jeremiah 25:1). The two writers most likely count differently: in Babylon a king’s first part-year on the throne was not counted as year one, while in Judah it usually was, and Daniel, writing in Babylon, uses Babylon’s count.

The Lord gave. The first great truth of the book comes in three words, and the title used, “the Lord”, means the Master. With the temple vessels set as trophies in a pagan treasury, it looked as though Babylon’s gods had won. Nebuchadnezzar did not take Jerusalem by his own strength. For generations the prophets had warned that this would come if Judah would not turn from its idols: Isaiah told King Hezekiah that “all that is in your house … shall be carried to Babylon” (Isaiah 39:6). God was not absent; he was keeping his word. The same verb returns twice in the chapter (vv. 9, 17), each time for his servants’ good.

The land of Shinar. This is the old name for the plain where people once built the tower of Babel (Genesis 11:2). The captives were taken to the place that stood for human pride raised against God, and the whole book shows God bringing that pride down. The vessels themselves reappear on the night Babylon falls (5:2–4, 30).

Who rules over it all. When life falls apart, the believer asks not only what has happened but who is ruling over what has happened. The same God who gave Jerusalem into Babylon’s hand later gave his own Son into the hands of sinful men: Jesus was “delivered up according to the definite plan and foreknowledge of God” (Acts 2:23). The darkest day in history became the day of our salvation, and no exile we pass through lies outside the hand that planned it.
verseByVerse.note: Shinar is the old name for Babylonia (Gen 10:10).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 3–7 — New Names in a New World
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Babylon sets out to remake the best of Judah’s young men. The king orders Ashpenaz to choose youths from the royal family and the nobility, gifted, healthy and good-looking, and to teach them for three years the literature and language of the Chaldeans (vv. 3–4). They will eat from the king’s own table (v. 5), and they are given new names honouring Babylon’s gods in place of names that honoured the God of Israel (vv. 6–7). Education, provision and identity: the empire’s method is not force but gradual reshaping, and the rest of the chapter answers whether these four will be reshaped.
verseByVerse.theology: The world will try to reshape God's people from the inside out: their education, their appetites and their names.

verseByVerse.quote: Then the king commanded Ashpenaz, his chief eunuch, to bring some of the people of Israel, both of the royal family and of the nobility, youths without blemish, of good appearance and skillful in all wisdom, endowed with knowledge, understanding learning, and competent to stand in the king's palace, and to teach them the literature and language of the Chaldeans. The king assigned them a daily portion of the food that the king ate, and of the wine that he drank. They were to be educated for three years, and at the end of that time they were to stand before the king.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Babylon took Judah’s brightest young men in order to remake them: trained in its learning, fed from the king’s table and bound to his service.

Some of the people of Israel. Babylon did not only take gold; it took people, the best young men of Judah’s leading families (“royal family” is literally of the seed of the kingdom, as the ESV notes). This too had been foretold: some of Hezekiah’s descendants “shall be eunuchs in the palace of the king of Babylon” (Isaiah 39:7).

The literature and language of the Chaldeans. The plan was clever: take gifted teenagers, the healthiest and quickest, and give them the finest education in the ancient world. The Chaldeans here are Babylon’s learned class. Their literature included mathematics and astronomy, but also astrology, magic and the reading of omens. These young Jews would learn to think like Babylonians, and serve Babylon for life.

Learning Babylon’s wisdom. Learning an unbelieving culture’s wisdom is not wrong in itself. Moses “was instructed in all the wisdom of the Egyptians” (Acts 7:22) without becoming an Egyptian at heart, and Daniel and his friends learned Babylon’s books very well. The danger was being shaped by Babylon’s view of the world until they forgot who they were.

The food that the king ate. The generosity was part of the strategy. To eat from the king’s own table was a great honour, but it also made the young men dependent on him: grateful, comfortable and loyal. After three years they were to “stand before the king”, that is, enter his service.

The danger of the king’s table. Christians often brace themselves for the furnace and the lions, and those chapters are coming. But Babylon’s first move was a scholarship, a place at court and dinner from the king’s kitchen, and that is still the more effective strategy. Very few people are argued out of their faith; far more are slowly made comfortable out of it, until their hopes, fears and weekends are arranged around the same things as everyone else’s, and God has become a kind of hobby. Comfort is a good gift and a demanding master: once it is the thing you cannot do without, you will give up almost anything to keep it. Paul’s warning fits Babylon exactly: “Do not be conformed to this world, but be transformed by the renewal of your mind” (Romans 12:2).

Another table. The answer is not to refuse every good thing Babylon offers; Daniel took the education. It is to have another table. Christ has spread one, where the bread is his body given for us, and he is a King who does not buy our loyalty but gives himself to win it. A heart fed at that table can sit at Babylon’s without being owned by it.

Uncertain wording. The word translated “eunuch” (saris) can mean a castrated man, but it was also used of high court officials in general: Potiphar, who had a wife, is called by it (Genesis 39:1, where the ESV has “officer”). So whether Daniel and his friends were literally made eunuchs is uncertain. Either way, they now belonged to a foreign king.

verseByVerse.quote: Among these were Daniel, Hananiah, Mishael, and Azariah of the tribe of Judah. And the chief of the eunuchs gave them names: Daniel he called Belteshazzar, Hananiah he called Shadrach, Mishael he called Meshach, and Azariah he called Abednego.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Babylon gave the four young men new names honouring its gods, but it could not change whose they were.

Of the tribe of Judah. The story narrows to four, of Judah, the royal tribe of David, from which the promised King would come (Genesis 49:10).

The chief of the eunuchs gave them names. A name told you whom a person belonged to, and each Hebrew name honoured Israel’s God: Daniel means “God is my judge”, Hananiah “the LORD has been gracious”, Mishael “Who is what God is?”, and Azariah “the LORD has helped”. The new names honoured Babylon’s gods: Nebuchadnezzar later says that Daniel was named Belteshazzar “after the name of my god” (4:8). Babylon wanted to erase their past and write a new identity over it.

Whose they were. The young men answered to the new names, and the book keeps using them. But their identity did not depend on what Babylon called them, only on whom they belonged to (see v. 19).

Our deeper name. That is true for every Christian. The world names us by our job, our failures, our background or other people’s opinion, but God has given his people a deeper name. We are “elect exiles” (1 Peter 1:1), chosen by God and living for now away from home, and the risen Christ promises the one who conquers “a new name written on the stone that no one knows except the one who receives it” (Revelation 2:17). No empire can take that name away.

Uncertain wording. Not all the meanings of the names are certain. Belteshazzar probably means “protect his life”, a prayer to a Babylonian god, and Abednego “servant of Nego”, perhaps a form of the god Nabu; Mishael’s meaning is likely but not sure, and the meanings of Shadrach and Meshach are unknown. The direction of the change is clear.
verseByVerse.note: Their Hebrew names honour God (Daniel, “God is my judge”); the new Babylonian names honour Babylon’s gods.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Faithfulness draws a line before God and holds it with courtesy, and God honours it. Daniel accepts Babylon’s education and names, but resolves not to defile himself with the king’s food and wine, and he asks permission rather than staging a protest (v. 8). God gives him favour with the chief official, who is nevertheless afraid for his own head (vv. 9–10). So Daniel proposes a fair ten-day test to the steward: vegetables and water, then judge by what you see (vv. 11–14). At the end the four look healthier than all the others, and the steward lets them keep to their plain food (vv. 15–16).
verseByVerse.theology: Faithfulness draws a clear line and holds it with courtesy, wisdom and trust in God.

verseByVerse.quote: But Daniel resolved that he would not defile himself with the king's food, or with the wine that he drank. Therefore he asked the chief of the eunuchs to allow him not to defile himself. And God gave Daniel favor and compassion in the sight of the chief of the eunuchs, and the chief of the eunuchs said to Daniel, "I fear my lord the king, who assigned your food and your drink; for why should he see that you were in worse condition than the youths who are of your own age? So you would endanger my head with the king."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Daniel accepted Babylon’s education and names, but drew a firm line at the king’s food, and God gave him favour with the official over him.

Daniel resolved. Literally, he set it on his heart, a settled decision made before God. Why this, of all things? The text does not say, and readers have suggested several reasons. Some of the food would certainly have broken the food laws God gave Israel (Leviticus 11). Much of Babylon’s meat and wine was first offered to its gods, and Israel had been warned never to eat what was sacrificed to idols (Exodus 34:15). And eating from the king’s table was a sign of belonging to the king and depending on him. It is probably wise to see all three in the background. But Daniel did not think this a lifelong rule against meat and wine: during a later time of mourning, “no meat or wine entered my mouth” (10:3), which suggests that at other times it did. His refusal here was about this table, this king and this moment.

This far and no further. There must be a place where God’s people say, This far and no further; if Daniel gave way everywhere, nothing would be left of him. Faithfulness in a hostile culture begins with small, private decisions made before God, long before any public test: the men who would face the furnace had first said no at the dinner table. For believers now, the Spirit within is the strength to keep such resolves (Galatians 5:16).

God gave Daniel favor and compassion. Once again God is the one who gave (v. 2), now favour in a Babylonian official’s heart. The same happened to Joseph in Egypt: “the LORD was with Joseph and showed him steadfast love and gave him favor in the sight of the keeper of the prison” (Genesis 39:21). “The king’s heart is a stream of water in the hand of the LORD; he turns it wherever he will” (Proverbs 21:1).

I fear my lord the king. The official liked Daniel but feared, with reason, for his own head. His answer is not quite a no, and Daniel finds a way through it.

What it does not mean. Daniel is no model for drawing lines everywhere or turning personal scruples into God’s law. He accepted a pagan curriculum and a new name, and refused where obedience to God was at stake; wisdom lies in knowing the difference (Romans 14:1–6).
verseByVerse.note: “Defile” is the language of the food laws (Lev 11:43-44).

verseByVerse.quote: Then Daniel said to the steward whom the chief of the eunuchs had assigned over Daniel, Hananiah, Mishael, and Azariah, "Test your servants for ten days; let us be given vegetables to eat and water to drink. Then let our appearance and the appearance of the youths who eat the king's food be observed by you, and deal with your servants according to what you see." So he listened to them in this matter, and tested them for ten days.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Daniel held his conviction with courtesy, offering a short, fair test that protected the official and left the decision with him.

Test your servants for ten days. Daniel makes no scene and goes over no one’s head. His plan protects everyone: it is short, it can be measured, and it leaves the decision with the steward who managed their food: “deal with your servants according to what you see”. Daniel calls himself and his friends “your servants”. He is firm about his conviction and gentle in the way he holds it.

Conviction with courtesy. Here is a model for believers under unbelieving authorities: conviction does not require rudeness. Peter tells Christians to give a reason for their hope “with gentleness and respect, having a good conscience” (1 Peter 3:15–16). Daniel looked for a way to be faithful to God while honouring those over him, and left the outcome with God.

Uncertain wording. “Vegetables” is literally things sown, probably food grown from seed in general, grains and pulses included. “Steward” translates a rare word, probably a Babylonian title; older translations took it as a name, Melzar.

verseByVerse.quote: At the end of ten days it was seen that they were better in appearance and fatter in flesh than all the youths who ate the king's food. So the steward took away their food and the wine they were to drink, and gave them vegetables.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God blessed their faithfulness: after ten days the four looked healthier than all who ate the king’s food, and their plain diet became the rule.

Fatter in flesh. Where being well fed was a sign of health, this was high praise, and vegetables do not normally do it in ten days. The point is that God blessed their faithfulness: “those who honor me I will honor” (1 Samuel 2:30).

So the steward took away their food. What began as a risky request became a settled way of life for the rest of their training.

Pointing beyond Daniel. Centuries later, another young man of the tribe of Judah was hungry in a hostile place, and the enemy offered him bread on terms that would have meant turning from his Father. Jesus refused: “It is written, ‘Man shall not live by bread alone’” (Luke 4:4). Daniel held his ground at a king’s table. Christ held his in the wilderness and at the cross, where the stakes were infinitely higher. He never once gave way, his obedience is counted as ours (Romans 5:19), and he helps us when we are tempted and when we fall: “we do not have a high priest who is unable to sympathize with our weaknesses, but one who in every respect has been tempted as we are, yet without sin” (Hebrews 4:15).

What it does not mean. This is not a chapter about diet; for Christians food itself is no longer the issue: “the kingdom of God is not a matter of eating and drinking but of righteousness and peace and joy in the Holy Spirit” (Romans 14:17). The lesson is not “eat vegetables” but trust God when obedience looks costly. Nor does God promise that faithfulness will always look better after ten days: the next chapters bring a furnace and a den of lions, and the three friends will say, “But if not” (3:18).

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The God who gave Jerusalem into Babylon’s hand also gives his servants all they need there. He gives the four learning and skill in all literature and wisdom, and Daniel understanding in all visions and dreams (v. 17). When the king examines the trainees, none compares with them, and they enter his service (vv. 18–19); in every question he puts to them they are ten times better than all his magicians and enchanters (v. 20). The chapter closes by looking ahead almost seventy years: Daniel was still there in the first year of Cyrus (v. 21), when Babylon had fallen and the exiles could go home.
verseByVerse.theology: God honours those who honour him, and his faithful servant outlasts the empire that captured him.

verseByVerse.quote: As for these four youths, God gave them learning and skill in all literature and wisdom, and Daniel had understanding in all visions and dreams. At the end of the time, when the king had commanded that they should be brought in, the chief of the eunuchs brought them in before Nebuchadnezzar. And the king spoke with them, and among all of them none was found like Daniel, Hananiah, Mishael, and Azariah. Therefore they stood before the king.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God gave the four a mastery of Babylon’s learning, and Daniel a gift no Babylonian book could give, so that at the king’s examination none could compare with them.

God gave them learning and skill. For the third time in the chapter, God gave (vv. 2, 9). Babylon gave the education; God gave the ability to master it. Daniel also received understanding in all visions and dreams, which prepares for the rest of the book and came from God, not from Babylon’s books of omens, as chapter 2 will show.

None was found like Daniel, Hananiah, Mishael, and Azariah. At the king’s examination the narrator uses their Hebrew names again. Babylon had renamed them, but in God’s story they are still who they were. “They stood before the king” means they entered his personal service.

Working in a secular world. Christians may study and work in a secular world. Daniel learned Babylon’s literature thoroughly and served its kings for most of seventy years, while drawing the line where obedience to God required it. Skill and knowledge are God’s gifts, and he can give them in Babylon.

verseByVerse.quote: And in every matter of wisdom and understanding about which the king inquired of them, he found them ten times better than all the magicians and enchanters that were in all his kingdom. And Daniel was there until the first year of King Cyrus.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The wisdom God gave far surpassed all Babylon’s experts, and Daniel outlasted the empire that had captured him.

Ten times better. That is, far better: Babylon’s magicians and enchanters could not compare with four exiles who feared the LORD.

An echo of Joseph. Pharaoh’s magicians could not interpret his dreams (Genesis 41:8), but Joseph could, and Pharaoh said, “Can we find a man like this, in whom is the Spirit of God?” (Genesis 41:38). In both stories the wisdom of the world is shown to be empty beside the wisdom that comes from God.

Until the first year of King Cyrus. Cyrus conquered Babylon in 539 BC, some sixty-six years after Daniel’s capture. Daniel lived on beyond it (10:1 records a vision in Cyrus’s third year); the point here is that he outlasted Babylon. Nebuchadnezzar looked unstoppable in verse 1; by the end of the chapter the empire is gone and the captive is still standing. And the first year of Cyrus was the year the exiles were allowed to go home (Ezra 1:1). Kingdoms rise and fall; God’s faithful servant remains. That is the whole book in a sentence.

Christ our wisdom. That wisdom has a name in the New Testament. Christ is the one “in whom are hidden all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge” (Colossians 2:3), who “became to us wisdom from God” (1 Corinthians 1:30). Daniel’s wisdom was a gift; Christ is God’s wisdom in person. And “if any of you lacks wisdom, let him ask God, who gives generously to all without reproach, and it will be given him” (James 1:5).

A map for exiles. For Christians living as exiles in a world that does not share their faith, Daniel 1 is a map. Do not run from Babylon, and do not become Babylon. Serve well and seek the good of the place where God has put you (Jeremiah 29:7), knowing that he put you there and keeps you there. Know where the line is, hold it with humility, and trust God with the outcome. The kingdoms of this world will pass; the King we serve will not.
verseByVerse.note: Cyrus’s first year over Babylon began in 539 BC.

1.title: Faithful in Babylon
1.overview:
Where we are. Daniel 1 opens the book and sets the scene for all that follows. It is 605 BC: Nebuchadnezzar of Babylon has come against Jerusalem, and among the hostages he carries off are four teenagers from Judah’s leading families (see the introduction).

The message. When God’s people are swept into a world that does not know him, he has not lost control and he has not left them. The Lord gave Jerusalem into Babylon’s hand, and the same Lord gives his servants favour, wisdom and endurance there. So they can serve Babylon well without becoming Babylon, drawing a line where loyalty to God requires it and trusting him with the outcome.

Why it was said. The first readers were exiles, or the children of exiles, who had to work out how to live in an empire that had burned their temple and wanted their minds, their appetites and even their names (see the introduction). The chapter answers their two great questions: has our God been beaten, and how do we stay his in a place like this?

How the chapter makes its case. Three times God “gave”. The Lord gave Jehoiakim into Nebuchadnezzar’s hand (vv. 1–2): the disaster is God’s judgment, not his defeat. Babylon then sets about remaking Judah’s best young men with an education, the king’s food and new names (vv. 3–7). Daniel accepts the training but resolves not to defile himself with the king’s food, and God gave him favour with the official, so that a courteous ten-day test ends in blessing (vv. 8–16). Then God gave the four a wisdom ten times better than all Babylon’s experts, and Daniel outlasts the empire that captured him (vv. 17–21).

Where it leads. To Christ chiefly by pattern, and by the need it exposes. Daniel is a young man of the tribe of Judah who stays faithful at a pagan king’s table. A greater Son of Judah refused bread on the devil’s terms (Luke 4:4) and stayed faithful all the way to the cross, where God gave him into the hands of sinful men for our salvation (Acts 2:23). Daniel’s faithfulness was real but not perfect, for he would later confess his own sin (9:20); Christ’s was perfect, and his obedience is counted to all who trust him.

For us. Christians are “elect exiles” (1 Peter 1:1), living in Babylon but not belonging to it. Babylon rarely begins with a furnace; it begins with a comfortable table. Do not run from it, and do not become it: know where your line is, hold it with courtesy, and when you fail, rest on the one who never did.
1.theology:
God rules over history, even over the defeat of his own people; Babylon's victory was God's gift and God's judgment (vv. 1-2; Isa 39:6-7; Acts 2:23).

God's people live as exiles in a world that seeks to reshape their minds, appetites and identity, and they are called not to be conformed to it (vv. 3-7; Rom 12:2; 1 Pet 1:1).

Faithfulness draws clear lines before God and holds them with wisdom, gentleness and respect toward those in authority (vv. 8-14; 1 Pet 3:15-16).

God gives favour, wisdom and blessing to those who honour him (vv. 9, 15-17, 20; Gen 39:21; Prov 21:1; 1 Sam 2:30; Jas 1:5).

Daniel's faithfulness in a hostile place foreshadows Christ, who refused to live by bread alone and was tempted in every way yet without sin, and who is God's wisdom in person (vv. 8, 17; Luke 4:4; Heb 4:15; Col 2:3; 1 Cor 1:30).

God's servants outlast the empires of this world (v. 21; Ezra 1:1).
1.examples: Think of a Christian student who masters a secular degree without letting it reshape what she loves, or an employee who will not falsify a report but offers his manager a better way instead of a public protest. Like Daniel, they learn Babylon's books, remember that they belong to God, and hold their line with courtesy.

keyVerse.quote: But Daniel resolved that he would not defile himself with the king’s food, or with the wine that he drank.
keyVerse.note: Everything Babylon has done to Daniel so far has been done to him: taken, trained, fed and renamed. Here, for the first time, he acts, and the whole book’s pattern of faithful exiles begins with this quiet decision made before God. It is a small line drawn at a dinner table, but it is the same allegiance that will later stand before the furnace and the lions.

1.reflection:
Babylon’s first move was not a threat but an education, a place at court and food from the king’s table (vv. 3–5). In what ways does the world around you try to reshape what you love through comfort and opportunity rather than pressure? How can you tell when a good gift has become a master?

Daniel accepted the education and the new name but drew a line at the king’s food (v. 8). How do you decide where your own lines must be, and how do you tell a conviction from God’s word from a personal preference?

Daniel held his conviction with courtesy, offering a fair test and leaving the decision with the official (vv. 11–14). What would firm conviction held with gentleness and respect look like in your workplace, school or family?

Three times the chapter says that God “gave” (vv. 2, 9, 17). How does knowing who rules over your circumstances, even painful ones, change the way you face them? Where do you most need to rest on Christ, who stayed faithful where we fail?

2.text: <sup>1</sup>In the second year of the reign of Nebuchadnezzar, Nebuchadnezzar had dreams; his spirit was troubled, and his sleep left him.<sup>2</sup>Then the king commanded that the magicians, the enchanters, the sorcerers, and the Chaldeans be summoned to tell the king his dreams. He went and said thus to him: "Do not destroy the wise men of Babylon; bring me in before the king, and I will show the king the interpretation."<sup>25</sup>Then Arioch brought in Daniel before the king in haste and said thus to him: "I have found among the exiles from Judah a man who will make known to the king the interpretation."<sup>26</sup>The king declared to Daniel, whose name was Belteshazzar, "Are you able to make known to me the dream that I have seen and its interpretation?"<sup>27</sup>Daniel answered the king and said, "No wise men, enchanters, magicians, or astrologers can show to the king the mystery that the king has asked,<sup>28</sup>but there is a God in heaven who reveals mysteries, and he has made known to King Nebuchadnezzar what will be in the latter days. But Daniel remained at the king's court.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–13 — A Dream No One Could Tell
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Human wisdom at its most impressive cannot reach the knowledge of God. Nebuchadnezzar is troubled by dreams and summons every kind of expert in Babylon (vv. 1–3). They ask to hear the dream, but he demands that they tell him the dream itself, on pain of death, as proof that their wisdom is real (vv. 4–6). When they stall, he sees through them (vv. 7–9), and they confess the truth that drives the chapter: no man on earth can do this, and the gods who could do not dwell with flesh (vv. 10–11). In a fury the king orders all the wise men killed, and Daniel and his friends are sought out with the rest (vv. 12–13).
verseByVerse.theology: Human wisdom reaches its limit where only God can speak.

verseByVerse.quote: In the second year of the reign of Nebuchadnezzar, Nebuchadnezzar had dreams; his spirit was troubled, and his sleep left him. Then the king commanded that the magicians, the enchanters, the sorcerers, and the Chaldeans be summoned to tell the king his dreams. So they came in and stood before the king. And the king said to them, "I had a dream, and my spirit is troubled to know the dream."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The most powerful man in the world lies awake, troubled by a dream: power cannot buy peace, and God is about to speak to a king who must learn who really rules.

In the second year of the reign of Nebuchadnezzar. How can this be the king’s second year when Daniel’s training was to last three (1:5)? The simplest answer is the way of counting met in 1:1. The part-year when the king came to the throne was not numbered, so the training could run through that part-year, year one and year two, and be finished early in year two. Whatever the exact timing, Daniel is still a young man, newly placed in the king’s service.

His spirit was troubled, and his sleep left him. Nebuchadnezzar had an empire and every comfort money could buy, but a dream frightened him and he could not shake it off. Power does not bring peace: “It is in vain that you rise up early and go late to rest, eating the bread of anxious toil; for he gives to his beloved sleep” (Psalm 127:2). And God sometimes troubles the sleep of the proud because he means to speak to them. This dream was the first of his messages to a king who needed to learn who really rules.

The magicians, the enchanters, the sorcerers, and the Chaldeans. The ancient world believed that dreams could carry messages from the gods, and Babylon’s experts kept long written lists of dream signs and their meanings. The king summons every kind of expert he has.

Why are the powerful so anxious? We might expect worry to shrink as control grows. Ordinary people today have more control over illness, distance and information than ancient kings had, yet our age is not known for its calm. The more we can steer, the more seems to depend on us, and the more the parts we cannot steer frighten us. Nebuchadnezzar is the patron of that condition: he controlled everything in his world except the one thing that kept him awake, what would come after him (v. 29). Søren Kierkegaard called anxiety the dizziness of freedom, the vertigo of a creature looking over the edge of possibilities it cannot master. God does not cure the king’s anxiety by giving him more control. He tells him that history is already in other hands, and that a kingdom is coming that will never be destroyed (v. 44). That is bad news for anyone whose peace depends on running the world, and very good news for anyone willing to stop trying. Jesus, the King of that kingdom, put it simply: “Therefore do not be anxious about tomorrow, for tomorrow will be anxious for itself” (Matthew 6:34).

verseByVerse.quote: Then the Chaldeans said to the king in Aramaic, "O king, live forever! Tell your servants the dream, and we will show the interpretation." The king answered and said to the Chaldeans, "The word from me is firm: if you do not make known to me the dream and its interpretation, you shall be torn limb from limb, and your houses shall be laid in ruins. But if you show the dream and its interpretation, you shall receive from me gifts and rewards and great honor. Therefore show me the dream and its interpretation."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The wise men ask to hear the dream, but the king, testing whether their wisdom is real, demands that they tell him the dream itself or die.

In Aramaic. Here the book switches from Hebrew to Aramaic, the empire’s common language, and stays in it to the end of chapter 7. Broadly, this part is about God’s rule over the nations, written in the language of the nations; chapters 8–12 return to Hebrew and to the future of God’s own people (see the introduction).

Tell your servants the dream. The request was perfectly reasonable: tell us the dream, and we will look up its meaning in our books.

You shall be torn limb from limb. The king’s demand was cruel, but it was also shrewd. Anyone can invent an interpretation once they know the dream. If these men truly had access to the gods, they should be able to tell him the dream itself, and only then could he trust their interpretation. Nebuchadnezzar was testing whether their wisdom was real.

Uncertain wording. “The word from me is firm” translates a rare word, probably borrowed from Persian, whose meaning is debated. Older translations took it to mean that the king had forgotten the dream: “The thing is gone from me” (KJV). Most now take it as a settled decree, and the king’s words in verse 9, that hearing the dream will show him they can interpret it, suggest that he remembered it well enough to check them. Either way, the threat stands.
verseByVerse.note: Aramaic was the common language of diplomacy across the empire (compare 2 Kgs 18:26).

verseByVerse.quote: They answered a second time and said, "Let the king tell his servants the dream, and we will show its interpretation." The king answered and said, "I know with certainty that you are trying to gain time, because you see that the word from me is firm— if you do not make the dream known to me, there is but one sentence for you. You have agreed to speak lying and corrupt words before me till the times change. Therefore tell me the dream, and I shall know that you can show me its interpretation." The Chaldeans answered the king and said, "There is not a man on earth who can meet the king's demand, for no great and powerful king has asked such a thing of any magician or enchanter or Chaldean. The thing that the king asks is difficult, and no one can show it to the king except the gods, whose dwelling is not with flesh."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The king sees through his experts’ stalling, and they confess that no man on earth can do what he asks, and that the gods who could do not live among men.

Lying and corrupt words. The king suspects what their answers had often been: words invented to please him and to buy time until he forgot or changed his mind. He sees through them.

Till the times change. The wise men hoped that circumstances would shift in their favour if they waited. A few verses later Daniel praises the God who actually controls such things: “He changes times and seasons” (v. 21).

There is not a man on earth. Here the wise men say more than they know. Human wisdom has reached its limit. Only divine beings could do it, and they are far away, “whose dwelling is not with flesh”. The gods of Babylon did not live among people or speak to them.

The God who took flesh. That is the hopeless conclusion of every religion built by human beings: if there is a God, he is far away and silent. The whole Bible answers it. The true God does speak, as this chapter is about to show, and one day he would do far more than send a message: “the Word became flesh and dwelt among us, and we have seen his glory” (John 1:14). The God who was thought to be far from flesh came and took on flesh in Jesus Christ.

verseByVerse.quote: Because of this the king was angry and very furious, and commanded that all the wise men of Babylon be destroyed. So the decree went out, and the wise men were about to be killed; and they sought Daniel and his companions, to kill them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
In a fury the king orders all his wise men killed, and the decree sweeps up Daniel and his friends, who had not even been in the room.

The king was angry and very furious. The same man who fed the four from his table in chapter 1 now wants them dead. Babylon’s favour was never safe ground.

Caught up in others’ decisions. Believers often find themselves caught up in the consequences of decisions made by powerful people who do not know God. Daniel had done nothing wrong, yet the executioners were on their way. The question the chapter now asks is what God’s people do when the sword is at the door.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 14–23 — The God Who Reveals Mysteries
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God’s people meet danger with prayer and answer his grace with praise. Daniel speaks wisely to the captain sent to kill him and asks the king for time (vv. 14–16). Then he gathers his friends to seek mercy from the God of heaven, and that night the mystery is revealed (vv. 17–19). Before doing anything else, Daniel blesses God in a hymn that states the theme of the whole book: wisdom and might belong to him; he changes times and seasons, removes kings and sets up kings, and reveals what is hidden in darkness (vv. 20–22). He thanks the God of his fathers for making known what “we asked” (v. 23).
verseByVerse.theology: When God's people are in danger, they pray together, and they praise God before they act.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Daniel replied with prudence and discretion to Arioch, the captain of the king's guard, who had gone out to kill the wise men of Babylon. He declared to Arioch, the king's captain, "Why is the decree of the king so urgent?" Then Arioch made the matter known to Daniel. And Daniel went in and requested the king to appoint him a time, that he might show the interpretation to the king.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Faced with the man sent to kill him, Daniel answers calmly and wisely, and asks the king for time, promising an answer he does not yet have.

With prudence and discretion. Daniel does not panic. He speaks calmly and wisely to Arioch, the very man who has come to kill him, and as in chapter 1 he is respectful toward those in authority even while they carry out an unjust order.

Requested the king to appoint him a time. The wise men were accused of stalling, yet Daniel asks for time and receives it. Perhaps his reputation from chapter 1 helped; certainly God was at work again in the king’s heart. And Daniel promises something he does not yet have. He does not know the dream. He is walking forward in faith, confident that God can do what no man on earth can.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Daniel went to his house and made the matter known to Hananiah, Mishael, and Azariah, his companions, and told them to seek mercy from the God of heaven concerning this mystery, so that Daniel and his companions might not be destroyed with the rest of the wise men of Babylon. Then the mystery was revealed to Daniel in a vision of the night. Then Daniel blessed the God of heaven.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Daniel’s first move is not a strategy meeting but a prayer meeting: he and his friends seek mercy from the God of heaven, and that night the mystery is revealed.

Made the matter known to Hananiah, Mishael, and Azariah. Daniel goes home and gathers his three friends to pray. He did not carry this burden alone; even the wisest believer needs the prayers of others. Jesus promised, “if two of you agree on earth about anything they ask, it will be done for them by my Father in heaven” (Matthew 18:19), and when Peter was in prison, “earnest prayer for him was made to God by the church” (Acts 12:5). Christian friendship is at its best when friends pray.

To seek mercy. They do not demand an answer from God as though he owed them one. They come as needy people asking for grace.

The God of heaven. Babylon’s astrologers studied the stars to read the future. These four young men prayed to the God who made the heavens and rules them.

Concerning this mystery. A mystery here is a secret that only God can make known. The New Testament uses the same idea for the gospel itself, the greatest secret of all: God’s plan, hidden for ages, to save people from every nation through Christ. Paul speaks of “the revelation of the mystery that was kept secret for long ages but has now been disclosed” (Romans 16:25–26). The God who revealed the king’s dream to Daniel has revealed his Son to us.

Then Daniel blessed the God of heaven. God answered that same night. And before Daniel hurries to the king to save his life, he stops to worship. His first response to answered prayer is praise.

verseByVerse.quote: Daniel answered and said: "Blessed be the name of God forever and ever, to whom belong wisdom and might. He changes times and seasons; he removes kings and sets up kings; he gives wisdom to the wise and knowledge to those who have understanding; he reveals deep and hidden things; he knows what is in the darkness, and the light dwells with him. To you, O God of my fathers, I give thanks and praise, for you have given me wisdom and might, and have now made known to me what we asked of you, for you have made known to us the king's matter."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Daniel’s hymn announces the theme of the whole book: wisdom and might belong to God, who rules history, sees into every darkness and has answered his people’s prayer.

To whom belong wisdom and might. This is one of the great hymns of the Bible. God has the two things the kings of Babylon thought were theirs: wisdom, which the wise men claimed, and might, which the king claimed. Both belong to God.

He removes kings and sets up kings. This is the heart of it. Nebuchadnezzar thinks he controls history, but every ruler holds power only as long as God allows. The rest of the book proves it again and again: Nebuchadnezzar humbled (chapter 4), Belshazzar removed in a single night (chapter 5), and the great empires rising and falling on God’s timetable (chapters 7–8, 11).

He knows what is in the darkness. What was dark to every wise man in Babylon is light to God; nothing is hidden from him. “For the Spirit searches everything, even the depths of God” (1 Corinthians 2:10).

O God of my fathers. The God of Abraham, Isaac and Jacob: in a foreign land, far from the temple, he is still Israel’s God. And the pronouns are plural: “what we asked of you” and “made known to us”. The answer came not to a lone genius but to a praying fellowship.

Comfort for anxious times. Elections, wars and changes of power can make us anxious. But no ruler takes office or leaves it without God’s permission, and Christ is “the ruler of kings on earth” (Revelation 1:5).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 24–30 — Not Because of Any Wisdom in Me
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The true servant of God points away from himself to the God who reveals mysteries. Daniel’s first words are a plea for the lives of Babylon’s wise men (v. 24). Arioch hurries him before the king as an exile from Judah who can do what the experts could not (v. 25), and the king asks whether he is able (v. 26). Daniel answers that no human wisdom can, but “there is a God in heaven who reveals mysteries”, and he has shown the king what will be in the latter days (vv. 27–29). The secret has been given to Daniel not because he is wiser than anyone else, but so that the king may know (v. 30).
verseByVerse.theology: The faithful witness points away from himself to God.

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore Daniel went in to Arioch, whom the king had appointed to destroy the wise men of Babylon. He went and said thus to him: "Do not destroy the wise men of Babylon; bring me in before the king, and I will show the king the interpretation." Then Arioch brought in Daniel before the king in haste and said thus to him: "I have found among the exiles from Judah a man who will make known to the king the interpretation." The king declared to Daniel, whose name was Belteshazzar, "Are you able to make known to me the dream that I have seen and its interpretation?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Daniel’s first words are a plea for the lives of Babylon’s wise men, and he is brought before the king as one of the conquered exiles.

Do not destroy the wise men of Babylon. These were the astrologers and magicians whose religion Daniel rejected, yet he pleads for their lives. God’s people are to seek the good even of those who do not share their faith (Jeremiah 29:7).

I have found among the exiles from Judah a man. Arioch is quick to take some of the credit; courtiers have always been like that. But his words also remind the king that the man who can do what Babylon’s experts cannot is one of the conquered people.

Whose name was Belteshazzar. The king knows him by the name given in honour of a Babylonian god. But the God who is about to answer the king’s question is not the god of that name. It is the God of the exile standing in front of him.

verseByVerse.quote: Daniel answered the king and said, "No wise men, enchanters, magicians, or astrologers can show to the king the mystery that the king has asked, but there is a God in heaven who reveals mysteries, and he has made known to King Nebuchadnezzar what will be in the latter days. Your dream and the visions of your head as you lay in bed are these: To you, O king, as you lay in bed came thoughts of what would be after this, and he who reveals mysteries made known to you what is to be. But as for me, this mystery has been revealed to me, not because of any wisdom that I have more than all the living, but in order that the interpretation may be made known to the king, and that you may know the thoughts of your mind.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Before the most powerful man on earth, Daniel takes no credit: no human being can reveal the dream, but there is a God in heaven who reveals mysteries.

No wise men, enchanters, magicians, or astrologers. The king asked, “Are you able?” Daniel’s answer begins with a no: no human being can do it, Daniel included. Then comes the great but: “but there is a God in heaven who reveals mysteries”.

In the latter days. The dream concerns the future God has planned. The New Testament says those days began with the coming of Christ: “in these last days he has spoken to us by his Son” (Hebrews 1:2).

Thoughts of what would be after this. Daniel gently tells the king what he had been thinking about before he fell asleep: the future of his empire and what would come after him. The great king was worried about what would outlast him, and God answered that question.

Not because of any wisdom that I have. With his life on the line, Daniel could easily have taken the credit and secured his career. Instead he preaches. Every gift God gives his people is for the sake of others and for the glory of God: “What do you have that you did not receive? If then you received it, why do you boast as if you did not receive it?” (1 Corinthians 4:7). The best servants of God are like windows: people look through them and see God.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 31–35 — The Image and the Stone
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Human power at its most dazzling stands on feet of clay, and God’s kingdom will sweep it away. Daniel describes the dream: a huge, brilliant and frightening statue, its head of gold, its chest and arms of silver, its middle of bronze, its legs of iron and its feet of iron mixed with clay (vv. 31–33). A stone cut out by no human hand strikes the feet, and the whole statue shatters at once and blows away like chaff until not a trace remains (vv. 34–35). Then the stone becomes a great mountain and fills the whole earth (v. 35). The rest of the chapter explains what Nebuchadnezzar saw.
verseByVerse.theology: All human empires, however glorious, will be swept away by a kingdom God himself establishes.

verseByVerse.quote: "You saw, O king, and behold, a great image. This image, mighty and of exceeding brightness, stood before you, and its appearance was frightening. The head of this image was of fine gold, its chest and arms of silver, its middle and thighs of bronze, its legs of iron, its feet partly of iron and partly of clay.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The king had seen a dazzling, frightening statue of a man, its metals growing cheaper but harder from head to foot, standing on feet that could not hold together.

A great image. A gigantic human figure, shining so brightly that it terrified him: human power at its most impressive.

Its feet partly of iron and partly of clay. From head to foot the metals become less precious (gold, then silver, bronze and iron) but harder and stronger, until at the very bottom they are mixed with clay. Human empires look magnificent at the top, but they rest on something fragile.
verseByVerse.note: The four metals are usually read as Babylon, Medo-Persia, Greece and Rome.

verseByVerse.quote: As you looked, a stone was cut out by no human hand, and it struck the image on its feet of iron and clay, and broke them in pieces. Then the iron, the clay, the bronze, the silver, and the gold, all together were broken in pieces, and became like the chaff of the summer threshing floors; and the wind carried them away, so that not a trace of them could be found. But the stone that struck the image became a great mountain and filled the whole earth.
verseByVerse.commentary:
A plain stone, made by God and not by human hands, shatters the whole statue, which blows away like chaff, and then grows into a mountain that fills the earth.

Cut out by no human hand. Beside a statue of gold and silver, a stone is plain and ordinary. But no quarry worker shaped this one; God made it. And it strikes the statue at its weakest point, the feet.

Like the chaff of the summer threshing floors. Everything collapses at once, “all together”, and is blown away like chaff, the light husks that farmers tossed into the wind at harvest. The Psalms describe the wicked in the same way: “like chaff that the wind drives away” (Psalm 1:4). All the glory of the world’s empires ends as dust on the wind, “so that not a trace of them could be found”.

Became a great mountain and filled the whole earth. But the stone grows. The humble thing that God made outlasts everything humans built, and takes the place they once held.

The stone the builders rejected. Jesus seems to have had this picture in mind. Quoting the psalm about “the stone that the builders rejected”, he warned, “Everyone who falls on that stone will be broken to pieces, and when it falls on anyone, it will crush him” (Luke 20:17–18). A stone that falls and crushes is the stone of Daniel’s dream, and Jesus claims it as himself. The stone that smashes the kingdoms of the world is Christ and the kingdom he brings.

Does God still reveal secrets through dreams like this? God may do as he pleases, and many believers have known him guide them in unusual ways. But this commentary holds, with many Reformed Christians, that new revelation ceased once Scripture was complete, while others see such gifts continuing; faithful believers differ here. All agree that we test everything by the Bible, where God has now spoken fully in his Son (Hebrews 1:1–2).
verseByVerse.note: “By no human hand” returns in 8:25, where the persecuting king is broken by God alone.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 36–45 — A Kingdom That Shall Never Be Destroyed
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Every human empire will pass, and God himself will set up a kingdom that never ends. The head of gold is Nebuchadnezzar, whose kingdom, power and glory were given him by the God of heaven (vv. 36–38). After him come a lesser kingdom, a third of bronze ruling all the earth, and a fourth as strong as iron, which crushes everything before it (vv. 39–40). Yet that fourth kingdom is divided and brittle, iron mixed with clay, unable to hold together (vv. 41–43). In the days of those kings the God of heaven will set up a kingdom that will never be destroyed or handed to another people; like the stone, it will break the others and stand forever. The dream is certain (vv. 44–45).
verseByVerse.theology: History moves toward the everlasting kingdom of God, fulfilled in Jesus Christ.

verseByVerse.quote: "This was the dream. Now we will tell the king its interpretation. You, O king, the king of kings, to whom the God of heaven has given the kingdom, the power, and the might, and the glory, and into whose hand he has given, wherever they dwell, the children of man, the beasts of the field, and the birds of the heavens, making you rule over them all—you are the head of gold.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Daniel tells the greatest king on earth that his kingdom, power and glory are God’s gift, and that he is only the head of gold.

Now we will tell the king its interpretation. Daniel says “we”. He may include the friends who prayed with him, or speak as God’s messenger together with the God who sent him. Either way, he does not present himself as a lone genius.

The king of kings, to whom the God of heaven has given. Daniel speaks with courtesy and honesty. Nebuchadnezzar is indeed the greatest ruler on earth, but Daniel makes sure he hears where that greatness came from: his kingdom, power, might and glory are on loan from God.

The beasts of the field, and the birds of the heavens. His rule sounds like the dominion God gave Adam at creation, “over the birds of the heavens and over every living thing that moves on the earth” (Genesis 1:28). Nebuchadnezzar has been given a rule something like Adam’s. But like Adam he will grasp at more, and in chapter 4 this king who ruled the beasts will be made to live like one.

You are the head of gold. The first kingdom is Babylon, and the text says so plainly. Nebuchadnezzar must have been pleased, but he was about to learn that the head of gold was only the top of a statue that would be completely destroyed.

The true King of kings. The book is preparing us for a better ruler. In chapter 7 Daniel will see “one like a son of man” who receives an everlasting dominion (7:13–14): Jesus, the true man who rules as God intended. “At present, we do not yet see everything in subjection to him. But we see him” (Hebrews 2:8–9). Only he truly deserves the title Daniel uses here. Paul speaks of God as “the blessed and only Sovereign, the King of kings and Lord of lords” (1 Timothy 6:15), and Revelation gives the same title to Christ: “the Lamb will conquer them, for he is Lord of lords and King of kings” (Revelation 17:14). Nebuchadnezzar’s title was borrowed; Christ’s is his own.

verseByVerse.quote: Another kingdom inferior to you shall arise after you, and yet a third kingdom of bronze, which shall rule over all the earth. And there shall be a fourth kingdom, strong as iron, because iron breaks to pieces and shatters all things. And like iron that crushes, it shall break and crush all these.
verseByVerse.commentary:
After Babylon come three more kingdoms in turn, the last as hard as iron, crushing everything before it; and every one of them will pass.

Another kingdom inferior to you. Inferior as silver is to gold. Daniel names only the first kingdom; the third “shall rule over all the earth”, and the fourth, “strong as iron”, breaks and crushes all that went before it.

Where Christians differ. Who are the other kingdoms? The traditional view, held by the early church, the Reformers and most evangelical interpreters today, sees four empires in order: Babylon (gold), then the Medo-Persian empire (silver), which conquered Babylon in 539 BC, then Greece under Alexander the Great and his successors (bronze), and finally Rome (iron), which crushed everything before it, the empire in which Jesus was born. Most critical scholars today read the sequence as Babylon, Media, Persia and Greece, and their case deserves to be heard at full strength. The book seems to place a Median ruler, Darius the Mede, between Babylon and Cyrus the Persian (5:31; 6:28; 9:1). The little horn of the fourth beast in chapter 7 shares the marks of Antiochus IV in chapter 8, which would make the fourth kingdom Greece. And this reading fits their view that the book was finished in the second century BC (see the introduction).

This commentary’s view. This commentary follows the traditional view in every chapter. The writing on the wall gives Babylon to “the Medes and Persians” together (5:28); chapter 8 pictures them as one ram, followed by “the king of Greece” (8:20–21); and the everlasting kingdom arrives “in the days of” the fourth kingdom (v. 44), as Christ came in the days of Rome. But both readings agree on the point that matters most: every human empire, however strong, will pass away.

verseByVerse.quote: And as you saw the feet and toes, partly of potter's clay and partly of iron, it shall be a divided kingdom, but some of the firmness of iron shall be in it, just as you saw iron mixed with the soft clay. And as the toes of the feet were partly iron and partly clay, so the kingdom shall be partly strong and partly brittle. As you saw the iron mixed with soft clay, so they will mix with one another in marriage, but they will not hold together, just as iron does not mix with clay.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The fourth kingdom keeps the strength of iron but is divided and brittle, and its attempts to hold itself together will fail.

Partly strong and partly brittle. The fourth kingdom keeps the strength of iron but is mixed with clay, and the two will never truly bond; it will be “a divided kingdom”. Rome was famous for its military power, but it was also a vast collection of peoples, languages and rival rulers that never truly held together, and in the end it broke apart.

They will mix with one another in marriage. The rulers of this kingdom will try to unite by intermarriage, perhaps royal marriage alliances like those described later in 11:6 and 11:17, or perhaps a wider mixing of peoples. Whatever the exact reference, it will not work. Human power cannot manufacture lasting unity. Only God’s kingdom joins people “from every tribe and language and people and nation” (Revelation 5:9) into one.

Uncertain wording. “In marriage” is literally by the seed of men, as the ESV notes. It most likely points to intermarriage, but it could describe a broader mixing of peoples, and what exactly it refers to is not known.

verseByVerse.quote: And in the days of those kings the God of heaven will set up a kingdom that shall never be destroyed, nor shall the kingdom be left to another people. It shall break in pieces all these kingdoms and bring them to an end, and it shall stand forever, just as you saw that a stone was cut from a mountain by no human hand, and that it broke in pieces the iron, the bronze, the clay, the silver, and the gold. A great God has made known to the king what shall be after this. The dream is certain, and its interpretation sure."
verseByVerse.commentary:
In the days of the fourth kingdom God himself will set up a kingdom that will never be destroyed, never be handed to another people and will stand forever; the dream is certain.

A kingdom that shall never be destroyed. This is the climax of the chapter and one of the great promises of the Old Testament. God’s kingdom will differ from every other in three ways: it “shall never be destroyed”; it will never be left “to another people”, as Babylon was handed to Persia; and it “shall stand forever”. For Jewish exiles who had lost their land, their temple and David’s throne, this answered the question the exile raised: had God’s promise of an everlasting kingdom for David’s house failed (2 Samuel 7:16)?

By no human hand. The words are repeated because they matter. God’s kingdom is not built by human politics, armies or cleverness. “Not by might, nor by power, but by my Spirit, says the LORD of hosts” (Zechariah 4:6). Jesus said, “My kingdom is not of this world” (John 18:36). The church does not advance Christ’s kingdom by seizing power as Babylon did, but by preaching the gospel.

The kingdom Jesus announced. When the angel announced the birth of Jesus, he used the same language: “he will reign over the house of Jacob forever, and of his kingdom there will be no end” (Luke 1:33). And Jesus began his ministry by saying, “The time is fulfilled, and the kingdom of God is at hand” (Mark 1:15). He was born “in the days of those kings”, while Rome ruled the world, and believers have already been brought, as Paul says, “to the kingdom of his beloved Son” (Colossians 1:13).

The dream is certain, and its interpretation sure. The whole message ends with certainty, so Christians can face the rise and fall of nations with confidence: “Therefore let us be grateful for receiving a kingdom that cannot be shaken, and thus let us offer to God acceptable worship, with reverence and awe” (Hebrews 12:28).

Where Christians differ. Christians agree that the stone is the kingdom of Christ. They differ on when it strikes the image. Many in the Reformed tradition believe the stone began its work at Christ’s first coming: his kingdom started small, like a mustard seed (Matthew 13:31–32), has been growing through the spread of the gospel ever since, and will fill the earth completely when he returns. Many other Christians, especially premillennialists and dispensationalists, believe the stone strikes at Christ’s second coming. They see the toes as a final form of the fourth empire, matching the ten horns of chapter 7, which Christ will destroy when he returns to reign. Both readings honour Christ as the King whose kingdom will outlast every other.

This commentary’s view. This commentary follows the Reformed, amillennial reading, which emphasises that the kingdom is already here and already growing, because Jesus announced it as present (Mark 1:15), though faithful Christians differ on this. Neither reading gives a date, and no one should try to calculate one from the toes.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 46–49 — God of Gods and Lord of Kings
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God honours those who honour him, and even a pagan king is brought to confess him. Nebuchadnezzar falls on his face before Daniel and orders offerings to be made (v. 46), and he confesses that Daniel’s God is “God of gods and Lord of kings, and a revealer of mysteries” (v. 47): a real step, though not yet faith in him as the only God. The king gives Daniel great gifts and makes him ruler of the province of Babylon and chief over all its wise men (v. 48). At Daniel’s request his three friends are given high office in the province, while Daniel remains at court (v. 49), which sets the stage for chapter 3.
verseByVerse.theology: God vindicates his servants and makes even pagan kings acknowledge him.

verseByVerse.quote: Then King Nebuchadnezzar fell upon his face and paid homage to Daniel, and commanded that an offering and incense be offered up to him. The king answered and said to Daniel, "Truly, your God is God of gods and Lord of kings, and a revealer of mysteries, for you have been able to reveal this mystery."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The king falls before Daniel and confesses that his God is God of gods and Lord of kings: a real step, but not yet true faith.

Nebuchadnezzar fell upon his face. The king of kings lies face down before a young captive and orders offerings and incense.

God of gods and Lord of kings. It is a real step, but it is not yet true faith. He still thinks of Daniel’s God as the greatest among many gods, not the only God, and in the very next chapter he sets up a golden image and demands that everyone worship it. A person can be deeply impressed by God’s power without bowing the knee to him. Nebuchadnezzar’s journey is not finished, and the book follows it to the end (4:34–37).

Did Daniel accept worship? The text does not record his response. But the king’s words that follow give the glory to Daniel’s God, “Truly, your God is God of gods” (v. 47), and Daniel had just told him that the dream came from “a God in heaven who reveals mysteries”, not from his own wisdom (vv. 27–30). The likeliest reading is that the honour was given to Daniel as God’s servant, not received as worship. Paul and Barnabas refused worship outright, “We also are men, of like nature with you” (Acts 14:14–15), and so did the angel in Revelation (Revelation 19:10).

verseByVerse.quote: Then the king gave Daniel high honors and many great gifts, and made him ruler over the whole province of Babylon and chief prefect over all the wise men of Babylon. Daniel made a request of the king, and he appointed Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego over the affairs of the province of Babylon. But Daniel remained at the king's court.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God lifts up the humble: the exile who was under sentence of death becomes ruler of the province, and he does not forget the friends who prayed with him.

Ruler over the whole province of Babylon. The exile under sentence of death a short time before is now ruler of the capital province and head of the wise men he had just saved. Like Joseph before him, Daniel goes from danger to the highest office in a foreign land (Genesis 41:39–43).

He appointed Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego. Daniel uses his new influence to lift up the friends who prayed with him. And this sets the stage for chapter 3, where those three, now high officials in the province, will face a test of their own.

The chapter as a whole. The chapter began with a king who could not sleep because he feared the future. It ends with the future revealed. Every kingdom of man will fall; one kingdom, set up by God and centred on his King, will fill the earth. Christians need not fear what tomorrow’s headlines bring. The stone has already been cut from the mountain, and it will not stop until it fills the whole earth.

2.title: The Stone That Filled the Earth
2.overview:
Where we are. Daniel and his friends have finished their training and entered the king’s service (1:19). Now, early in Nebuchadnezzar’s reign, the most powerful man in the world cannot sleep. This is the first of the book’s Aramaic chapters (2:4–7:28), and its four kingdoms return, as heaven sees them, in chapter 7.

The message. Human empires, however dazzling, are temporary and fragile, and the God of heaven, who alone knows the future, will set up a kingdom that shall never be destroyed. The world’s wisdom cannot reach him, but he reveals his secrets to those who seek his mercy, and his kingdom comes by his own hand, not by man’s.

Why it was said. Exiles who had lost their land, their temple and David’s throne needed to know whether God’s kingdom had died with Jerusalem (see the introduction). Here Babylon’s own king learns that his empire is only the head of a statue that will be blown away like chaff.

How the chapter makes its case. Babylon’s wisdom fails: no man on earth can tell the king his dream, and he orders all his wise men killed, Daniel included (vv. 1–13). Daniel asks for time, gathers his friends to seek mercy, receives the mystery in the night and blesses the God who “removes kings and sets up kings” (vv. 14–23). Before the king he gives the glory away: “there is a God in heaven who reveals mysteries” (vv. 24–30). The dream is a dazzling statue on feet of iron and clay, struck by a stone cut out by no human hand that becomes a mountain filling the earth (vv. 31–35). Its meaning is four kingdoms, beginning with Babylon, and in their days the everlasting kingdom of God (vv. 36–45). The king falls on his face and confesses Daniel’s God, impressed but not yet converted (vv. 46–49).

Where it leads. To Christ above all by promise. The kingdom that shall never be destroyed is the kingdom Jesus announced as at hand (Mark 1:15), born in the days of Rome; the angel promised that “of his kingdom there will be no end” (Luke 1:33), and Jesus took the crushing stone as a picture of himself (Luke 20:17–18). And the wise men’s despair that the gods do not dwell “with flesh” (v. 11) is answered when the Word became flesh (John 1:14).

For us. Nations, leaders and headlines rise and fall, and none of them is the stone. We can meet frightening news as Daniel did, praying with friends and praising God before the way ahead is clear, and we can serve the kingdoms of this world without fearing or worshipping them, because in Christ we are “receiving a kingdom that cannot be shaken” (Hebrews 12:28).
2.theology:
Human wisdom cannot reach the knowledge of God; the true God reveals what no man on earth can know (vv. 10-11, 27-28; 1 Cor 1:20; 2:10).

The God who was thought to dwell far from flesh has spoken, and in Christ the Word became flesh (v. 11; John 1:14).

God's people meet danger with shared prayer for mercy and answer God's grace with praise (vv. 17-23; Matt 18:19; Acts 12:5).

God rules history: he removes kings and sets up kings, and every earthly power is his gift (vv. 21, 37-38; Rev 1:5; 1 Tim 6:15).

God's faithful servants give the glory to God and not to themselves (vv. 27-30; 1 Cor 4:7).

All human empires will pass away, and God will set up a kingdom that shall never be destroyed, fulfilled in the kingdom of Jesus Christ, the stone the builders rejected (vv. 34-35, 44-45; Luke 1:33; 20:17-18; Mark 1:15; Col 1:13; Heb 12:28).

God's kingdom comes by his power, not by human hands (vv. 34, 45; Zech 4:6; John 18:36).
2.examples: When the executioners were coming, Daniel called a prayer meeting, and when the answer came he stopped to praise God before he ran to save his life. Believers facing a frightening diagnosis or a threatened job can do the same: pray with friends first, and give thanks before the next step. And when the news is full of powerful nations, the statue on feet of clay reminds us how fragile they are, while the plain stone that becomes a mountain reminds us whose kingdom lasts.

keyVerse.quote: And in the days of those kings the God of heaven will set up a kingdom that shall never be destroyed, nor shall the kingdom be left to another people. It shall break in pieces all these kingdoms and bring them to an end, and it shall stand forever
keyVerse.note: This is the interpretation of the stone and the heart of the chapter: every empire in the statue passes, and only the kingdom God himself sets up lasts. It is one of the Old Testament’s great promises of the kingdom of God, which Jesus announced as at hand while Rome ruled the world (Mark 1:15). For exiles who had lost David’s throne, and for believers under any power, it says who will have the last word.

2.reflection:
When the executioners were on their way, Daniel’s first move was to ask his friends to pray, and his first response to the answer was praise (vv. 17–23). What does your first response to a crisis tend to be, and who prays with you when it comes?

The wise men said that the gods do not dwell “with flesh” (v. 11). How does the coming of Christ in the flesh answer the fear that God is far away and silent?

Daniel refused to take the credit: “not because of any wisdom that I have” (v. 30). Where are you tempted to let your gifts or achievements point to yourself rather than to God?

The statue looked magnificent but stood on feet of iron and clay, and the stone was cut “by no human hand” (vv. 33–34). Which powers or institutions are you tempted to fear, or to trust, too much? What does it look like to seek Christ’s kingdom without trying to build it by worldly power?

3.text: <sup>1</sup>King Nebuchadnezzar made an image of gold, whose height was sixty cubits and its breadth six cubits. He set it up on the plain of Dura, in the province of Babylon.<sup>2</sup>Then King Nebuchadnezzar sent to gather the satraps, the prefects, and the governors, the counselors, the treasurers, the justices, the magistrates, and all the officials of the provinces to come to the dedication of the image that King Nebuchadnezzar had set up.<sup>3</sup>Then the satraps, the prefects, and the governors, the counselors, the treasurers, the justices, the magistrates, and all the officials of the provinces gathered for the dedication of the image that King Nebuchadnezzar had set up.
