And they stood before the image that Nebuchadnezzar had set up.<sup>4</sup>And the herald proclaimed aloud, "You are commanded, O peoples, nations, and languages,<sup>5</sup>that when you hear the sound of the horn, pipe, lyre, trigon, harp, bagpipe, and every kind of music, you are to fall down and worship the golden image that King Nebuchadnezzar has set up.<sup>6</sup>And whoever does not fall down and worship shall immediately be cast into a burning fiery furnace."<sup>7</sup>Therefore, as soon as all the peoples heard the sound of the horn, pipe, lyre, trigon, harp, bagpipe, and every kind of music, all the peoples, nations, and languages fell down and worshiped the golden image that King Nebuchadnezzar had set up.<sup>8</sup>Therefore at that time certain Chaldeans came forward and maliciously accused the Jews.<sup>9</sup>They declared to King Nebuchadnezzar, "O king, live forever!<sup>10</sup>You, O king, have made a decree, that every man who hears the sound of the horn, pipe, lyre, trigon, harp, bagpipe, and every kind of music, shall fall down and worship the golden image.<sup>11</sup>And whoever does not fall down and worship shall be cast into a burning fiery furnace.<sup>12</sup>There are certain Jews whom you have appointed over the affairs of the province of Babylon: Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego. These men, O king, pay no attention to you; they do not serve your gods or worship the golden image that you have set up."<sup>13</sup>Then Nebuchadnezzar in furious rage commanded that Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego be brought. So they brought these men before the king.<sup>14</sup>Nebuchadnezzar answered and said to them, "Is it true, O Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego, that you do not serve my gods or worship the golden image that I have set up?<sup>15</sup>Now if you are ready when you hear the sound of the horn, pipe, lyre, trigon, harp, bagpipe, and every kind of music, to fall down and worship the image that I have made, well and good. But if you do not worship, you shall immediately be cast into a burning fiery furnace. And who is the god who will deliver you out of my hands?"<sup>16</sup>Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego answered and said to the king, "O Nebuchadnezzar, we have no need to answer you in this matter.<sup>17</sup>If this be so, our God whom we serve is able to deliver us from the burning fiery furnace, and he will deliver us out of your hand, O king.<sup>18</sup>But if not, be it known to you, O king, that we will not serve your gods or worship the golden image that you have set up."<sup>19</sup>Then Nebuchadnezzar was filled with fury, and the expression of his face was changed against Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego. He ordered the furnace heated seven times more than it was usually heated.<sup>20</sup>And he ordered some of the mighty men of his army to bind Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego, and to cast them into the burning fiery furnace.<sup>21</sup>Then these men were bound in their cloaks, their tunics, their hats, and their other garments, and they were thrown into the burning fiery furnace.<sup>22</sup>Because the king's order was urgent and the furnace overheated, the flame of the fire killed those men who took up Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego.<sup>23</sup>And these three men, Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego, fell bound into the burning fiery furnace.<sup>24</sup>Then King Nebuchadnezzar was astonished and rose up in haste. He declared to his counselors, "Did we not cast three men bound into the fire?" They answered and said to the king, "True, O king."<sup>25</sup>He answered and said, "But I see four men unbound, walking in the midst of the fire, and they are not hurt; and the appearance of the fourth is like a son of the gods."<sup>26</sup>Then Nebuchadnezzar came near to the door of the burning fiery furnace; he declared, "Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego, servants of the Most High God, come out, and come here!" Then Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego came out from the fire.<sup>27</sup>And the satraps, the prefects, the governors, and the king's counselors gathered together and saw that the fire had not had any power over the bodies of those men. The hair of their heads was not singed, their cloaks were not harmed, and no smell of fire had come upon them.<sup>28</sup>Nebuchadnezzar answered and said, "Blessed be the God of Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego, who has sent his angel and delivered his servants, who trusted in him, and set aside the king's command, and yielded up their bodies rather than serve and worship any god except their own God.<sup>29</sup>Therefore I make a decree: Any people, nation, or language that speaks anything against the God of Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego shall be torn limb from limb, and their houses laid in ruins, for there is no other god who is able to rescue in this way."<sup>30</sup>Then the king promoted Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego in the province of Babylon.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Every power that demands the worship belonging to God must be refused. Nebuchadnezzar, so recently told that he was only a head of gold, sets up an image of gold ninety feet high on the plain of Dura and summons every official of the empire to its dedication (vv. 1–3). The lists repeat, and so does the phrase “the image that King Nebuchadnezzar had set up”: the whole state stands before a god a man has made. A herald announces that at the sound of the music all peoples, nations and languages must fall down and worship, or be thrown into a burning fiery furnace (vv. 4–6). The band plays, and everyone bows (v. 7).
verseByVerse.theology: Every earthly power that demands the worship belonging to God must be refused.

verseByVerse.quote: King Nebuchadnezzar made an image of gold, whose height was sixty cubits and its breadth six cubits. He set it up on the plain of Dura, in the province of Babylon. Then King Nebuchadnezzar sent to gather the satraps, the prefects, and the governors, the counselors, the treasurers, the justices, the magistrates, and all the officials of the provinces to come to the dedication of the image that King Nebuchadnezzar had set up. Then the satraps, the prefects, and the governors, the counselors, the treasurers, the justices, the magistrates, and all the officials of the provinces gathered for the dedication of the image that King Nebuchadnezzar had set up. And they stood before the image that Nebuchadnezzar had set up.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Told that he was only a head of gold, Nebuchadnezzar sets up an image of gold and gathers the whole state to honour it: a god that a man has made.

Whose height was sixty cubits. About ninety feet tall and only nine wide, the image may have been a statue on a high base or a pillar, probably gold-plated rather than solid gold, blazing in the sun over the flat plain. Where the plain of Dura lay is not known.

An image of gold. The text does not say what the image represented. It may have been one of Babylon’s gods, or the king himself, or both at once, since in the ancient world loyalty to the king and loyalty to his gods went together. Many readers have noticed the link with chapter 2. There God showed Nebuchadnezzar that he was only a head of gold, and that his kingdom would pass away; here he builds an image that is gold from top to bottom. Intended or not, it looks like a king answering God’s message with his own: my kingdom will last.

The image that King Nebuchadnezzar had set up. The writer gives the long list of officials twice, and this phrase again and again. The effect is deliberate, and a little humorous. The whole machinery of the state lines up before a statue, and the repeated phrase keeps reminding us where this god came from: a man set it up.

The truth about idols. That is always the truth about idols: “Their idols are silver and gold, the work of human hands” (Psalm 115:4). And the psalm adds a warning: “Those who make them become like them” (Psalm 115:8). The officials on the plain of Dura stood as still and silent as the statue they served.
verseByVerse.note: Sixty by six cubits is about 90 by 9 feet. Dura was a plain near Babylon.

verseByVerse.quote: And the herald proclaimed aloud, "You are commanded, O peoples, nations, and languages, that when you hear the sound of the horn, pipe, lyre, trigon, harp, bagpipe, and every kind of music, you are to fall down and worship the golden image that King Nebuchadnezzar has set up. And whoever does not fall down and worship shall immediately be cast into a burning fiery furnace." Therefore, as soon as all the peoples heard the sound of the horn, pipe, lyre, trigon, harp, bagpipe, and every kind of music, all the peoples, nations, and languages fell down and worshiped the golden image that King Nebuchadnezzar had set up.
verseByVerse.commentary:
At the sound of the music the whole empire must bow to the king’s image or burn, and everyone bows.

O peoples, nations, and languages. This was a religious ceremony and also a test of loyalty for an empire of many peoples, and the king wanted one act of worship to unite them all. The music was the signal, from a full royal orchestra of horns, pipes and stringed instruments. The writer lists the instruments four times (vv. 5, 7, 10, 15): every time the band plays, everyone falls down.

A burning fiery furnace. The furnace was probably a large kiln used for baking bricks or smelting metal, with an opening at the top for loading and a door at the side (v. 26).

As soon as all the peoples heard. The moment the music sounded, everyone bowed. No one wanted to be the one left standing; bowing seemed a small price for safety and a career. Worship can be stirred up from outside in this way: powerful music, a great crowd and the pressure to join in can carry people along without thinking. The question is always who is being worshipped.

Why is it so hard to be the one left standing? In the 1950s the psychologist Solomon Asch ran a simple experiment. A student sat with a group judging which of three lines matched another in length. The answer was obvious, but the others in the room had been told to give the same wrong answer, and most of the students went along with them at least once, against the plain evidence of their eyes. We like to think we would have stood on the plain of Dura, yet most of us bow to far smaller pressures: a laugh round a dinner table, the drift of an office, the opinions it is safe to hold online. The pull is the deep human need to belong and to be approved. That need is not wicked; we were made for approval. The trouble is seeking it from the crowd, because the crowd’s approval has to be earned again every day. The three men could stand because they already had the approval that mattered, from the God they served. In Christ that approval is given, not earned: “There is therefore now no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus” (Romans 8:1). Those who have it can afford to be the odd ones out.

The scene repeated. This scene will be repeated. In Revelation John sees a beast whose image causes “those who would not worship the image of the beast to be slain” (Revelation 13:15). Every age has its golden images: the state, success, money, pleasure, the opinion of the crowd. And every age asks believers whether they will bow when everyone else does. “Little children, keep yourselves from idols” (1 John 5:21).

Uncertain wording. Several of the instruments cannot be identified with certainty. The trigon was probably a small triangular harp, and the word translated “bagpipe” may instead be a kind of drum, or may mean the instruments sounding together. Three of the names (lyre, harp and bagpipe) are Greek words, a point often raised in the debate over the book’s date (see the introduction).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 8–18 — We Will Not Serve Your Gods
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: True faith trusts that God is able to deliver, and obeys him even if he does not. Rival Chaldeans maliciously accuse the three Jews whom the king had promoted: they do not serve his gods or worship his image (vv. 8–12). In a furious rage the king has them brought, offers them a second chance to bow, and throws down the challenge of the chapter: “who is the god who will deliver you out of my hands?” (vv. 13–15). Their answer is calm. There is nothing to discuss: their God is able to deliver them, and he will; “But if not”, they will still not serve the king’s gods or worship his image (vv. 16–18).
verseByVerse.theology: True faith trusts God's power and obeys him whatever he chooses to do.

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore at that time certain Chaldeans came forward and maliciously accused the Jews. They declared to King Nebuchadnezzar, "O king, live forever! You, O king, have made a decree, that every man who hears the sound of the horn, pipe, lyre, trigon, harp, bagpipe, and every kind of music, shall fall down and worship the golden image. And whoever does not fall down and worship shall be cast into a burning fiery furnace. There are certain Jews whom you have appointed over the affairs of the province of Babylon: Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego. These men, O king, pay no attention to you; they do not serve your gods or worship the golden image that you have set up."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Rivals accuse the three Jews of disloyalty to the king, when their only refusal was to worship his gods.

Certain Chaldeans came forward. Among thousands of bowing officials, three men were still standing, and someone noticed. Members of the learned class came forward to accuse them, and “maliciously accused” (literally, ate the pieces of) captures the idea that this was personal. These three had been promoted over the province of Babylon (2:49), and their rivals saw an opportunity.

Whom you have appointed. The accusers are clever. They flatter the king, quote his own decree back to him and remind him that he himself had promoted these men. The charge is presented as ingratitude and disloyalty: “These men, O king, pay no attention to you.” That was not true. The three had served the king faithfully; they simply would not worship his gods. Their refusal rested on the first words of God’s covenant with Israel, “You shall have no other gods before me”, and on its word about every carved image, “You shall not bow down to them or serve them” (Exodus 20:3, 5).

Accused of disloyalty. Christians are often accused in the same way: refusing to join in what everyone else does is described as hatred, arrogance or disloyalty. But refusing to worship a ruler is not refusing to respect him. These men gave the king their work and their honour. They would not give him their worship.

Where was Daniel? The text does not say. He may have been away on the king’s business, but it is better not to guess. The story is about these three men and their God.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Nebuchadnezzar in furious rage commanded that Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego be brought. So they brought these men before the king. Nebuchadnezzar answered and said to them, "Is it true, O Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego, that you do not serve my gods or worship the golden image that I have set up? Now if you are ready when you hear the sound of the horn, pipe, lyre, trigon, harp, bagpipe, and every kind of music, to fall down and worship the image that I have made, well and good. But if you do not worship, you shall immediately be cast into a burning fiery furnace. And who is the god who will deliver you out of my hands?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
The furious king offers the three a second chance to bow, and throws down the chapter’s challenge: what god can deliver them from his hand?

In furious rage. Yet the king does not execute them at once; he asks, “Is it true?”, as if giving them a chance to deny it.

Well and good. The band will play again, and all they need do is bow once. (The ESV notes that “well and good” is not in the Aramaic: the sentence simply breaks off, as angry people’s sentences often do, and the meaning is plain.) This is the most dangerous kind of temptation, the one that comes with a reasonable offer: just once, just outwardly, and everything will be forgiven.

Who is the god who will deliver you out of my hands? This is the king’s real challenge. More than a century earlier, the Assyrian king Sennacherib’s spokesman had mocked Jerusalem with almost the same words: “Who among all the gods of the lands have delivered their lands out of my hand, that the LORD should deliver Jerusalem out of my hand?” (2 Kings 18:35). God answered Sennacherib by destroying his army. Nebuchadnezzar has forgotten that he himself confessed Daniel’s God as “God of gods and Lord of kings” (2:47). Now he claims that no god can match him, and the stage is set for God to answer.

verseByVerse.quote: Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego answered and said to the king, "O Nebuchadnezzar, we have no need to answer you in this matter. If this be so, our God whom we serve is able to deliver us from the burning fiery furnace, and he will deliver us out of your hand, O king. But if not, be it known to you, O king, that we will not serve your gods or worship the golden image that you have set up."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The three men are sure that God is able to deliver them, but their obedience does not depend on whether he does: even if he lets them burn, they will not bow.

We have no need to answer you in this matter. Their answer is calm and short, not rude: they mean that there is nothing to discuss and no defence to prepare. The question had been settled in their hearts long before the music played, as Daniel’s was in 1:8.

Our God whom we serve is able to deliver us. They are confident of two things: God is able, and God will rescue them out of the king’s hand, whether by saving them from the fire or by taking them through death into his presence. Either way the king will not have the last word.

But if not. These are three of the bravest words in the Bible. They believe God can keep them alive; they do not claim a promise that he will. But their obedience does not depend on the outcome. Even if God lets them burn, they will not bow.

Faith, not bargaining. Bargaining says, I will serve God if he protects me. Faith says, I will serve God because he is God, and I trust him with whatever he decides. Job said it this way: “Though he slay me, I will hope in him” (Job 13:15). The apostles said it before their own rulers: “We must obey God rather than men” (Acts 5:29).

Real furnaces today. Many Christians today face real furnaces, and every believer meets moments where faithfulness costs a job, a friendship or a reputation. We need both halves of this answer: God is able, and even if he does not deliver us as we hope, we will not bow. Such courage is not found in ourselves; it is “the Spirit of glory and of God” resting on his people (1 Peter 4:14). And where we have given way, as Peter did when he denied Jesus beside a fire, Christ stood firm for us to the end, and the way back is the same mercy that restored Peter. “And do not fear those who kill the body but cannot kill the soul” (Matthew 10:28). Hebrews honours both kinds of faithful people: those who “quenched the power of fire” (Hebrews 11:34), and those who “were tortured, refusing to accept release, so that they might rise again to a better life” (Hebrews 11:35).

Uncertain wording. The opening of verse 17 is hard to translate. The ESV has “If this be so”, and notes another possible reading: “If our God whom we serve is able to deliver us, he will deliver us from the burning fiery furnace and out of your hand, O king.” Either way, the “if” is not a doubt about God’s power. It takes up the king’s challenge: if it comes to a contest between you and our God, our God will deliver us.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 19–27 — Four Men in the Fire
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God does not always keep his people out of the fire, but he is present with them in it. The king, his face twisted with rage, orders the furnace heated seven times hotter, and the three are bound in all their clothes and thrown in; the flames kill the soldiers who throw them (vv. 19–23). Then the king leaps up: he sees four men, unbound, walking in the fire, unhurt, and the fourth looks like a son of the gods (vv. 24–25). He calls the three out as “servants of the Most High God”, and the gathered officials see that the fire has not touched their bodies, their hair or their cloaks, nor left even its smell (vv. 26–27).
verseByVerse.theology: God does not always keep his people out of the fire, but he goes with them into it.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Nebuchadnezzar was filled with fury, and the expression of his face was changed against Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego. He ordered the furnace heated seven times more than it was usually heated. And he ordered some of the mighty men of his army to bind Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego, and to cast them into the burning fiery furnace. Then these men were bound in their cloaks, their tunics, their hats, and their other garments, and they were thrown into the burning fiery furnace. Because the king's order was urgent and the furnace overheated, the flame of the fire killed those men who took up Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego. And these three men, Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego, fell bound into the burning fiery furnace.
verseByVerse.commentary:
In his fury the king has the furnace heated as hot as it will go, and the three fall bound into the fire; to every eye, the idol has won.

Seven times more than it was usually heated. A moment before, the king was offering a second chance; now his face twists with rage. “Seven times more” means as hot as possible, a senseless order, since a hotter fire would not make them more dead. The man who ruled the world could not rule his own temper.

Bound in their cloaks, their tunics, their hats. They were thrown in fully dressed, in all their official clothes. The detail matters later: clothing is the first thing to burn, yet theirs will come out unharmed (v. 27).

The flame of the fire killed those men. The king’s fury killed his own soldiers at the opening of the furnace. The fire was real.

Fell bound into the burning fiery furnace. The sentence is slow and heavy: “these three men … fell bound”. The story seems to be over. The idol has won; the faithful are gone.

Uncertain wording. The words for their clothes are rare, probably borrowed from Persian, and the exact meaning of each is uncertain; the first, for example, may mean trousers rather than cloaks. The point is plain: they went in fully clothed.

verseByVerse.quote: Then King Nebuchadnezzar was astonished and rose up in haste. He declared to his counselors, "Did we not cast three men bound into the fire?" They answered and said to the king, "True, O king." He answered and said, "But I see four men unbound, walking in the midst of the fire, and they are not hurt; and the appearance of the fourth is like a son of the gods."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The king sees not three bound men but four, unbound and unhurt, walking in the fire: God did not keep his servants out of the furnace, but met them in it.

Four men unbound, walking in the midst of the fire. The king leaps from his seat. Everything has changed. Not three but four. Not bound but unbound. Not falling but walking, as calmly as if they were in a garden. Not burned but “not hurt”. The only thing the fire destroyed was the ropes that tied them.

Like a son of the gods. Nebuchadnezzar, a pagan, describes the fourth in pagan terms, meaning a divine or heavenly being. In verse 28 he calls him God’s “angel”.

Met in the fire. Whoever the fourth man was (see below), the heart of the matter is the same. God did not keep his servants out of the fire. He met them in it. Long before, God had promised: “when you walk through fire you shall not be burned, and the flame shall not consume you” (Isaiah 43:2). And the risen Christ has promised every believer the same presence: “behold, I am with you always, to the end of the age” (Matthew 28:20). Believers are not promised a life without furnaces. They are promised that they will never be in the furnace alone.

But what of those God did not bring out alive? Many faithful Christians have died in the fire, and many families have prayed for a rescue that did not come. Their faith was not weaker than these three men’s; the three themselves said, “But if not” (v. 18). Christ was with the martyrs in death as surely as he was in the furnace, and he says to every one of them, “Be faithful unto death, and I will give you the crown of life” (Revelation 2:10).

Where Christians differ. Who was the fourth man? Some believe that God sent an angel, as he did for Daniel in the lions’ den (6:22). Many others, in the Reformed tradition and long before it, believe that this was an appearance of the Son of God himself before he was born in Bethlehem, like the angel of the LORD who appeared to Moses “in a flame of fire” in a bush that “was not consumed” (Exodus 3:2). The text does not settle the question, and faithful Christians hold both views.

This commentary’s view. This commentary leans to the second: in the Old Testament the angel of the LORD repeatedly speaks and acts as God himself (Genesis 16:13; Exodus 3:2–6), and the one who walks with his servants in the fire fits that pattern.

Uncertain wording. The KJV translated “like the Son of God”, but the Aramaic word here is plural, “gods”, and on a pagan king’s lips the ESV’s rendering is almost certainly right: he saw a divine being. Even so, he said more than he knew.
verseByVerse.note: “A son of the gods” is Nebuchadnezzar’s pagan description; many have seen in the fourth figure the Son of God.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Nebuchadnezzar came near to the door of the burning fiery furnace; he declared, "Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego, servants of the Most High God, come out, and come here!" Then Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego came out from the fire. And the satraps, the prefects, the governors, and the king's counselors gathered together and saw that the fire had not had any power over the bodies of those men. The hair of their heads was not singed, their cloaks were not harmed, and no smell of fire had come upon them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The king calls the three out as servants of the Most High God, and the whole assembly sees that the fire has not touched them: God’s deliverance is complete.

Servants of the Most High God. The king who had asked “who is the god who will deliver you?” now comes to the door of the furnace and calls them by this title. “Most High” means the God above all gods, and it will become one of the most important names for God in the book (4:17). The contest of verse 15 is over, and the king has announced the winner himself.

No smell of fire had come upon them. The officials who had bowed before the image now crowd round to inspect three men. Their bodies were untouched, their hair was not singed, their cloaks were not harmed, and there was not even the smell of fire on them. Anyone who has stood near a bonfire knows how the smoke gets into your clothes; these men walked out of a blazing furnace smelling of nothing at all. God’s deliverance was complete, and the very crowd gathered to worship an idol became witnesses of the living God.

A greater fire. Many Christians have seen here a picture of something greater. The fire that no human being can survive is the judgment of God against sin. Jesus did not walk through that fire untouched. He took it upon himself on the cross, so that all who trust him come through it without even the smell of fire upon them. Through his death he delivered “all those who through fear of death were subject to lifelong slavery” (Hebrews 2:15).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 28–30 — No Other God Who Is Able to Rescue
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Even a pagan king must confess that no other god can rescue like this one, though admiring God is not yet bowing to him. Nebuchadnezzar blesses the God of Shadrach, Meshach and Abednego, who sent his angel and delivered his servants, and he describes their faith well: they trusted in him, set aside the king’s command and yielded up their bodies rather than worship any other god (v. 28). Yet he answers with another threat of violence, decreeing death for anyone who speaks against their God (v. 29). Then he promotes the three in the province of Babylon (v. 30): the men thrown down into the fire are lifted up.
verseByVerse.theology: God's rescue of his faithful servants compels even their enemies to acknowledge him.

verseByVerse.quote: Nebuchadnezzar answered and said, "Blessed be the God of Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego, who has sent his angel and delivered his servants, who trusted in him, and set aside the king's command, and yielded up their bodies rather than serve and worship any god except their own God. Therefore I make a decree: Any people, nation, or language that speaks anything against the God of Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego shall be torn limb from limb, and their houses laid in ruins, for there is no other god who is able to rescue in this way." Then the king promoted Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego in the province of Babylon.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The king blesses the God who rescued his servants and confesses that no other god can save like this, yet he still tries to command faith by force: admiring God is not yet bowing to him.

Blessed be the God of Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego. The king’s words sum up the chapter. He praises the God “who has sent his angel and delivered his servants”, and he describes their faith accurately. They “trusted in him”. They “set aside the king’s command” (the ESV notes that the Aramaic says they “changed” it, as if their obedience to God overruled the king’s word). And they “yielded up their bodies”, choosing to die rather than worship anyone but God.

Yielded up their bodies. That is what the New Testament asks of every Christian: “present your bodies as a living sacrifice, holy and acceptable to God, which is your spiritual worship” (Romans 12:1). The three offered their bodies to the fire, and God gave them back. Our bodies belong to him too, in life and in death.

There is no other god who is able to rescue in this way. The king has learned something, but not enough. His response is to threaten violence, the same method he used to force people to worship his image; he still thinks faith can be commanded by decree. He honours the God of the three men, but he does not yet bow to him as his own God. That will take another humbling, in chapter 4.

Admiring is not turning. People can be impressed by God’s power without surrendering their lives to him. One day “every knee should bow … and every tongue confess that Jesus Christ is Lord” (Philippians 2:10–11). The question is whether we bow now in faith, or later when it is too late.

Then the king promoted Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego. The chapter ends where chapter 2 ended, with God’s faithful servants lifted up. The men who were thrown down into the fire are raised up in the kingdom. That is the pattern of the whole Bible, and it reaches its fullest form in Christ, who went down into death and was raised and exalted above every name. “In the world you will have tribulation. But take heart; I have overcome the world” (John 16:33).

3.title: But If Not
3.overview:
Where we are. Nebuchadnezzar has just confessed Daniel’s God as “God of gods and Lord of kings” (2:47) and promoted Daniel’s three friends to high office (2:49). Now the king who was told he was only a head of gold sets up an image of gold, and the friends meet the test that the quiet resolve of chapter 1 prepared them for.

The message. No earthly power may have the worship that belongs to God alone, and those who refuse to give it are never alone. God is able to deliver his people from the fire; whether he does or not, they must not bow; and when he lets them go into the furnace, he goes in with them.

Why it was said. Jews scattered through the empire faced constant pressure to honour the gods of the state, with careers and sometimes lives at stake (see the introduction). The chapter shows them what faithfulness looks like, and what their God is like.

How the chapter makes its case. At the sound of the music the whole empire bows to a golden image (vv. 1–7). Three men stand. Accused by rivals and given a second chance by a furious king who asks “who is the god who will deliver you out of my hands?”, they answer that their God is able, “But if not”, they will not serve the king’s gods (vv. 8–18). The furnace is heated seven times hotter and they fall in bound; then the king sees four men walking unhurt in the fire, and the three come out without even the smell of smoke (vv. 19–27). The king blesses their God, yet still tries to command faith by decree (vv. 28–30).

Where it leads. To Christ by the presence of God with his people, and by pattern. This commentary takes the fourth man as the Son of God appearing before his birth (see the note on vv. 24–25): the one who walked with his servants in the fire later came in the flesh as Immanuel, God with us. And the furnace points to a greater fire. These three were brought through unharmed; Jesus went into the fire of God’s judgment against sin and was not spared, so that all who trust him come through it with not even the smell of fire upon them (Hebrews 2:14–15).

For us. The golden image today is seldom a statue. It is whatever the crowd bows to and asks us to bow to as the price of belonging. We need both halves of the three men’s answer: God is able, and even if not, we will not bow. Where we have bowed, Christ stood firm for us and restores us; and when we go into the fire, we do not go alone.
3.theology:
Idols are made by human hands, and every power that demands the worship belonging to God must be refused (vv. 1-7; Exod 20:3-5; Ps 115:4-8; Rev 13:15; 1 John 5:21).

Faithful believers may be maliciously accused, but they can honour rulers while refusing to worship them (vv. 8-12; Acts 5:29).

True faith trusts that God is able to deliver and obeys him even if he does not (vv. 16-18; Job 13:15; Matt 10:28; Heb 11:34-35).

God does not always keep his people out of the fire, but he is present with them in it (vv. 24-25; Isa 43:2; Matt 28:20).

God's deliverance is complete, and it points to Christ, who bore the fire of judgment so that his people are delivered from the fear of death (vv. 26-27; Heb 2:14-15).

Believers offer their bodies to God as living sacrifices (v. 28; Rom 12:1).

Admiring God's power is not the same as bowing to him in faith (vv. 28-29; Phil 2:10-11).
3.examples: The golden image rarely looks like a statue today. It may be a workplace that expects you to sign a statement you believe is false, or friends who make one small compromise the price of belonging. The offer is always the king's: just bow once. The three men's answer still serves: God is able, But if not, we will not bow, and we will not be alone in the fire.

keyVerse.quote: If this be so, our God whom we serve is able to deliver us from the burning fiery furnace, and he will deliver us out of your hand, O king. But if not, be it known to you, O king, that we will not serve your gods or worship the golden image that you have set up.
keyVerse.note: These two verses are the answer to the king’s question, “who is the god who will deliver you?” (v. 15), and the heart of the chapter. They hold together confidence in God’s power and obedience that does not depend on the outcome: God is able, and even if he does not rescue us, we will not bow. That is the difference between faith and bargaining.

3.reflection:
Everyone on the plain of Dura bowed when the music played (v. 7). What are the golden images in your world that everyone is expected to honour, and where do you feel the pressure to bow just once in order to belong?

The three men served the king faithfully but would not worship his gods (vv. 12, 18). How can we tell the difference between respecting those in authority and giving them the loyalty that belongs to God alone?

“Our God whom we serve is able … But if not” (vv. 17–18). How is this answer different from bargaining with God? Where are you tempted to make your obedience depend on how things turn out?

God did not keep his servants out of the fire but met them in it (v. 25). How do Christ’s presence with his people, and his going into the fire of judgment for us, give you courage for the trials you face or fear?

4.text: <sup>1</sup>King Nebuchadnezzar to all peoples, nations, and languages, that dwell in all the earth: Peace be multiplied to you!<sup>2</sup>It has seemed good to me to show the signs and wonders that the Most High God has done for me.<sup>3</sup>How great are his signs, how mighty his wonders! His kingdom is an everlasting kingdom, and his dominion endures from generation to generation.<sup>4</sup>I, Nebuchadnezzar, was at ease in my house and prospering in my palace.<sup>5</sup>I saw a dream that made me afraid. As I lay in bed the fancies and the visions of my head alarmed me.<sup>6</sup>So I made a decree that all the wise men of Babylon should be brought before me, that they might make known to me the interpretation of the dream.<sup>7</sup>Then the magicians, the enchanters, the Chaldeans, and the astrologers came in, and I told them the dream, but they could not make known to me its interpretation.<sup>8</sup>At last Daniel came in before me—he who was named Belteshazzar after the name of my god, and in whom is the spirit of the holy gods —and I told him the dream, saying,<sup>9</sup>"O Belteshazzar, chief of the magicians, because I know that the spirit of the holy gods is in you and that no mystery is too difficult for you, tell me the visions of my dream that I saw and their interpretation.<sup>10</sup>The visions of my head as I lay in bed were these: I saw, and behold, a tree in the midst of the earth, and its height was great.<sup>11</sup>The tree grew and became strong, and its top reached to heaven, and it was visible to the end of the whole earth.<sup>12</sup>Its leaves were beautiful and its fruit abundant, and in it was food for all. The beasts of the field found shade under it, and the birds of the heavens lived in its branches, and all flesh was fed from it.<sup>13</sup>"I saw in the visions of my head as I lay in bed, and behold, a watcher, a holy one, came down from heaven.<sup>14</sup>He proclaimed aloud and said thus: 'Chop down the tree and lop off its branches, strip off its leaves and scatter its fruit. Let the beasts flee from under it and the birds from its branches.<sup>15</sup>But leave the stump of its roots in the earth, bound with a band of iron and bronze, amid the tender grass of the field. Let him be wet with the dew of heaven. Let his portion be with the beasts in the grass of the earth.<sup>16</sup>Let his mind be changed from a man's, and let a beast's mind be given to him; and let seven periods of time pass over him.<sup>17</sup>The sentence is by the decree of the watchers, the decision by the word of the holy ones, to the end that the living may know that the Most High rules the kingdom of men and gives it to whom he will and sets over it the lowliest of men.'<sup>18</sup>This dream I, King Nebuchadnezzar, saw. And you, O Belteshazzar, tell me the interpretation, because all the wise men of my kingdom are not able to make known to me the interpretation, but you are able, for the spirit of the holy gods is in you."<sup>19</sup>Then Daniel, whose name was Belteshazzar, was dismayed for a while, and his thoughts alarmed him. The king answered and said, "Belteshazzar, let not the dream or the interpretation alarm you." Belteshazzar answered and said, "My lord, may the dream be for those who hate you and its interpretation for your enemies!<sup>20</sup>The tree you saw, which grew and became strong, so that its top reached to heaven, and it was visible to the end of the whole earth,<sup>21</sup>whose leaves were beautiful and its fruit abundant, and in which was food for all, under which beasts of the field found shade, and in whose branches the birds of the heavens lived—<sup>22</sup>it is you, O king, who have grown and become strong. Your greatness has grown and reaches to heaven, and your dominion to the ends of the earth.<sup>23</sup>And because the king saw a watcher, a holy one, coming down from heaven and saying, 'Chop down the tree and destroy it, but leave the stump of its roots in the earth, bound with a band of iron and bronze, in the tender grass of the field, and let him be wet with the dew of heaven, and let his portion be with the beasts of the field, till seven periods of time pass over him,'<sup>24</sup>this is the interpretation, O king: It is a decree of the Most High, which has come upon my lord the king,<sup>25</sup>that you shall be driven from among men, and your dwelling shall be with the beasts of the field. You shall be made to eat grass like an ox, and you shall be wet with the dew of heaven, and seven periods of time shall pass over you, till you know that the Most High rules the kingdom of men and gives it to whom he will.<sup>26</sup>And as it was commanded to leave the stump of the roots of the tree, your kingdom shall be confirmed for you from the time that you know that Heaven rules.<sup>27</sup>Therefore, O king, let my counsel be acceptable to you: break off your sins by practicing righteousness, and your iniquities by showing mercy to the oppressed, that there may perhaps be a lengthening of your prosperity."<sup>28</sup>All this came upon King Nebuchadnezzar.<sup>29</sup>At the end of twelve months he was walking on the roof of the royal palace of Babylon,<sup>30</sup>and the king answered and said, "Is not this great Babylon, which I have built by my mighty power as a royal residence and for the glory of my majesty?"<sup>31</sup>While the words were still in the king's mouth, there fell a voice from heaven, "O King Nebuchadnezzar, to you it is spoken: The kingdom has departed from you,<sup>32</sup>and you shall be driven from among men, and your dwelling shall be with the beasts of the field. And you shall be made to eat grass like an ox, and seven periods of time shall pass over you, until you know that the Most High rules the kingdom of men and gives it to whom he will."<sup>33</sup>Immediately the word was fulfilled against Nebuchadnezzar. He was driven from among men and ate grass like an ox, and his body was wet with the dew of heaven till his hair grew as long as eagles' feathers, and his nails were like birds' claws.<sup>34</sup>At the end of the days I, Nebuchadnezzar, lifted my eyes to heaven, and my reason returned to me, and I blessed the Most High, and praised and honored him who lives forever, for his dominion is an everlasting dominion, and his kingdom endures from generation to generation;<sup>35</sup>all the inhabitants of the earth are accounted as nothing, and he does according to his will among the host of heaven and among the inhabitants of the earth; and none can stay his hand or say to him, "What have you done?"<sup>36</sup>At the same time my reason returned to me, and for the glory of my kingdom, my majesty and splendor returned to me. My counselors and my lords sought me, and I was established in my kingdom, and still more greatness was added to me.<sup>37</sup>Now I, Nebuchadnezzar, praise and extol and honor the King of heaven, for all his works are right and his ways are just; and those who walk in pride he is able to humble.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–18 — The King Tells His Dream
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The Most High rules the kingdom of men, and this chapter is a pagan emperor’s own confession of it. Nebuchadnezzar writes to the whole world in praise of the God whose kingdom is everlasting (vv. 1–3). He tells how a dream frightened him at the height of his success, how his wise men failed again, and how he finally turned to Daniel (vv. 4–9). The dream shows a world-sheltering tree (vv. 10–12) felled at a watcher’s command, its stump spared and the man it stands for given a beast’s mind for seven periods of time (vv. 13–16), so that the living may know who really rules (vv. 17–18).
verseByVerse.theology: God speaks even to proud rulers, warning them before he acts.

verseByVerse.quote: King Nebuchadnezzar to all peoples, nations, and languages, that dwell in all the earth: Peace be multiplied to you! It has seemed good to me to show the signs and wonders that the Most High God has done for me. How great are his signs, how mighty his wonders! His kingdom is an everlasting kingdom, and his dominion endures from generation to generation.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The king who burned Jerusalem’s temple opens his letter to the world by praising the God of Israel, whose kingdom alone lasts for ever. The chapter is his own testimony, and he begins where his story ends.

King Nebuchadnezzar to all peoples. An open letter from Nebuchadnezzar himself, to the same “peoples, nations, and languages” he once commanded to bow to his image (3:4). Royal inscriptions recorded a king’s victories; this one records his humiliation. Only grace makes a proud man willing to tell the story against himself (compare 1 Timothy 1:15–16).

His kingdom is an everlasting kingdom. In chapters 2 and 3 the king admired Daniel’s God. Here he confesses, in words close to the Psalms: “Your kingdom is an everlasting kingdom, and your dominion endures throughout all generations” (Psalm 145:13). The rest of the chapter tells how he learned it.
verseByVerse.note: Daniel 4:1–3 is 3:31–33 in the Aramaic numbering, so Aramaic verse numbers in this chapter run three behind English ones (ESV note).

verseByVerse.quote: I, Nebuchadnezzar, was at ease in my house and prospering in my palace. I saw a dream that made me afraid. As I lay in bed the fancies and the visions of my head alarmed me. So I made a decree that all the wise men of Babylon should be brought before me, that they might make known to me the interpretation of the dream. Then the magicians, the enchanters, the Chaldeans, and the astrologers came in, and I told them the dream, but they could not make known to me its interpretation. At last Daniel came in before me—he who was named Belteshazzar after the name of my god, and in whom is the spirit of the holy gods —and I told him the dream, saying, "O Belteshazzar, chief of the magicians, because I know that the spirit of the holy gods is in you and that no mystery is too difficult for you, tell me the visions of my dream that I saw and their interpretation.
verseByVerse.commentary:
At the height of his success the king is frightened by a dream; once again Babylon’s wise men fail, and at last he turns to Daniel.

At ease in my house and prospering in my palace. The story begins at the peak, and that is often the most dangerous moment in a life. Trouble drives people to God; comfort lets them forget him. Jesus told of a rich man who said to his soul, “relax, eat, drink, be merry”, and God said, “Fool! This night your soul is required of you” (Luke 12:19–20).

They could not make known to me its interpretation. This time the king told them the dream (v. 7), and it made no difference. The problem was never lack of information but lack of access to the God who sends the dream.

At last Daniel came in before me. Why try the wise men first, after chapter 2? Perhaps because Daniel’s God made him uncomfortable. Proud people often turn to God only when everything else has failed.

Named Belteshazzar after the name of my god. The king still thinks of Daniel by a name that honours his own god. And “chief of the magicians” (v. 9) means Daniel had been set over the wise men (2:48), not that he practised their arts; he claimed no wisdom but what God gave (2:27–28).

Uncertain wording. “The spirit of the holy gods” (vv. 8, 9, 18) could also be translated “Spirit of the holy God” (ESV note), since the plural word can be used of the one God. From a king who still worshipped many gods, “gods” is the likelier sense. Either way, he recognises in Daniel a wisdom from heaven.

verseByVerse.quote: The visions of my head as I lay in bed were these: I saw, and behold, a tree in the midst of the earth, and its height was great. The tree grew and became strong, and its top reached to heaven, and it was visible to the end of the whole earth. Its leaves were beautiful and its fruit abundant, and in it was food for all. The beasts of the field found shade under it, and the birds of the heavens lived in its branches, and all flesh was fed from it.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The king sees a magnificent tree that shelters and feeds the whole world, a picture of his own empire at its height.

A tree in the midst of the earth. The ancient world often pictured a great king or empire as a great tree. Ezekiel had described Assyria in the same way, as a cedar “of towering height, its top among the clouds”, with “all the birds of the heavens” nesting in its boughs (Ezekiel 31:3, 6).

Its top reached to heaven. The picture is not all bad: the empire did bring order, food and protection to many peoples, as government is meant to (Romans 13:4). But this phrase is ominous. It recalls the builders of Babel, who wanted “a tower with its top in the heavens” to make a name for themselves (Genesis 11:4). A tree that grows toward heaven is a king who is starting to think he belongs there.

Another tree. Jesus pictured the kingdom of heaven as a tree too, grown from the smallest of seeds until “the birds of the air come and make nests in its branches” (Matthew 13:32). Nebuchadnezzar’s tree is felled at its height; Christ’s kingdom begins with a carpenter, twelve followers and a cross, and fills the earth (2:35). The shelter the empire gave for a while, his kingdom gives for ever.

verseByVerse.quote: "I saw in the visions of my head as I lay in bed, and behold, a watcher, a holy one, came down from heaven. He proclaimed aloud and said thus: 'Chop down the tree and lop off its branches, strip off its leaves and scatter its fruit. Let the beasts flee from under it and the birds from its branches. But leave the stump of its roots in the earth, bound with a band of iron and bronze, amid the tender grass of the field. Let him be wet with the dew of heaven. Let his portion be with the beasts in the grass of the earth. Let his mind be changed from a man's, and let a beast's mind be given to him; and let seven periods of time pass over him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
A messenger from heaven orders the tree cut down, but its stump is spared: the king will be brought low and lose his human mind for a set time, yet not destroyed.

A watcher, a holy one. An angel, one of God’s messengers who watch over the affairs of the earth (see “Uncertain wording” below).

Leave the stump of its roots in the earth. There is mercy in the sentence: the stump is protected so that it can grow again. The judgment will not be the end.

Let him be wet with the dew of heaven. In the middle of the sentence the picture shifts from a tree to a man: “Let his portion be with the beasts.” The dream is beginning to interpret itself. This tree is a person.

Let seven periods of time pass over him. Seven often suggests completeness: it will last exactly as long as God has decided, until his work in the king is done.

Hope in a stump. Isaiah used the same picture for David’s royal house: cut down, yet “a shoot from the stump of Jesse” would grow (Isaiah 11:1). The God who spared a stump for a pagan king spared one for David’s line, and from it came Christ.

Uncertain wording. “Watcher” translates an Aramaic word found in the Bible only in this chapter (vv. 13, 17, 23); it probably means a wakeful one, and “a holy one” shows it is an angel. The “band of iron and bronze” may protect the stump or picture the king restrained like a madman; the first fits the stump’s purpose (v. 26). And “seven periods of time” does not say how long a period is. Many take it as seven years, which is possible but not stated.

verseByVerse.quote: The sentence is by the decree of the watchers, the decision by the word of the holy ones, to the end that the living may know that the Most High rules the kingdom of men and gives it to whom he will and sets over it the lowliest of men.' This dream I, King Nebuchadnezzar, saw. And you, O Belteshazzar, tell me the interpretation, because all the wise men of my kingdom are not able to make known to me the interpretation, but you are able, for the spirit of the holy gods is in you."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The point of the whole dream is that every living person should know that God rules all human government, gives power to whom he chooses, and can lift up the lowliest. This is the key sentence of the chapter, and perhaps of the book.

The decree of the watchers. Heavenly messengers announce it, but it is “a decree of the Most High” (v. 24): the angels proclaim; the decision is God’s.

Three truths. God rules over all human government. He gives it to whom he will: no one holds power except by his gift. And he can set over it “the lowliest of men”, raising the humble and bringing down the proud whenever he chooses.

To the end that the living may know. The lesson is for “the living”, everyone who reads the story. “The LORD has established his throne in the heavens, and his kingdom rules over all” (Psalm 103:19). For exiles ruled by the king who had burned their temple, it was strong comfort: their conqueror held his throne only by God’s gift, and God could take it from him in a moment.

The lowliest of men. In Jesus God did exactly this. He set over the world one who was laid in a manger and died on a cross, and gave him “all authority in heaven and on earth” (Matthew 28:18).

In everyday life. Whoever rules your country holds office under the Most High. That frees Christians from both panic and idolatry about politics: we pray for rulers (1 Timothy 2:1–2) and honour them, but none of them is ultimate.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 19–27 — It Is You, O King
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God tells the proud the truth before he humbles them, and he tells it through a servant who wishes them well. Daniel is appalled by what he sees and longs for the dream to fall on the king’s enemies, but he does not soften it: the great tree is the king himself (vv. 19–22). The decree of the Most High will drive him out to live with the beasts until he knows that Heaven rules, yet the stump means his kingdom will be given back (vv. 23–26). So Daniel urges him to break off his sins by doing right and showing mercy to the oppressed, in case God delays the blow (v. 27).
verseByVerse.theology: Faithful love tells the truth and calls for repentance while there is still time.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Daniel, whose name was Belteshazzar, was dismayed for a while, and his thoughts alarmed him. The king answered and said, "Belteshazzar, let not the dream or the interpretation alarm you." Belteshazzar answered and said, "My lord, may the dream be for those who hate you and its interpretation for your enemies! The tree you saw, which grew and became strong, so that its top reached to heaven, and it was visible to the end of the whole earth, whose leaves were beautiful and its fruit abundant, and in which was food for all, under which beasts of the field found shade, and in whose branches the birds of the heavens lived— it is you, O king, who have grown and become strong. Your greatness has grown and reaches to heaven, and your dominion to the ends of the earth.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Daniel is appalled at the sentence and wishes his master well, yet he tells him plainly that the great tree is the king himself. Goodwill and honesty go together.

Dismayed for a while. Daniel understands at once, and it shocks him into silence: he must deliver this to a king who has killed people for less.

May the dream be for those who hate you! Daniel does not rejoice that the king who destroyed Jerusalem is about to be judged; after many years in his service, he wishes him well. That is what it means to “seek the welfare of the city where I have sent you into exile, and pray to the LORD on its behalf” (Jeremiah 29:7). Christians are told to pray “for kings and all who are in high positions” (1 Timothy 2:2), including those who do not know God.

It is you, O king. Daniel repeats the description of the tree (vv. 20–21) and then says the hardest words of the chapter. Like Nathan telling David, “You are the man!” (2 Samuel 12:7), he does not soften the truth. Love that will not tell the truth is not love.

Truth in love. Jesus spoke this way: “Jesus, looking at him, loved him”, and then told the rich young man the one thing he did not want to hear (Mark 10:21). Christ never flattered, and never told the truth to wound.

How do I tell hard truth to someone above me? As Daniel did: with real goodwill, plain words, and a way of escape held out (v. 27). Pray first, choose your moment, and leave the outcome to God.

verseByVerse.quote: And because the king saw a watcher, a holy one, coming down from heaven and saying, 'Chop down the tree and destroy it, but leave the stump of its roots in the earth, bound with a band of iron and bronze, in the tender grass of the field, and let him be wet with the dew of heaven, and let his portion be with the beasts of the field, till seven periods of time pass over him,' this is the interpretation, O king: It is a decree of the Most High, which has come upon my lord the king, that you shall be driven from among men, and your dwelling shall be with the beasts of the field. You shall be made to eat grass like an ox, and you shall be wet with the dew of heaven, and seven periods of time shall pass over you, till you know that the Most High rules the kingdom of men and gives it to whom he will. And as it was commanded to leave the stump of the roots of the tree, your kingdom shall be confirmed for you from the time that you know that Heaven rules.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The sentence is God’s own decree: the king will live like a beast until he acknowledges that the Most High rules, and then his kingdom will be given back. The judgment has a goal, and the goal is restoration.

It is a decree of the Most High. Daniel makes sure the king knows who stands behind the watcher’s words.

Made to eat grass like an ox. The punishment fits the sin: a king who thinks himself more than a man will be made less than one. “Man in his pomp yet without understanding is like the beasts that perish” (Psalm 49:20). Pride is already a kind of madness, and God will let the king’s outward life show what his heart has become.

Till you know that the Most High rules. The word “till” matters. God’s aim is not to destroy Nebuchadnezzar but to bring him to his senses. That is the shape of God’s discipline of his own children too: painful for the moment, “but later it yields the peaceful fruit of righteousness to those who have been trained by it” (Hebrews 12:11).

Your kingdom shall be confirmed for you. The stump means hope: his kingdom will be given back once he learns the lesson. “Heaven rules” is a reverent way of saying “God rules”, as Matthew speaks of “the kingdom of heaven”.

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore, O king, let my counsel be acceptable to you: break off your sins by practicing righteousness, and your iniquities by showing mercy to the oppressed, that there may perhaps be a lengthening of your prosperity."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Daniel urges the king to turn from his sins now, showing it in justice and mercy to the oppressed, in case God may yet delay the judgment. Warnings are given so that people can turn.

Showing mercy to the oppressed. Daniel does not stop at the interpretation; he pleads, and names the sin. Nebuchadnezzar’s great sin was pride, and its fruit was oppression: an empire built by conquest leaves many people crushed and poor. Real repentance shows itself in conduct. This is not a way of earning forgiveness; it is what turning looks like. John the Baptist said the same: “Bear fruits in keeping with repentance” (Luke 3:8). “Whoever conceals his transgressions will not prosper, but he who confesses and forsakes them will obtain mercy” (Proverbs 28:13).

That there may perhaps be a lengthening of your prosperity. Daniel promises no more than “perhaps”, but he knows that God delights to show mercy to those who turn: “I have no pleasure in the death of the wicked, but that the wicked turn from his way and live” (Ezekiel 33:11). The gospel goes further than Daniel’s “perhaps”. To all who turn to Christ, mercy is not possible but promised (John 6:37).

Uncertain wording. The verb translated “break off” can also mean “redeem”. The old Latin Bible read “redeem your sins with alms”, and the verse was later used to teach that almsgiving makes satisfaction for sin, which the Reformers rejected. The context favours “break off”: the point is a change of life, not a payment. Only Christ’s ransom pays for sin (Mark 10:45).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 28–33 — Is Not This Great Babylon?
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Pride claims God’s gifts as its own achievement, and God answers it in a moment. Daniel’s warning stands for a whole year of patience (vv. 28–29). Then, on the roof of his palace, the king looks out over the city and credits it all to his own power and glory (v. 30). While the words are still in his mouth a voice from heaven passes sentence, and at once the greatest king on earth is driven out to eat grass like an ox, his hair and nails grown like a bird’s (vv. 31–33). The man who would not live as a creature under God lives like a beast.
verseByVerse.theology: Pride goes before a fall, and God can humble the greatest in a moment.

verseByVerse.quote: All this came upon King Nebuchadnezzar. At the end of twelve months he was walking on the roof of the royal palace of Babylon, and the king answered and said, "Is not this great Babylon, which I have built by my mighty power as a royal residence and for the glory of my majesty?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
After a year of God’s patience, the king looks over his capital and claims every bit of it as his own achievement for his own glory. This is the sin the whole chapter is about.

A change of voice. The letter is in the king’s own voice, as “I”, but his madness is told about him, as “he” (vv. 28–33), until his reason returns (v. 34). It is as though, during that time, there was no “I” left to tell the story.

At the end of twelve months. A whole year to take the warning to heart was patience, not forgetfulness: “do you presume on the riches of his kindness and forbearance and patience, not knowing that God’s kindness is meant to lead you to repentance?” (Romans 2:4). A delay in judgment is always an invitation to repent. The king did not accept it.

Walking on the roof of the royal palace of Babylon. He looks out over one of the wonders of the ancient world, much of it his own building, and speaks to no one but himself. His surviving inscriptions boast in much the same way.

Is not this great Babylon? Listen to the pronouns: “which I have built by my mighty power … for the glory of my majesty”. There is no mention of God, who had given him “the kingdom, the power, and the might, and the glory” (2:37). He has taken every gift and claimed it as his own. “What do you have that you did not receive? If then you received it, why do you boast as if you did not receive it?” (1 Corinthians 4:7).

The opposite of Christ. The Son of God could have stood on any roof in creation and said, “I built this”, and it would have been true (John 1:3). Instead he said, “I do nothing on my own authority” (John 8:28).

In everyday life. This sin needs no golden statue. It lives quietly in anyone who looks at a career, a family or a ministry and thinks, “I built this.” The cure is not trying to feel small but gratitude: naming the Giver of each thing.
verseByVerse.note: Nebuchadnezzar rebuilt much of Babylon; bricks stamped with his name have been found throughout its ruins.

verseByVerse.quote: While the words were still in the king's mouth, there fell a voice from heaven, "O King Nebuchadnezzar, to you it is spoken: The kingdom has departed from you, and you shall be driven from among men, and your dwelling shall be with the beasts of the field. And you shall be made to eat grass like an ox, and seven periods of time shall pass over you, until you know that the Most High rules the kingdom of men and gives it to whom he will." Immediately the word was fulfilled against Nebuchadnezzar. He was driven from among men and ate grass like an ox, and his body was wet with the dew of heaven till his hair grew as long as eagles' feathers, and his nails were like birds' claws.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God answers the boast instantly: the king is struck down from his throne and lives like an animal until he learns who rules. Pride does not lift a person above humanity but drags him below it.

While the words were still in the king’s mouth. The year of patience ended with one proud sentence. Centuries later the same happened to King Herod. When the crowd shouted, “The voice of a god, and not of a man!”, “Immediately an angel of the Lord struck him down, because he did not give God the glory” (Acts 12:22–23). “Pride goes before destruction, and a haughty spirit before a fall” (Proverbs 16:18).

He was driven from among men. Some compare his condition to a rare mental illness in which a person believes he is an animal, but Scripture is not interested in the medical name. It tells us the cause: God did it, for a reason.

What pride does. When we refuse to live as creatures under God, we do not become gods; we become beasts. The psalmist confessed his own bitterness toward God in the same terms: “I was brutish and ignorant; I was like a beast toward you” (Psalm 73:22).

Is the story historical? Babylonian records are silent, which is not surprising: royal records did not record a king’s disgrace. A fragment found among the Dead Sea Scrolls, the Prayer of Nabonidus, tells of a Babylonian king struck with illness for seven years until a Jewish exile helped him, which suggests that such a story was told about Babylon’s kings. Many scholars think the story was first told of Nabonidus, who left Babylon for some ten years in the Arabian desert, and was later attached to Nebuchadnezzar. Others answer that the two accounts differ in most details and need not be the same story. Daniel gives it as the king’s own testimony, and this commentary reads it as real history, while granting that outside evidence is thin.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 34–37 — My Reason Returned to Me
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Looking up to God is where sanity returns, and the God who humbles the proud also restores the humbled. At the end of the appointed time the king lifts his eyes to heaven, his reason comes back, and his first act is worship: the Most High lives for ever, his kingdom endures, and no one can stay his hand (vv. 34–35). His kingdom and honour are given back with more besides (v. 36), and his last recorded words praise the King of heaven, whose works are right and whose ways are just, and who is able to humble those who walk in pride (v. 37).
verseByVerse.theology: The humbled sinner who looks up to heaven finds his sanity and learns to praise the King of heaven.

verseByVerse.quote: At the end of the days I, Nebuchadnezzar, lifted my eyes to heaven, and my reason returned to me, and I blessed the Most High, and praised and honored him who lives forever, for his dominion is an everlasting dominion, and his kingdom endures from generation to generation; all the inhabitants of the earth are accounted as nothing, and he does according to his will among the host of heaven and among the inhabitants of the earth; and none can stay his hand or say to him, "What have you done?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
When the king looks up to heaven his reason returns, and his first sane act is to worship the eternal God, whose rule no one can resist. Coming to God is coming to our senses.

I, Nebuchadnezzar, lifted my eyes to heaven. Now the king speaks again as “I”, and the order matters: first he lifted his eyes, then his reason returned. An animal looks down at the ground; a man made in God’s image looks up. The moment he looked to heaven, he began to be human again.

Coming to our senses. That is what repentance is. When the prodigal son sat among the pigs, “he came to himself” and said, “I will arise and go to my father” (Luke 15:17–18). Sin is madness; turning to God is sanity. The king’s first act as a sane man was worship: “I blessed the Most High.”

Accounted as nothing. The man who said, “Is not this great Babylon?” now says that all the earth’s inhabitants, himself included, “are accounted as nothing” beside God, as Isaiah said: “All the nations are as nothing before him” (Isaiah 40:17). No one can “stay his hand”, that is, stop him, or demand that he explain himself: “who are you, O man, to answer back to God?” (Romans 9:20). For those who trust him this is the safest truth in the world: the one who cannot be stopped is the one who gave his Son for his people (Romans 8:31–32).

Isn’t faith the opposite of reason? This chapter tells the story the other way round. The king did not reason his way back and then find God; he looked up, and his reason came back. G. K. Chesterton, in Orthodoxy, observed that the madman is not the man who has lost his reason but the one who has lost everything except his reason. A mind sealed inside itself can be perfectly logical and still badly wrong, like a king on a roof explaining that everything in sight exists because of him. Faith does not switch the mind off; it lets it out of that small circle, to see the world as it is, with God at the centre. When Festus told Paul that his learning had driven him mad, Paul answered, “I am not out of my mind, most excellent Festus, but I am speaking true and rational words” (Acts 26:25). Worship is not where reason ends. It is where reason comes home.

verseByVerse.quote: At the same time my reason returned to me, and for the glory of my kingdom, my majesty and splendor returned to me. My counselors and my lords sought me, and I was established in my kingdom, and still more greatness was added to me. Now I, Nebuchadnezzar, praise and extol and honor the King of heaven, for all his works are right and his ways are just; and those who walk in pride he is able to humble.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The humbled king is restored with even greater honour, and his last words praise the King of heaven, who is right in all he does and able to humble the proud.

Still more greatness was added to me. The stump grew again, as Daniel had said. God humbled the king in order to lift him up.

The King of heaven. The king’s last words in the book are a confession: a King above himself, whose dealings with him, even the time in the field, were “right” and “just”.

Those who walk in pride he is able to humble. That lesson is written across the Bible: “God opposes the proud but gives grace to the humble” (James 4:6); “everyone who exalts himself will be humbled, and he who humbles himself will be exalted” (Luke 14:11).

The one who walked the other way. Nebuchadnezzar grasped at heaven and was thrown down; Christ, “though he was in the form of God, did not count equality with God a thing to be grasped”. He humbled himself to death on a cross, “Therefore God has highly exalted him and bestowed on him the name that is above every name” (Philippians 2:6, 9). The king was humbled against his will for his own sin; Christ humbled himself willingly for ours. The way up in God’s kingdom is always the way down: “Humble yourselves, therefore, under the mighty hand of God so that at the proper time he may exalt you” (1 Peter 5:6).

Where Christians differ: was Nebuchadnezzar truly converted? Some believe so: he praises and honours the King of heaven and confesses that all his works are right (v. 37), in words no pagan king spoke of his own gods. Others are more cautious: he still speaks of “my majesty and splendor” (v. 36), and we are not told he abandoned Babylon’s gods. This commentary’s view: we should not claim more than Scripture says, but his confession is the strongest sign in the book of a real humbling before God, and the God who drove a proud king into the field can bring him to faith.

4.title: The Most High Rules
4.overview:
Where we are. Chapter 3 ended with Nebuchadnezzar praising the God of Shadrach, Meshach and Abednego, yet still a king of many gods and quick with threats. Chapter 4 is the last we hear of him, and he tells it himself, in an open letter to his whole empire.

The message. The Most High rules the kingdom of men and gives it to whom he will (v. 17). Pride takes God’s gifts and calls them achievements, and it makes a person less than human; but God humbles the proud in order to restore them, and the one who lifts his eyes to heaven gets his sanity back.

Why it was said. The exiles lived under the very king who had burned their temple (see the introduction). They needed to know that their conqueror held his throne on loan, and that God could take it from him in a sentence or give it back. And the man who destroyed Jerusalem ends by praising the King of heaven.

How the chapter makes its case. The king opens with praise and tells of a dream his wise men cannot interpret: a great tree sheltering the world, cut down at the command of a holy watcher, its stump left bound in the field, “to the end that the living may know that the Most High rules” (vv. 1–18). Daniel, dismayed, tells him plainly, “it is you, O king”, and urges him to break off his sins while there is time (vv. 19–27). A year later he boasts of “great Babylon, which I have built”, and is driven out to live like an ox (vv. 28–33). At the end of the days he lifts his eyes to heaven, his reason returns, and he blesses the Most High and is restored (vv. 34–37).

Where it leads. To Christ chiefly by contrast, and by the character of God revealed in him. Nebuchadnezzar reached for heaven and was brought down among the beasts; the Son of God, “though he was in the form of God, did not count equality with God a thing to be grasped”, humbled himself to the cross and was highly exalted (Philippians 2:6–9). The God who “sets over it the lowliest of men” (v. 17) has set over all things a man born among the animals and crucified.

For us. Whatever we have built, a career, a family, a church or a reputation, was given. The cure for pride is not trying to feel small but looking up: thanking the Giver, confessing that he rules, and trusting the one who humbled himself for proud people like us. And no one is too proud or too far gone for God to reach.
4.theology:
The Most High rules the kingdom of men, gives it to whom he will, and can set over it the lowliest of men (vv. 17, 25, 32; Ps 103:19).

God warns the proud before he judges them, and his patience is meant to lead to repentance (vv. 27, 29; Rom 2:4; Ezek 33:11).

True repentance breaks off sin and bears fruit in righteousness and mercy to the oppressed (v. 27; Luke 3:8; Prov 28:13).

Pride claims God's gifts as one's own achievement, and it makes a person less than human; God humbles the proud (vv. 30-33, 37; 1 Cor 4:7; Prov 16:18; Acts 12:23; Ps 49:20).

Looking up to God in humility restores true sanity and leads to worship (vv. 34-35; Luke 15:17-18).

God's servants love and pray for rulers even while telling them hard truths (vv. 19-22; Jer 29:7; 1 Tim 2:1-2).

Nebuchadnezzar's grasping pride is the opposite of Christ, who humbled himself and was exalted above every name (v. 37; Phil 2:6-9; Luke 14:11; Jas 4:6; 1 Pet 5:6).
4.examples: Nebuchadnezzar's boast can be heard in anyone who looks at a business, a family or a ministry and says, "I built this." The cure is to look up, as he finally did, and give thanks to the one who gave it all. And Daniel shows how to bring hard news to a powerful person: with real goodwill, plainly, and with a call to turn while there is still time.

keyVerse.quote: Now I, Nebuchadnezzar, praise and extol and honor the King of heaven, for all his works are right and his ways are just; and those who walk in pride he is able to humble.
keyVerse.note: The chapter ends where it began, with the king’s praise, and this sentence is the lesson of his whole story told in his own words. The most powerful man on earth confesses a King above him, calls God’s dealings with him just, and warns the world from experience that pride will be humbled. It points beyond itself to Christ, the one who humbled himself and was exalted.

4.reflection:
Nebuchadnezzar was most in danger when he was “at ease” and “prospering” (v. 4). Why is success often more dangerous to the soul than trouble? Where are you most tempted to say, “I built this”?

Daniel was dismayed by the dream, wished the king well, and still told him, “it is you, O king” (vv. 19–22). What can we learn from him about speaking hard truth to people we respect or fear? Is there someone you need to speak to in this way?

The king’s reason returned when he lifted his eyes to heaven (v. 34). How does this chapter challenge the idea that faith is the opposite of reason? What changes when we see ourselves as creatures under God rather than at the centre?

Nebuchadnezzar was humbled against his will; Christ humbled himself willingly (Philippians 2:6–9). How does Christ’s humility for us make it possible to “humble yourselves” (1 Peter 5:6) without despair?
