verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–9 — A Feast and a Hand
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Contempt for the living God is answered by God himself, suddenly and in public. On the night Babylon is to fall, Belshazzar throws a vast drinking feast, sends for the gold and silver vessels taken from God’s temple, and toasts his idols from them (vv. 1–4). At once the fingers of a human hand write on the palace wall, and the king collapses in terror (vv. 5–6). He offers purple, a gold chain and the third place in the kingdom to anyone who can read it, but for the third time in the book Babylon’s wise men fail (vv. 7–9).
verseByVerse.theology: God will not be mocked, and his judgment can interrupt the proudest celebration in an instant.

verseByVerse.quote: King Belshazzar made a great feast for a thousand of his lords and drank wine in front of the thousand. Belshazzar, when he tasted the wine, commanded that the vessels of gold and of silver that Nebuchadnezzar his father had taken out of the temple in Jerusalem be brought, that the king and his lords, his wives, and his concubines might drink from them. Then they brought in the golden vessels that had been taken out of the temple, the house of God in Jerusalem, and the king and his lords, his wives, and his concubines drank from them. They drank wine and praised the gods of gold and silver, bronze, iron, wood, and stone.
verseByVerse.commentary:
On Babylon’s last night its ruler throws a drunken feast and uses the vessels from God’s temple to toast his idols: deliberate contempt for the living God.

Twenty years on. Nebuchadnezzar died in 562 BC, and several short reigns followed. The last king of Babylon was Nabonidus, who spent years away from the capital and left his son Belshazzar in charge of the city. So Belshazzar ruled Babylon, but under his father.

King Belshazzar made a great feast. The date is October 539 BC. The armies of the Medes and Persians under Cyrus were already in the region and had defeated Babylon’s forces nearby, and in the city the king threw a party. Ancient historians later recorded that Babylon fell while its people were celebrating a festival.

When he tasted the wine. The drink loosened whatever restraint he had left. He called for the sacred vessels carried to Babylon in 1:2, which had sat in a treasury for nearly seventy years, and used them as party cups.

Deliberate contempt. This was not bad manners but contempt: drinking from the vessels of the living God while praising idols, with an enemy army at the gates. The prophets had seen this night coming. Isaiah described Babylon’s leaders at a feast: “They prepare the table, they spread the rugs, they eat, they drink. Arise, O princes; oil the shield!” (Isaiah 21:5). Jeremiah said God would punish Babylon with “the vengeance for his temple” (Jeremiah 51:11). “Do not be deceived: God is not mocked” (Galatians 6:7).

The other cup. Jeremiah had also said that the nations, and last of all Babylon, would be made to drink “this cup of the wine of wrath” from God’s hand (Jeremiah 25:15, 26). Belshazzar lifted God’s cups in mockery on the very night that cup reached him. In Gethsemane Jesus prayed, “Remove this cup from me. Yet not what I will, but what you will” (Mark 14:36), and drank it for people who had despised holy things as surely as Belshazzar, so that it would never be handed to them.

Uncertain wording. “Nebuchadnezzar his father” (v. 2): Belshazzar’s father was Nabonidus, who as far as the records show was not of Nebuchadnezzar’s family. But “father” can also mean ancestor or predecessor (ESV note), and “son” can mean successor (v. 22). Some suggest Belshazzar descended from Nebuchadnezzar through his mother, but no record confirms it. The likeliest meaning is that Nebuchadnezzar was his great predecessor on the throne.
verseByVerse.note: Belshazzar’s name means “Bel, protect the king”.

verseByVerse.quote: Immediately the fingers of a human hand appeared and wrote on the plaster of the wall of the king's palace, opposite the lampstand. And the king saw the hand as it wrote. Then the king's color changed, and his thoughts alarmed him; his limbs gave way, and his knees knocked together.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God interrupts the party with a hand writing on the wall, and the proud king collapses in terror.

Immediately the fingers of a human hand appeared. God did not wait. In the middle of the laughter, opposite the lampstand where everyone could see, the fingers of a hand began to write. The finger of God had once written his law on tablets of stone (Exodus 31:18); now it writes his verdict on a palace wall.

His knees knocked together. The king’s face went white, his legs gave way, his knees knocked together. A few moments before he was mocking the God of Israel; now he could not stand. That is how quickly human arrogance collapses when God acts. “It is a fearful thing to fall into the hands of the living God” (Hebrews 10:31).

verseByVerse.quote: The king called loudly to bring in the enchanters, the Chaldeans, and the astrologers. The king declared to the wise men of Babylon, "Whoever reads this writing, and shows me its interpretation, shall be clothed with purple and have a chain of gold around his neck and shall be the third ruler in the kingdom." Then all the king's wise men came in, but they could not read the writing or make known to the king the interpretation. Then King Belshazzar was greatly alarmed, and his color changed, and his lords were perplexed.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The terrified king offers rich rewards to anyone who can read the writing, but all of Babylon’s learning cannot do it.

The third ruler in the kingdom. Why third and not second? Because Belshazzar himself was only second: his father Nabonidus was still king, and the best he could offer was the place below himself. This small detail fits exactly what we now know of Babylon’s final years. For a long time critics doubted that Belshazzar had ever existed, since later Greek historians do not name him; Babylonian texts found since the nineteenth century name him as Nabonidus’s son, entrusted with the kingship in Babylon (see the introduction).

They could not read the writing. For the third time in the book, Babylon’s wise men fail (2:10–11; 4:7). They could not even read the words, let alone explain them. All the learning of Babylon was useless in the one moment it was needed.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 10–16 — There Is a Man in Your Kingdom
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God keeps his faithful servants, even when the powerful forget them, and brings them out when he has work for them. Hearing the uproar, the queen comes into the hall and reminds the king of a man Nebuchadnezzar trusted, in whom was the spirit of the holy gods and a gift for interpreting dreams and riddles (vv. 10–12). So the forgotten Daniel, now an old man, is brought in. The king greets him as one of the exiles of Judah and repeats his offer of rewards (vv. 13–16).
verseByVerse.theology: God's faithful servant may be forgotten by the powerful, but he is not forgotten by God.

verseByVerse.quote: The queen, because of the words of the king and his lords, came into the banqueting hall, and the queen declared, "O king, live forever! Let not your thoughts alarm you or your color change. There is a man in your kingdom in whom is the spirit of the holy gods. In the days of your father, light and understanding and wisdom like the wisdom of the gods were found in him, and King Nebuchadnezzar, your father—your father the king— made him chief of the magicians, enchanters, Chaldeans, and astrologers, because an excellent spirit, knowledge, and understanding to interpret dreams, explain riddles, and solve problems were found in this Daniel, whom the king named Belteshazzar. Now let Daniel be called, and he will show the interpretation."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The queen remembers the man the king has forgotten: Daniel, whom Nebuchadnezzar trusted because God’s wisdom was in him. God’s servants may be pushed aside by the powerful, but they are never lost to God.

The queen. The ESV notes that “queen” may mean “queen mother”. That fits: Belshazzar’s wives were already at the feast (v. 2), but this woman comes in from outside, hearing the uproar, and she remembers the days of Nebuchadnezzar. She was likely an older woman of the royal family.

There is a man in your kingdom. The king did not know Daniel. The man who once ruled the province of Babylon was no longer among the king’s advisers. He may still have held a lesser office, for in Belshazzar’s third year he was still going “about the king’s business” (8:27), but the new rulers had pushed him to the edges.

Forgotten, but not by God. Like Joseph, whom Pharaoh’s cupbearer forgot for two full years (Genesis 40:23; 41:1, 9), Daniel was remembered at the moment God chose. Faithful people often spend years out of the spotlight, but God knows exactly where they are. If you feel overlooked in your church, your work or your family, you are not overlooked by him.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Daniel was brought in before the king. The king answered and said to Daniel, "You are that Daniel, one of the exiles of Judah, whom the king my father brought from Judah. I have heard of you that the spirit of the gods is in you, and that light and understanding and excellent wisdom are found in you. Now the wise men, the enchanters, have been brought in before me to read this writing and make known to me its interpretation, but they could not show the interpretation of the matter. But I have heard that you can give interpretations and solve problems. Now if you can read the writing and make known to me its interpretation, you shall be clothed with purple and have a chain of gold around your neck and shall be the third ruler in the kingdom."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The king greets the aged Daniel as a foreign captive and offers to buy his help, assuming, like everything else that night, that God’s servant has a price.

One of the exiles of Judah. Daniel is now an old man, probably in his eighties. After a lifetime of service, to this king he is still a foreign captive, and there may be a sneer in the words.

You shall be clothed with purple. The king repeats his offer. He has spent the evening treating holy things as his to use as he pleased, and he assumes that anyone can be bought.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 17–24 — You Have Not Humbled Your Heart
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Sin against knowledge is the most serious sin, and Daniel names it before he reads the verdict. He refuses the king’s gifts, because God’s word is not for sale (v. 17). He reminds Belshazzar that every scrap of Nebuchadnezzar’s greatness was God’s gift, and that God brought him down when he grew proud until he knew that the Most High rules (vv. 18–21). Then the charge: you knew all this and did not humble your heart; you defiled God’s vessels, praised dead idols, and did not honour the God who holds your breath. That is why the hand was sent (vv. 22–24).
verseByVerse.theology: To sin against the light we have been given is a grave sin.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Daniel answered and said before the king, "Let your gifts be for yourself, and give your rewards to another. Nevertheless, I will read the writing to the king and make known to him the interpretation. O king, the Most High God gave Nebuchadnezzar your father kingship and greatness and glory and majesty. And because of the greatness that he gave him, all peoples, nations, and languages trembled and feared before him. Whom he would, he killed, and whom he would, he kept alive; whom he would, he raised up, and whom he would, he humbled. But when his heart was lifted up and his spirit was hardened so that he dealt proudly, he was brought down from his kingly throne, and his glory was taken from him. He was driven from among the children of mankind, and his mind was made like that of a beast, and his dwelling was with the wild donkeys. He was fed grass like an ox, and his body was wet with the dew of heaven, until he knew that the Most High God rules the kingdom of mankind and sets over it whom he will.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Daniel refuses to be paid for God’s word, and before reading the verdict he reminds the king that all Nebuchadnezzar’s greatness came from God, who humbled him when he grew proud.

Let your gifts be for yourself. Daniel is blunt but not rude: his message is not for sale. Elisha refused Naaman’s gifts in the same way: “As the LORD lives, before whom I stand, I will receive none” (2 Kings 5:16). Jesus told his disciples, “You received without paying; give without pay” (Matthew 10:8). A servant of God who can be bought cannot be trusted to tell the truth. Besides, Daniel knew something the king did not: by morning Babylon’s honours would be worthless.

The Most High God gave Nebuchadnezzar your father kingship. Before Daniel reads the writing, he preaches, beginning with history. Nebuchadnezzar held the power of life and death over everyone, but all of it was given to him by the Most High God. When his heart was lifted up, God took away his throne and his reason until he confessed that the Most High rules (chapter 4). He learned the lesson and was restored.

A sermon on the last night. Even now, with the verdict already written, God sends a preacher to tell the king why. He does not judge in silence. That is the character of the God who sent his Son “not … to condemn the world, but in order that the world might be saved through him” (John 3:17), and who still warns before he judges.

verseByVerse.quote: And you his son, Belshazzar, have not humbled your heart, though you knew all this, but you have lifted up yourself against the Lord of heaven. And the vessels of his house have been brought in before you, and you and your lords, your wives, and your concubines have drunk wine from them. And you have praised the gods of silver and gold, of bronze, iron, wood, and stone, which do not see or hear or know, but the God in whose hand is your breath, and whose are all your ways, you have not honored. "Then from his presence the hand was sent, and this writing was inscribed.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Belshazzar’s guilt is that he knew what God had done to Nebuchadnezzar and still exalted himself, defiled God’s holy things, and refused to honour the God who gives him every breath.

Though you knew all this. Here is the charge that seals his fate. He was not ignorant: the story of Nebuchadnezzar had been proclaimed to the whole empire (4:1). He had the warning, and he ignored it.

Sinning against knowledge. Sinning in ignorance is serious; sinning against knowledge is worse. “Everyone to whom much was given, of him much will be required” (Luke 12:48). That should sober everyone who grew up hearing the gospel: knowing the truth does not save; humbling ourselves before the God who offers mercy does. “Today, if you hear his voice, do not harden your hearts” (Hebrews 3:15).

Which do not see or hear or know. Daniel names the sins: pride against God, contempt for holy things, and the worship of idols that cannot see, hear or know (Psalm 115:4–7). Then he puts his finger on the deepest one of all.

The God in whose hand is your breath. Every breath Belshazzar took that night, every mouthful of wine and every word of praise to his idols, was given to him by the God he mocked. That is true of every human being: God “himself gives to all mankind life and breath and everything” (Acts 17:25). The heart of sin is not only doing bad things. It is living on God’s gifts while refusing to honour the Giver.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 25–31 — MENE, MENE, TEKEL, and PARSIN
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God’s verdict is short, certain and carried out at once. The writing reads MENE, MENE, TEKEL, and PARSIN, and Daniel gives its meaning: God has numbered the days of the kingdom and ended it; the king has been weighed and found wanting; his kingdom is divided and given to the Medes and Persians (vv. 25–28). Belshazzar keeps his promise and Daniel is robed in purple (v. 29), but there is no repentance. That very night the king is killed, and Darius the Mede receives the kingdom (vv. 30–31).
verseByVerse.theology: God weighs every life, and his word of judgment comes true exactly as he says.

verseByVerse.quote: And this is the writing that was inscribed: MENE, MENE, TEKEL, and PARSIN. This is the interpretation of the matter: MENE, God has numbered the days of your kingdom and brought it to an end; TEKEL, you have been weighed in the balances and found wanting; PERES, your kingdom is divided and given to the Medes and Persians."
verseByVerse.commentary:
God’s verdict is written in three words: the king’s days are counted and finished, he has been weighed and found too light, and his kingdom is handed to the Medes and Persians.

MENE, God has numbered the days of your kingdom. “Mene” sounds like the Aramaic for “numbered”. God had counted Belshazzar’s days, and the last one had arrived. Every kingdom, and every life, has a number of days, and God knows it. The word is written twice, perhaps for emphasis: it is certain.

TEKEL, you have been weighed in the balances and found wanting. “Tekel” sounds like the word for “weighed”. Picture a merchant’s scale: God put Belshazzar on it, and he was too light, all show and no substance. “By him actions are weighed” (1 Samuel 2:3); “In the balances they go up; they are together lighter than a breath” (Psalm 62:9).

PERES, your kingdom is divided. “Peres” is the singular of “parsin”, and it sounds like both “divided” and “Persia” (ESV note). The kingdom is being broken up and handed to the Persians. This was not a warning with time to repent, but a verdict.

All of us on the scale. This is the most searching sentence in the chapter, because it is true of us all. If God put any of us on his scale, we would be found wanting: “all have sinned and fall short of the glory of God” (Romans 3:23). The only hope for anyone weighed by God is that someone else’s goodness be counted as ours, and that is the gospel. Christ’s perfect obedience is put to the account of everyone who trusts him: “For our sake he made him to be sin who knew no sin, so that in him we might become the righteousness of God” (2 Corinthians 5:21). Paul’s great desire was to “be found in him, not having a righteousness of my own” (Philippians 3:9). In Christ, those who were found wanting are found complete.

The scales we live on. Modern people may not believe in a divine scale, but we have never lived on so many earthly ones: rated by employers and customers, graded, ranked, counted in followers, weighing ourselves against everyone we scroll past before breakfast. Two responses are on offer. One is to load the scale, working harder and presenting a better self; but there is always a heavier weight on the other side. The other is to deny the scale: nobody gets to judge me; yet we go on feeling the verdicts we say we reject. Belshazzar tried a third way, the oldest of all: drink, laugh and ignore the writing for one more night. The gospel answers all three. The scale is real, and we are found wanting. But Christ has stepped onto it in our place, and for those who trust him the verdict is already given, and tomorrow’s numbers cannot revise it.

Uncertain wording. The four words are probably also names of weights: a mina, a shekel (tekel) and halves (parsin), and the “u” of the Aramaic “u-parsin” simply means “and”. Read as a list of nouns they look like a meaningless string of weights, which may be one reason the wise men could make nothing of them, though why they could not even read the words is not known. Daniel reads them as verbs, numbered, weighed, divided, and so as a sentence from God. Exactly how each weight relates to the message is uncertain; the meaning Daniel gives is not.
verseByVerse.note: Many scholars note that the three words are also names of weights: a mina, a shekel (tekel) and half-minas (parsin).

verseByVerse.quote: Then Belshazzar gave the command, and Daniel was clothed with purple, a chain of gold was put around his neck, and a proclamation was made about him, that he should be the third ruler in the kingdom. That very night Belshazzar the Chaldean king was killed. And Darius the Mede received the kingdom, being about sixty-two years old.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The king honours Daniel but does not repent, and that same night he is killed and his kingdom passes to the Medes and Persians, exactly as God had written.

Daniel was clothed with purple. Belshazzar keeps his word, but shows no sign of repentance. He treats God’s judgment as a clever puzzle solved, not a call to turn.

That very night Belshazzar the Chaldean king was killed. The Medes and Persians entered the city that night, and Babylon, the head of gold in Nebuchadnezzar’s dream (2:38), fell almost without a battle. The king who began the evening mocking God did not live to see the morning. The prophets had foretold it: “Fallen, fallen is Babylon” (Isaiah 21:9); God would make Babylon’s leaders drunk so that they would “sleep a perpetual sleep and not wake” (Jeremiah 51:57).

Two proud kings. Chapters 4 and 5 stand side by side on purpose. Both kings were proud, and both were warned. One humbled himself and was restored; the other did not and was destroyed. “He who is often reproved, yet stiffens his neck, will suddenly be broken beyond healing” (Proverbs 29:1). The difference was not the size of their sins but what they did with God’s warning. “Behold, now is the favorable time; behold, now is the day of salvation” (2 Corinthians 6:2).

Daniel still standing. Babylon had fallen and the king who mocked God was dead, but God’s servant was still there. As 1:21 says, “Daniel was there”, and the empire was not.

Why did Daniel accept the honours he had refused? He had refused them as payment for God’s word (v. 17). Once the message had been given freely, accepting the king’s command compromised nothing, and Daniel knew the honours would last only hours.

Who was Darius the Mede? No other ancient record we have mentions a ruler by that name, so Christians have offered different suggestions. Some think he was Gubaru, the governor Cyrus set over Babylon, or Ugbaru, the general who took the city; Daniel says he “was made king” (9:1), as a ruler appointed under a greater king would be. Others take 6:28 to mean “Darius, that is, Cyrus”, so that Darius the Mede is another title for Cyrus. Many critical scholars think the writer confused later traditions about the Persian king Darius I. This commentary takes Darius the Mede as a real ruler, while granting that we do not have enough evidence to be certain who he was. What matters is that the kingdom passed exactly as the writing said, to the Medes and Persians.
verseByVerse.note: Babylon fell to the Medes and Persians in October 539 BC. Daniel 5:31 is 6:1 in Aramaic (ESV note).

5.title: Weighed and Found Wanting
5.overview:
Where we are. More than twenty years have passed since chapter 4. Nebuchadnezzar is dead, the armies of the Medes and Persians are at hand, and this is Babylon’s last night. Chapter 5 is the twin of chapter 4: another proud king, another message from God, but a very different ending.

The message. God weighs every ruler and every life, and the one who knew the truth and still would not humble himself is found wanting. Holy things cannot be mocked for ever: the God “in whose hand is your breath” (v. 23) numbers the days of every kingdom, and his word comes true that very night.

Why it was said. The exiles had watched Babylon carry off the vessels of God’s house (1:2), and the prophets had promised that Babylon’s turn would come (see the introduction). This chapter shows God keeping that promise to the hour: the empire that seemed permanent falls in one night, and the old exile who served God faithfully is still standing.

How the chapter makes its case. Belshazzar feasts with a thousand lords, drinks from the temple vessels and praises his idols, until a hand writes on the wall and his wise men cannot read it (vv. 1–9). The queen remembers Daniel, forgotten since Nebuchadnezzar’s day, and he is brought in (vv. 10–16). Daniel refuses the king’s gifts, reminds him how God humbled Nebuchadnezzar, and charges him: “you … have not humbled your heart, though you knew all this” (vv. 17–24). The writing means numbered, weighed and divided, and that very night Belshazzar is killed and Darius the Mede receives the kingdom (vv. 25–31).

Where it leads. To Christ chiefly by the need it exposes. “Weighed in the balances and found wanting” is not only Belshazzar’s verdict; it is ours, for “all have sinned and fall short of the glory of God” (Romans 3:23). The gospel does not tell us we weigh more than we thought. It tells us that Christ stepped onto the scale for us: “For our sake he made him to be sin who knew no sin, so that in him we might become the righteousness of God” (2 Corinthians 5:21). And the cup of wrath that Babylon was made to drink, Christ drank in the place of his people (Mark 14:36).

For us. Knowing the story is not the same as humbling yourself before it. Many fill their lives with noise to avoid thinking about the God who weighs them, as Belshazzar partied with an army at the gates. Today, while it is called today, is the time to stop relying on our own weight and trust Christ, whose righteousness is the only weight that holds.
5.theology:
God is not mocked; contempt for what is holy brings his judgment, as the prophets foretold (vv. 1-6; Gal 6:7; Isa 21:5, 9; Jer 51:11, 57; Heb 10:31).

God's servants may be forgotten by the powerful but are kept by God for his purposes (vv. 10-13).

God's message cannot be bought (v. 17; 2 Kgs 5:16; Matt 10:8).

To sin against knowledge is especially serious; those who have heard the warnings must humble themselves (v. 22; Luke 12:48; Heb 3:15; Prov 29:1).

Every human being lives on God's gifts of life and breath and owes him honour (v. 23; Acts 17:25).

God numbers and weighs every life; all are found wanting, and the only hope is the righteousness of God in Christ (vv. 26-27; Rom 3:23; 2 Cor 5:21; Phil 3:9).

God's word of judgment comes true exactly as spoken, and kingdoms pass as he decrees (vv. 28, 30-31; 2 Cor 6:2).
5.examples: Belshazzar partied while an enemy army waited outside, and many still fill their lives with noise to avoid thinking about the God who will weigh them. The writing on the wall is not only a verdict on him. It is a warning to everyone who has heard the story of God's mercy and judgment and has not yet humbled their heart. The only way to pass God’s weighing is to trust in Christ, whose righteousness is counted to those who belong to him.

keyVerse.quote: TEKEL, you have been weighed in the balances and found wanting
keyVerse.note: This is the heart of the writing on the wall and of the chapter. A king who had every advantage, and who knew what God had done to Nebuchadnezzar, is put on God’s scale and found too light. The verdict reaches every reader, for all are found wanting before God, and it prepares for the gospel, in which Christ’s righteousness is counted to those who trust him.

5.reflection:
Belshazzar threw a party with an enemy army outside the walls (vv. 1–4). In what ways do people today fill their lives with noise and pleasure to avoid thinking about God? Are there ways you do this?

Daniel’s charge was “you … have not humbled your heart, though you knew all this” (v. 22). Why is sin against knowledge so serious? What does this mean for those of us who have heard the gospel many times?

Daniel says the deepest sin is refusing to honour “the God in whose hand is your breath” (v. 23). What would it look like this week to honour God as the Giver of your life, gifts and opportunities?

“Weighed in the balances and found wanting” (v. 27) is true of all of us. What earthly scales do you find yourself living on? How does Christ’s righteousness, counted to us (Philippians 3:9), set us free from them?

And he labored till the sun went down to rescue him.<sup>15</sup>Then these men came by agreement to the king and said to the king, "Know, O king, that it is a law of the Medes and Persians that no injunction or ordinance that the king establishes can be changed."<sup>16</sup>Then the king commanded, and Daniel was brought and cast into the den of lions. The king declared to Daniel, "May your God, whom you serve continually, deliver you!"<sup>17</sup>And a stone was brought and laid on the mouth of the den, and the king sealed it with his own signet and with the signet of his lords, that nothing might be changed concerning Daniel.<sup>18</sup>Then the king went to his palace and spent the night fasting; no diversions were brought to him, and sleep fled from him.<sup>19</sup>Then, at break of day, the king arose and went in haste to the den of lions.<sup>20</sup>As he came near to the den where Daniel was, he cried out in a tone of anguish. The king declared to Daniel, "O Daniel, servant of the living God, has your God, whom you serve continually, been able to deliver you from the lions?"<sup>21</sup>Then Daniel said to the king, "O king, live forever!<sup>22</sup>My God sent his angel and shut the lions' mouths, and they have not harmed me, because I was found blameless before him; and also before you, O king, I have done no harm."<sup>23</sup>Then the king was exceedingly glad, and commanded that Daniel be taken up out of the den. verseByVerse.sectionOverview: A faithful believer can be so good at his work that the only charge his enemies can bring is his faith. Daniel, set over the empire’s governors to protect the king’s interests, outshines every colleague, and the king plans to put him over the whole kingdom (vv. 1–3). Envious rivals comb his record and find nothing, so they decide to attack him through the law of his God (vv. 4–5). With flattery and a lie about everyone being agreed, they persuade Darius to sign an irrevocable decree that for thirty days no one may pray to any god or man except the king, on pain of the lions’ den (vv. 6–9).
verseByVerse.theology: A faithful life leaves enemies nothing to attack but its faith.

verseByVerse.quote: It pleased Darius to set over the kingdom 120 satraps, to be throughout the whole kingdom; and over them three high officials, of whom Daniel was one, to whom these satraps should give account, so that the king might suffer no loss. Then this Daniel became distinguished above all the other high officials and satraps, because an excellent spirit was in him. And the king planned to set him over the whole kingdom.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Under the new Persian government the aged Daniel rises above all his colleagues because of the excellent spirit in him, and the king plans to set him over the whole kingdom.

120 satraps. The Medes and Persians organised their huge territory carefully. Satraps were provincial governors, and over them Darius set three senior officials “so that the king might suffer no loss”: their job was to stop corruption and make sure the taxes reached the king.

Three high officials, of whom Daniel was one. Daniel was now an old man, probably over eighty, who had served the kings of Babylon most of his life. A new ruler might easily have removed the old regime’s officials. God had kept Daniel through the fall of an empire and placed him again at the centre of power.

An excellent spirit was in him. This includes ability but also character: wisdom, honesty and steadiness. Daniel’s faith did not make him a poor employee; it made him an outstanding one. Excellent, honest work in an ordinary job is one of the ways God’s people honour the God who placed them there (Colossians 3:23).

The historical details. This Darius is the Mede of 5:31 (see the note there on who he may have been). The 120 satraps are more than the twenty or so great provinces of the later Persian empire, so the word is probably used here in a broader sense for regional officials, much as Esther counts 127 provinces (Esther 1:1).

verseByVerse.quote: Then the high officials and the satraps sought to find a ground for complaint against Daniel with regard to the kingdom, but they could find no ground for complaint or any fault, because he was faithful, and no error or fault was found in him. Then these men said, "We shall not find any ground for complaint against this Daniel unless we find it in connection with the law of his God."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Envious rivals search Daniel’s whole career for something to use against him and find nothing, so they decide to attack him through his faith.

Sought to find a ground for complaint against Daniel. Success brought envy. The other officials probably did not want a foreign Jew promoted over them, and they may have feared an honest man who would stop them filling their own pockets.

They could find no ground for complaint. A lifetime of public service examined by enemies, and clean. Their own verdict was that they would find nothing “unless we find it in connection with the law of his God”. What a thing for enemies to say.

Honourable conduct among unbelievers. This is what Peter asks of Christians: “Keep your conduct among the Gentiles honorable, so that when they speak against you as evildoers, they may see your good deeds” (1 Peter 2:12). Paul tells Titus to live “so that an opponent may be put to shame, having nothing evil to say about us” (Titus 2:8). The world will still oppose believers, but let it be for their faith and not for their wrongdoing.

A clean record in Christ. Jesus’ enemies too “watched him and sent spies” to catch him (Luke 20:20), and in the end could only bring false witnesses. None of us has a record like Daniel’s before God, let alone like Christ’s. But only Christ’s record is wholly clean, and when we trust him his righteousness is counted as ours (Philippians 3:9); the Spirit he gives then begins to make our conduct honourable in the world’s sight.

parallels.desc: enemies watch Jesus to trap him

verseByVerse.quote: Then these high officials and satraps came by agreement to the king and said to him, "O King Darius, live forever! All the high officials of the kingdom, the prefects and the satraps, the counselors and the governors are agreed that the king should establish an ordinance and enforce an injunction, that whoever makes petition to any god or man for thirty days, except to you, O king, shall be cast into the den of lions. Now, O king, establish the injunction and sign the document, so that it cannot be changed, according to the law of the Medes and the Persians, which cannot be revoked." Therefore King Darius signed the document and injunction.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The officials flatter the king into signing an irrevocable law that turns Daniel’s faithfulness into a crime.

All the high officials of the kingdom. Their claim was a lie. There were only three high officials (v. 2), and one of them was Daniel, who had certainly not agreed. The conspirators flattered the king with a proposal that for thirty days he alone would receive prayers; to a new ruler it may have seemed harmless. But the trap was built for one man. They knew Daniel’s habit of prayer and made a law that would turn his faithfulness into a crime.

Which cannot be revoked. According to Daniel and Esther, once the Persian king signed and sealed a law, even he could not cancel it: “an edict written in the name of the king and sealed with the king’s ring cannot be revoked” (Esther 8:8). In practice the king could be trapped by his own word.

King Darius signed the document. Flattery works. Darius signed without asking the obvious questions: who suggested this, and why? Leaders who love praise are easily used by those who give it.

One mediator. For thirty days the king was to be the only one through whom any prayer could go. Scripture gives that place to one man only: “there is one God, and there is one mediator between God and men, the man Christ Jesus” (1 Timothy 2:5). Every ruler who claims it is a counterfeit; the true Mediator never closes the door to anyone who comes through him (Hebrews 4:16).

Uncertain wording. “Came by agreement” (also vv. 11, 15) translates an Aramaic verb whose exact sense is uncertain. The ESV notes that it could be “came thronging”: it may mean coming as a crowd, in a rush, or by conspiracy. Any of these fits a group acting together to pressure the king.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 10–15 — As He Had Done Previously
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Faithfulness that has been practised in ordinary days holds firm when it becomes a crime. Knowing the decree is signed, Daniel goes home and kneels at his open window toward Jerusalem three times a day, praying and giving thanks as he had always done (v. 10). The conspirators find him at prayer, make the king confirm the law, and then accuse Daniel of ignoring the king (vv. 11–13). Darius is distressed and labours till sunset to save him, but the rivals remind him that a law of the Medes and Persians cannot be changed (vv. 14–15).
verseByVerse.theology: Faithful prayer is a steady habit, kept openly when it becomes costly.

verseByVerse.quote: When Daniel knew that the document had been signed, he went to his house where he had windows in his upper chamber open toward Jerusalem. He got down on his knees three times a day and prayed and gave thanks before his God, as he had done previously.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Knowing exactly what it will cost, Daniel goes home and prays as he always had, toward Jerusalem, three times a day, giving thanks. This verse is the heart of the chapter.

When Daniel knew. He was not caught unaware. He knew what the law said and what it would cost. He went to his house, where he always prayed: he neither staged a demonstration nor hid.

Windows in his upper chamber open toward Jerusalem. When Solomon dedicated the temple, he prayed that if Israel ever went into exile for their sins and prayed “toward their land … the city that you have chosen, and the house that I have built for your name”, God would hear and forgive (1 Kings 8:48–49). Jerusalem lay in ruins and the temple was gone, but Daniel was still leaning on God’s promise to hear his people in exile.

He got down on his knees three times a day. A settled rhythm of prayer, like the psalmist’s: “Evening and morning and at noon I utter my complaint and moan, and he hears my voice” (Psalm 55:17). His prayer life was built before the crisis came.

Prayed and gave thanks before his God. With the lions waiting, Daniel gave thanks. “Give thanks in all circumstances; for this is the will of God in Christ Jesus for you” (1 Thessalonians 5:18).

As he had done previously. He neither started nor stopped praying because of the crisis. Courage in the great moment grows out of faithfulness in ten thousand ordinary ones. On the night he was betrayed, Jesus too went out “as was his custom” to the Mount of Olives to pray (Luke 22:39), to a place his betrayer knew well (John 18:2). He did not change his habit to avoid the cost; he walked into it, for us.

Why did Daniel not simply close his windows or pray silently for thirty days? God hears silent prayers. But to change his lifelong habit at the moment the king demanded it would have been to accept that the king had authority over his worship. Daniel was loyal to the king in everything else; here he had to obey God rather than man (Acts 5:29). Jesus warned against praying in public “that they may be seen by others” (Matthew 6:5). Daniel was not showing off. He was refusing to hide.

Should Christians face Jerusalem or keep set hours? Daniel faced Jerusalem because the temple was where God had promised to hear (1 Kings 8:48–49). Jesus says true worshippers worship “in spirit and truth”, not on a mountain or in a city (John 4:21–24), and Christ himself is now where we meet God (Hebrews 10:19–22). No direction or hour binds us. But a steady habit of prayer, kept when it becomes costly, is a pattern every believer can follow.
verseByVerse.note: An upper room on the flat roof was a natural place for quiet prayer (compare Acts 10:9).

verseByVerse.quote: Then these men came by agreement and found Daniel making petition and plea before his God. Then they came near and said before the king, concerning the injunction, "O king! Did you not sign an injunction, that anyone who makes petition to any god or man within thirty days except to you, O king, shall be cast into the den of lions?" The king answered and said, "The thing stands fast, according to the law of the Medes and Persians, which cannot be revoked." Then they answered and said before the king, "Daniel, who is one of the exiles from Judah, pays no attention to you, O king, or the injunction you have signed, but makes his petition three times a day."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The conspirators catch Daniel at prayer, make the king confirm the law, and then accuse Daniel of disloyalty.

Making petition and plea before his God. They came together to watch, and they found exactly what they expected.

The thing stands fast. They make the king confirm the law before naming Daniel, and he does so, not yet knowing whom it will catch.

One of the exiles from Judah. Their words are full of contempt. And they accuse him of disrespecting the king, the same false charge made against his friends in 3:12.

Accused for loyalty to God. Faithful believers are often accused of disloyalty when their only offence is loyalty to God. Jesus warned, “If they persecuted me, they will also persecute you” (John 15:20). “Indeed, all who desire to live a godly life in Christ Jesus will be persecuted” (2 Timothy 3:12).

verseByVerse.quote: Then the king, when he heard these words, was much distressed and set his mind to deliver Daniel. And he labored till the sun went down to rescue him. Then these men came by agreement to the king and said to the king, "Know, O king, that it is a law of the Medes and Persians that no injunction or ordinance that the king establishes can be changed."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The king sees that he has been tricked into condemning the man he trusts most, labours all day to save him, and is trapped by his own law.

Much distressed. Darius spends the day seeking a legal way out. At sunset the conspirators return and remind him of his own law: his word has become a chain around him.

Pilate and Jesus. The scene has a striking parallel in the Gospels. Pilate knew that Jesus was innocent: “I find no guilt in this man” (Luke 23:4). He tried again and again to release him, “desiring to release Jesus” (Luke 23:20), and like Darius he knew why the accusers wanted him dead: “it was out of envy that they had delivered him up” (Matthew 27:18). But there is a great difference. Darius was trapped by a law; Pilate by his own cowardice. And behind both scenes stood the purposes of God, who meant the second to save the world (Acts 4:27–28).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 16–24 — He Shut the Lions' Mouths
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God is able to deliver those who trust him, and no human seal can keep him out. Daniel is thrown into the den, and the king, hoping that Daniel’s God will save him, seals the stone with his own signet and his lords’ (vv. 16–17). After a sleepless night the king hurries to the den at dawn and calls out (vv. 18–20). Daniel answers that God sent his angel and shut the lions’ mouths, and he is lifted out without a scratch, because he trusted in his God (vv. 21–23). His accusers, with their families, are thrown in and destroyed at once (v. 24).
verseByVerse.theology: God is able to deliver those who trust him, and his justice finally overtakes their enemies.

verseByVerse.quote: Then the king commanded, and Daniel was brought and cast into the den of lions. The king declared to Daniel, "May your God, whom you serve continually, deliver you!" And a stone was brought and laid on the mouth of the den, and the king sealed it with his own signet and with the signet of his lords, that nothing might be changed concerning Daniel.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Daniel is thrown to the lions and the den is sealed by both king and lords, so that no human hand can interfere.

The den of lions. Probably a pit in the ground with an opening at the top, through which the victim was thrown. Lions were kept by Mesopotamian kings, and royal lion hunts were a favourite subject of their art.

May your God, whom you serve continually, deliver you! The king’s last words to Daniel are a mixture of hope and helplessness. He had noticed that Daniel served his God “continually”, and now he pinned his hope on that God.

A stone was brought and laid on the mouth of the den. Wet clay over the stone, stamped with the rings, would show if it were moved. The lords’ seal meant the king could not secretly rescue Daniel; the king’s seal meant the lords could not secretly make sure he died. The seal had a purpose its makers never intended: it proved that whatever happened in the den was God’s doing alone. Centuries later another stone was sealed for the same reason, and it proved the same thing (Matthew 27:66).

verseByVerse.quote: Then the king went to his palace and spent the night fasting; no diversions were brought to him, and sleep fled from him. Then, at break of day, the king arose and went in haste to the den of lions. As he came near to the den where Daniel was, he cried out in a tone of anguish. The king declared to Daniel, "O Daniel, servant of the living God, has your God, whom you serve continually, been able to deliver you from the lions?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
The king spends a sleepless night and at first light hurries to the den, calling to Daniel and asking whether his living God has been able to save him.

Sleep fled from him. The contrast is almost humorous. In the pit, Daniel was with the lions; in the palace, the king was the one who could not rest. The man in the den was in God’s hands; the man on the throne was in torment.

Servant of the living God. The king calls out in anguish, afraid of the silence that might answer. Yet now he speaks of “the living God”, and his question is the question of the whole book: is this God able? Nebuchadnezzar had asked it mockingly (3:15); Darius asks it in hope.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Daniel said to the king, "O king, live forever! My God sent his angel and shut the lions' mouths, and they have not harmed me, because I was found blameless before him; and also before you, O king, I have done no harm." Then the king was exceedingly glad, and commanded that Daniel be taken up out of the den. So Daniel was taken up out of the den, and no kind of harm was found on him, because he had trusted in his God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Daniel answers from the den that God sent his angel and shut the lions’ mouths, and he is lifted out unharmed, because he trusted in his God.

O king, live forever! The voice from the pit is calm and courteous. Daniel greets the king who condemned him without bitterness. Like his Lord after him, “When he was reviled, he did not revile in return” (1 Peter 2:23).

My God sent his angel and shut the lions’ mouths. Daniel gives God all the credit. The lions were hungry (v. 24); God closed their mouths. “The angel of the LORD encamps around those who fear him, and delivers them” (Psalm 34:7). Hebrews remembers Daniel among those who by faith “stopped the mouths of lions” (Hebrews 11:33).

Blameless before him. Daniel declares his innocence twice: before God, and before the king, “I have done no harm.” He had broken the king’s law, but he had not wronged the king. Obeying God rather than man is not disloyalty.

Because he had trusted in his God. As in the furnace, the deliverance was complete, and the writer tells us why: not because Daniel was an extraordinary man, though he was, but because he trusted God. “Without faith it is impossible to please him, for whoever would draw near to God must believe that he exists and that he rewards those who seek him” (Hebrews 11:6).

Pointing forward to Christ. Daniel was innocent, condemned through envy, put into a pit, sealed in with a stone, and brought out alive at dawn. Jesus was innocent, condemned through envy, laid in a tomb and sealed in, as his enemies “made the tomb secure by sealing the stone and setting a guard” (Matthew 27:66). But Jesus was not spared death. He went all the way into it, bearing the sins of his people, and early on the first day of the week the stone was rolled away and he came out alive, “because it was not possible for him to be held by it” (Acts 2:24). Daniel was delivered from death; Christ conquered it.

Not every believer is rescued. God does not promise that every faithful believer will be rescued from every lion. Many have died for their faith, and Hebrews honours them too (Hebrews 11:35–38). Paul, near the end of his life, could say, “I was rescued from the lion’s mouth”, and in the next breath, “The Lord will rescue me from every evil deed and bring me safely into his heavenly kingdom” (2 Timothy 4:17–18), though he knew he would soon be executed. Because Christ conquered death, the final deliverance is certain for all who trust him, whether God brings them out of the den in this life or through death into his presence.

verseByVerse.quote: And the king commanded, and those men who had maliciously accused Daniel were brought and cast into the den of lions—they, their children, and their wives. And before they reached the bottom of the den, the lions overpowered them and broke all their bones in pieces.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The accusers suffer the fate they planned for Daniel, but the king’s cruelty to their families is recorded, not approved.

Those men who had maliciously accused Daniel. This verse is hard to read. The accusers fell into the pit they had dug for another, as Scripture often describes the wicked doing (Psalm 7:15). The lions were clearly neither tame nor full: they seized the men “before they reached the bottom of the den”. Daniel’s survival was no accident.

They, their children, and their wives. Ancient Persian kings often destroyed a traitor’s whole family. The Bible records it; it does not approve it. God’s law for Israel said plainly, “nor shall children be put to death because of their fathers. Each one shall be put to death for his own sin” (Deuteronomy 24:16). The end of those families shows how deeply the sin of a few leaders can wound those who depend on them, and that the justice of human kings, even when it punishes real wrong, is never the perfect justice of God.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 25–28 — His Kingdom Shall Never Be Destroyed
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The living God is honoured before the whole world through one faithful man. The king whose decree had demanded that all prayer go to him now writes to every people and language, commanding them to tremble before the God of Daniel: the living God, enduring for ever, whose kingdom shall never be destroyed, who delivers and rescues and has saved Daniel from the lions (vv. 25–27). The story half of the book closes quietly: Daniel prospered during the reign of Darius and the reign of Cyrus the Persian (v. 28). Kings change; God’s servant remains.
verseByVerse.theology: The deliverance of one faithful servant proclaims the living God to the nations.

verseByVerse.quote: Then King Darius wrote to all the peoples, nations, and languages that dwell in all the earth: "Peace be multiplied to you. I make a decree, that in all my royal dominion people are to tremble and fear before the God of Daniel, for he is the living God, enduring forever; his kingdom shall never be destroyed, and his dominion shall be to the end. He delivers and rescues; he works signs and wonders in heaven and on earth, he who has saved Daniel from the power of the lions."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The king whose law demanded that all prayer go to him now commands the whole empire to fear Daniel’s God, the living God whose kingdom will never end.

Then King Darius wrote. The chapter ends with a pagan king writing to the whole world, as Nebuchadnezzar did in chapter 4. The thirty-day law demanded that everyone pray to the king; the new decree tells everyone to fear Daniel’s God.

He is the living God, enduring forever. Darius’s confession sounds like the message of the whole book. God is “the living God”, unlike the dead idols of the nations; he endures for ever, while kings and empires come and go; “his kingdom shall never be destroyed”, almost the very words Daniel spoke of the stone that fills the earth (2:44); and “He delivers and rescues”.

What it means that God is the living God. To modern ears “the living God” can sound like a pious extra. In Babylon it was a fighting word. The gods of the city had mouths but did not speak and eyes but did not see (Psalm 115:5); they had to be carried in procession, and could be carried off as plunder (11:8). A living God acts on his own. He speaks when you have not asked him to, and he can contradict you, which is exactly why we prefer the other kind. Our idols today are careers, comfort and causes, and they share the old flaw: they cannot help you when the stone is rolled over the den. The living God can. He shut the lions’ mouths, and he did far more at a sealed tomb: the risen Christ calls himself “the living one. I died, and behold I am alive forevermore” (Revelation 1:18).

In everyday life. When you pray, are you only telling God your plans, or are you listening for a God who may say no, and trusting him when he does? Daniel set out only to be faithful, and God made his quiet faithfulness a testimony across an empire.

verseByVerse.quote: So this Daniel prospered during the reign of Darius and the reign of Cyrus the Persian.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Daniel prospered under Darius and Cyrus: kings come and go, but God’s faithful servant remains. The story half of the book ends here.

So this Daniel prospered. The man who entered Babylon as a captive teenager outlived Nebuchadnezzar, saw Babylon fall, survived the lions and served the kings of Persia with honour, to the first year of Cyrus and beyond (1:21; 10:1).

The first six chapters. They have taught one lesson from many angles: the Most High rules, and he is able to keep those who trust him, even in Babylon. The visions that follow will show the kingdoms of this world as savage beasts, more and more hostile to God’s people, but the lesson of the lions’ den stands behind every one. “Behold, the Lion of the tribe of Judah, the Root of David, has conquered” (Revelation 5:5).

Uncertain wording. “During the reign of Darius and the reign of Cyrus the Persian”: the Aramaic “and” can sometimes mean “that is”, so some read “the reign of Darius, that is, the reign of Cyrus the Persian”, making Darius the Mede another title for Cyrus. The ordinary reading, two reigns one after the other, is just as possible (see the note on 5:29–31).

6.title: The Living God, Enduring Forever
6.overview:
Where we are. Babylon has fallen (5:30–31), and Daniel, now over eighty, serves the new Persian government under Darius the Mede. This last court story matches chapter 3: there his friends faced a furnace for refusing to worship; here Daniel faces lions for refusing to stop praying.

The message. God’s people can serve an unbelieving government with excellence and still refuse when it claims what belongs to God alone, and the living God is able to deliver them. Courage in the crisis grows out of faithfulness in ordinary days, and the king who condemned Daniel ends by telling the world that Daniel’s God “delivers and rescues” (v. 27).

Why it was said. Under a new empire (see the introduction) the exiles faced the old question: could they be loyal subjects and faithful worshippers at once? This chapter answers yes, up to the point where the state demands what God forbids, and it shows that even an “unchangeable” law of the Medes and Persians cannot bind the living God.

How the chapter makes its case. Daniel serves so well that his jealous rivals can find no fault in him except his faith, so they flatter the king into a thirty-day law against praying to anyone but him (vv. 1–9). Daniel goes home and prays as he always had, the conspirators report him, and the king is trapped by his own decree (vv. 10–15). Daniel is thrown to the lions and the den is sealed; at dawn he is found unharmed, because God shut the lions’ mouths, and his accusers suffer the fate they planned (vv. 16–24). Darius proclaims the living God to the whole empire, and Daniel prospers (vv. 25–28).

Where it leads. To Christ chiefly by pattern. An innocent man, condemned through envy by a ruler who wanted to release him, shut in a pit under a sealed stone and brought out alive at dawn: it is the shape of the Gospels’ last chapters. Yet the difference is the point. Daniel was kept from death; Jesus went into it, bearing the sins of his people, and rose because “it was not possible for him to be held by it” (Acts 2:24). The God of whom Darius said “his kingdom shall never be destroyed” (v. 26) has given that kingdom to his risen Son.

For us. Daniel’s courage at the window was built in years of prayer no one noticed. Keep your ordinary habits of prayer and honest work now, so that when faith becomes costly, at work, in the family or before the authorities, you are already where you need to be. And whether God shuts the lions’ mouths or brings you through death, in Christ you are safe.
6.theology:
Believers honour God by excellent, honest work, so that opponents can find no fault but their faith (vv. 3-5; 1 Pet 2:12; Titus 2:7-8).

Faithful prayer is a settled habit that does not stop when it becomes costly; God's people obey God rather than men while remaining loyal servants in everything else (vv. 10, 22; 1 Kgs 8:48-49; Ps 55:17; 1 Thess 5:17-18).

The godly will be falsely accused and persecuted, as their Lord was (vv. 5, 13; John 15:20; 2 Tim 3:12; Matt 27:18).

God is able to deliver those who trust in him, and his final deliverance of his people is certain even when he does not spare them from death (vv. 22-23; Ps 34:7; Heb 11:6, 33; 2 Tim 4:17-18).

Many Christians have seen in Daniel's condemnation, sealed stone and dawn deliverance a foreshadowing of Christ, who was condemned through envy, sealed in a tomb and raised from death (vv. 14-23; Luke 23:4, 20; Matt 27:66; Acts 2:24).

Human justice, even when it punishes real wrong, falls short of God's perfect justice (v. 24; Deut 24:16).

The living God endures forever, his kingdom shall never be destroyed, and he delivers and rescues (vv. 26-27; 2:44; Rev 5:5).
6.examples: Daniel's courage at the window was built in years of ordinary prayer that no one noticed. A believer who keeps a daily time of prayer when life is calm is laying up strength for the day it becomes costly, whether that means praying openly at work, holding to Christ under family pressure, or simply giving thanks on the worst day of the year. If our prayer has been patchy, the way back is not a grim resolve to try harder. It is simply to start praying again, because the God who promised to hear is still listening.

keyVerse.quote: When Daniel knew that the document had been signed, he went to his house where he had windows in his upper chamber open toward Jerusalem. He got down on his knees three times a day and prayed and gave thanks before his God, as he had done previously.
keyVerse.note: Everything in the chapter turns on this verse. Daniel knows the cost and changes nothing: no protest, no hiding, only the prayer and thanksgiving he had always offered, leaning on God’s promise to hear his exiled people. It shows that faithfulness in the crisis is built in ordinary days, and that loyalty to God comes before every law that would forbid it.

6.reflection:
Daniel’s enemies could find no fault in his work, only in his faith (vv. 4–5). What would it look like for your work, honesty and attitude to commend the gospel where you are? Where is that hardest?

Daniel prayed “as he had done previously” (v. 10). What ordinary habits of prayer are you building now? What would help you keep them when they become inconvenient or costly?

Daniel obeyed the king in everything except what would deny God. How do we tell the difference between submitting to authorities and obeying God rather than men (Acts 5:29)? Where might that line be tested for Christians today?

God shut the lions’ mouths for Daniel, but did not spare Christ from death, nor many faithful martyrs. How does Christ’s resurrection give us confidence whether or not God rescues us from a particular trouble?

Then as I looked its wings were plucked off, and it was lifted up from the ground and made to stand on two feet like a man, and the mind of a man was given to it.<sup>5</sup>And behold, another beast, a second one, like a bear. It was raised up on one side. It had three ribs in its mouth between its teeth; and it was told, 'Arise, devour much flesh.'<sup>6</sup>After this I looked, and behold, another, like a leopard, with four wings of a bird on its back. And the beast had four heads, and dominion was given to it.<sup>7</sup>After this I saw in the night visions, and behold, a fourth beast, terrifying and dreadful and exceedingly strong. It had great iron teeth; it devoured and broke in pieces and stamped what was left with its feet. It was different from all the beasts that were before it, and it had ten horns.<sup>8</sup>I considered the horns, and behold, there came up among them another horn, a little one, before which three of the first horns were plucked up by the roots. And behold, in this horn were eyes like the eyes of a man, and a mouth speaking great things.<sup>9</sup>"As I looked, thrones were placed, and the Ancient of Days took his seat; his clothing was white as snow, and the hair of his head like pure wool; his throne was fiery flames; its wheels were burning fire.<sup>10</sup>A stream of fire issued and came out from before him; a thousand thousands served him, and ten thousand times ten thousand stood before him; the court sat in judgment, and the books were opened.<sup>11</sup>"I looked then because of the sound of the great words that the horn was speaking. And as I looked, the beast was killed, and its body destroyed and given over to be burned with fire.<sup>12</sup>As for the rest of the beasts, their dominion was taken away, but their lives were prolonged for a season and a time.<sup>13</sup>"I saw in the night visions, and behold, with the clouds of heaven there came one like a son of man, and he came to the Ancient of Days and was presented before him.<sup>14</sup>And to him was given dominion and glory and a kingdom, that all peoples, nations, and languages should serve him; his dominion is an everlasting dominion, which shall not pass away, and his kingdom one that shall not be destroyed.<sup>15</sup>"As for me, Daniel, my spirit within me was anxious, and the visions of my head alarmed me.<sup>16</sup>I approached one of those who stood there and asked him the truth concerning all this. So he told me and made known to me the interpretation of the things.<sup>17</sup>'These four great beasts are four kings who shall arise out of the earth.<sup>18</sup>But the saints of the Most High shall receive the kingdom and possess the kingdom forever, forever and ever.'<sup>19</sup>"Then I desired to know the truth about the fourth beast, which was different from all the rest, exceedingly terrifying, with its teeth of iron and claws of bronze, and which devoured and broke in pieces and stamped what was left with its feet,<sup>20</sup>and about the ten horns that were on its head, and the other horn that came up and before which three of them fell, the horn that had eyes and a mouth that spoke great things, and that seemed greater than its companions.<sup>21</sup>As I looked, this horn made war with the saints and prevailed over them,<sup>22</sup>until the Ancient of Days came, and judgment was given for the saints of the Most High, and the time came when the saints possessed the kingdom.<sup>23</sup>"Thus he said: 'As for the fourth beast, there shall be a fourth kingdom on earth, which shall be different from all the kingdoms, and it shall devour the whole earth, and trample it down, and break it to pieces.<sup>24</sup>As for the ten horns, out of this kingdom ten kings shall arise, and another shall arise after them; he shall be different from the former ones, and shall put down three kings.<sup>25</sup>He shall speak words against the Most High, and shall wear out the saints of the Most High, and shall think to change the times and the law; verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–8 — Four Beasts from the Sea
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The empires that dazzle the world are, in heaven’s sight, beasts rising out of chaos, and each holds power only as it is given. Daniel writes down a night vision: heaven’s four winds stir up the great sea, and four great beasts come up out of it (vv. 1–3). A winged lion is humbled and given a human mind; a lopsided bear is told to devour; a four-headed, four-winged leopard is given dominion (vv. 4–6). Then comes a fourth beast unlike any animal, with iron teeth and ten horns, among which a little horn with human eyes and a boasting mouth uproots three others (vv. 7–8).
verseByVerse.theology: Behind the glory of human empires lies a beastly, devouring power that sets itself against God.

verseByVerse.quote: In the first year of Belshazzar king of Babylon, Daniel saw a dream and visions of his head as he lay in his bed. Then he wrote down the dream and told the sum of the matter. Daniel declared, "I saw in my vision by night, and behold, the four winds of heaven were stirring up the great sea. And four great beasts came up out of the sea, different from one another.
verseByVerse.commentary:
In a night vision Daniel sees the restless sea of the nations, stirred by heaven’s winds, and four great beasts rising from it. Even the storms of history blow at God’s command.

In the first year of Belshazzar king of Babylon. With chapter 7 stories give way to visions in Daniel’s own voice, arranged by theme rather than strict date. This one came years before Babylon fell in chapter 5. It is still in Aramaic, so it belongs with chapters 2–6, but it looks forward to chapters 8–12: the hinge of the book (see the introduction).

The great sea. In the Bible the sea often pictures the restless, chaotic world of nations opposed to God: “the roar of nations; they roar like the roaring of mighty waters” (Isaiah 17:12); “the wicked are like the tossing sea; for it cannot be quiet” (Isaiah 57:20). The “four winds of heaven” suggest a storm from every direction, and that heaven is stirring it. Even the turmoil of world history is under God’s hand.

Four great beasts came up out of the sea. They are the four kingdoms of chapter 2’s statue, seen as they really are. A pagan king saw a shining statue; God’s prophet sees devouring beasts. The empires the world admires are, in heaven’s sight, savage animals.
verseByVerse.note: The first year of Belshazzar was about 553 BC, before chapter 5.

verseByVerse.quote: The first was like a lion and had eagles' wings. Then as I looked its wings were plucked off, and it was lifted up from the ground and made to stand on two feet like a man, and the mind of a man was given to it. And behold, another beast, a second one, like a bear. It was raised up on one side. It had three ribs in its mouth between its teeth; and it was told, 'Arise, devour much flesh.' After this I looked, and behold, another, like a leopard, with four wings of a bird on its back. And the beast had four heads, and dominion was given to it.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The first three beasts picture Babylon, Medo-Persia and Greece: a winged lion humbled and given a human mind, a lopsided bear told to devour, and a swift four-headed leopard. Each receives its power from above.

The first was like a lion. Babylon, the head of gold of chapter 2. The lion was king of beasts and the eagle king of birds, a fitting image for Nebuchadnezzar’s mighty and swift empire. Jeremiah pictured Babylon as a lion leaving its thicket (Jeremiah 4:7), and Ezekiel pictured its king as a great eagle (Ezekiel 17:3, 12). Lions in glazed brick lined Babylon’s Processional Way, and winged beasts were common in Mesopotamian art, so an exile would have recognised the picture at once.

The mind of a man was given to it. The wings are torn off, and the beast stands up like a man and receives a human mind. This probably recalls chapter 4, where Nebuchadnezzar lost his reason, lived like a beast, and had his reason restored.

Like a bear. The silver of chapter 2: the empire of the Medes and Persians. It is “raised up on one side”, probably because of its two partners Persia became the stronger, as the ram of chapter 8 has one horn higher than the other (8:3, 20). And it is told to devour: even the beasts act only when permitted.

Like a leopard. The bronze: Greece. The leopard is fast, and with four wings faster still, which fits Alexander the Great, who in about ten years built an empire from Greece to the borders of India. The four heads fit what followed his early death, when his empire was divided among his generals into four main kingdoms, as chapter 8 says: “four kingdoms shall arise from his nation, but not with his power” (8:22).

Dominion was given to it. Every empire receives its power from the Most High. When John saw the beast rising from the sea in Revelation, it combined all of these: “like a leopard; its feet were like a bear’s, and its mouth was like a lion’s mouth” (Revelation 13:2). The same beastly power runs through every age until Christ comes.

Uncertain wording. Two details of the bear are not explained. “Raised up on one side” may picture one partner stronger than the other, as above, or a beast rearing to strike. The “three ribs” in its mouth probably stand for conquered lands, and suggestions include Lydia, Babylon and Egypt, all taken by Cyrus and his son; but the text does not say, and no identification is certain.

verseByVerse.quote: After this I saw in the night visions, and behold, a fourth beast, terrifying and dreadful and exceedingly strong. It had great iron teeth; it devoured and broke in pieces and stamped what was left with its feet. It was different from all the beasts that were before it, and it had ten horns. I considered the horns, and behold, there came up among them another horn, a little one, before which three of the first horns were plucked up by the roots. And behold, in this horn were eyes like the eyes of a man, and a mouth speaking great things.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The fourth beast, more terrible than any animal, crushes everything, and from its ten horns rises a little horn with human eyes and a boasting mouth. This horn will be the focus of the rest of the chapter.

A fourth beast, terrifying and dreadful. So terrible that Daniel cannot compare it to any known animal. Its “iron teeth” link it to the legs of iron in chapter 2, and this commentary, with the early church and the Reformers, takes it as Rome, which crushed every power in its path (see the notes on 2:39–40).

It had ten horns. In the Bible a horn is a symbol of strength, especially a king’s power. The angel will explain that the ten horns are ten kings (v. 24).

Another horn, a little one. Daniel’s attention fixes on a little horn that grows among the others and uproots three of them. It has “eyes like the eyes of a man”, suggesting intelligence and watchfulness, and “a mouth speaking great things”, boastful words against God (v. 25).

Where Christians differ: which kingdom is the fourth beast, and who is the little horn? Many modern scholars read the four kingdoms as Babylon, Media, Persia and Greece, making the fourth beast Greece and the little horn Antiochus IV, the Greek king who persecuted the Jews in the 160s BC. Their reason is weighty: chapter 8 describes him with very similar marks, a boastful horn that attacks God’s people and stops their worship, and he did try to abolish the Jewish festivals and law (v. 25). Many Protestants in the centuries after the Reformation saw the horn as the papacy. Many others see a final ruler who will oppose God and persecute his people at the end of history, the one Paul calls “the man of lawlessness” who “exalts himself against every so-called god or object of worship” (2 Thessalonians 2:3–4), and whom Revelation pictures as a beast with “a mouth uttering haughty and blasphemous words” (Revelation 13:5). This commentary’s view: the fourth beast is Rome, and the little horn is that final enemy. The chapter itself says the horn’s defeat is followed directly by the final judgment and the everlasting kingdom (vv. 26–27). Antiochus, the horn of chapter 8, who grows from the Greek goat, is a preview of him, and John adds the balance: “as you have heard that antichrist is coming, so now many antichrists have come” (1 John 2:18). The final enemy is foreshadowed by many proud rulers before him.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 9–14 — The Ancient of Days and the Son of Man
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Above the raging beasts sits the eternal Judge, and he gives the everlasting kingdom to one like a son of man. Thrones are set, and the Ancient of Days takes his seat in dazzling white on a throne of fire, served by countless thousands; the court sits and the books are opened (vv. 9–10). While the horn is still boasting, the fourth beast is killed and burned, and the others lose their dominion (vv. 11–12). Then one like a son of man comes with the clouds of heaven to the Ancient of Days and receives dominion, glory and a kingdom that all peoples will serve and that will never pass away (vv. 13–14).
verseByVerse.theology: God sits in judgment over the beasts and gives the everlasting kingdom to the Son of Man, Jesus Christ.

verseByVerse.quote: "As I looked, thrones were placed, and the Ancient of Days took his seat; his clothing was white as snow, and the hair of his head like pure wool; his throne was fiery flames; its wheels were burning fire. A stream of fire issued and came out from before him; a thousand thousands served him, and ten thousand times ten thousand stood before him; the court sat in judgment, and the books were opened.
verseByVerse.commentary:
While the horn is still boasting on earth, Daniel sees heaven’s court: the eternal God takes his throne in blazing holiness, surrounded by countless servants, and the books are opened.

Thrones were placed. The scene moves suddenly from the stormy sea to heaven’s courtroom. Thrones are set, and a judge takes his seat. Who sits on the other thrones is not said; Revelation later shows the saints seated on thrones with authority to judge (Revelation 20:4).

The Ancient of Days took his seat. A title found only in this chapter: the one who is old beyond all time, the eternal God. The beasts are new arrivals in history; he was there before them all. White clothing speaks of purity, white hair of wisdom and eternal age. His throne is “fiery flames” with “wheels” of fire, like the throne on wheels that Ezekiel saw by the Chebar canal (Ezekiel 1). Fire speaks of holiness and judgment.

The hair of his head like pure wool. In the New Testament something astonishing happens. When John sees the risen Jesus, he describes him with the words of this verse: “The hairs of his head were white, like white wool, like snow” (Revelation 1:14). The features of the Ancient of Days belong to Christ. He shares the eternal glory of God.

The books were opened. Countless servants surround the throne, “ten thousand times ten thousand”, and the books record what the beasts have done. Nothing has been forgotten. Revelation uses the same picture: “the dead were judged by what was written in the books, according to what they had done” (Revelation 20:12). This is deep comfort for God’s persecuted people. Tyrants may seem to act without consequences, but every cruelty and every martyr is recorded, and the court will sit.

verseByVerse.quote: "I looked then because of the sound of the great words that the horn was speaking. And as I looked, the beast was killed, and its body destroyed and given over to be burned with fire. As for the rest of the beasts, their dominion was taken away, but their lives were prolonged for a season and a time.
verseByVerse.commentary:
With no battle at all, the boasting beast is killed and burned, while the earlier beasts lose their power but are allowed to live on for a time.

The beast was killed. Daniel’s eyes are drawn back to earth by the noise of the horn’s boasting, and the verdict is carried out. All its loud words cannot save it. “He who sits in the heavens laughs; the Lord holds them in derision” (Psalm 2:4).

Their lives were prolonged for a season and a time. The earlier beasts lose their power to rule but are not destroyed at once: each conquered empire lived on for a while inside the one that conquered it. The fourth beast is completely destroyed at the final judgment.

verseByVerse.quote: "I saw in the night visions, and behold, with the clouds of heaven there came one like a son of man, and he came to the Ancient of Days and was presented before him. And to him was given dominion and glory and a kingdom, that all peoples, nations, and languages should serve him; his dominion is an everlasting dominion, which shall not pass away, and his kingdom one that shall not be destroyed.
verseByVerse.commentary:
After the beasts comes one like a son of man, a truly human figure who travels as only God travels, and the Ancient of Days gives him an everlasting kingdom over all peoples. This is the high point of the chapter and one of the most important promises in the Bible, and Jesus claimed it as his own.

One like a son of man. That is, one who looks like a human being. The contrast is deliberate. The kingdoms of the world are beastly; God’s kingdom will be ruled by one who is truly human, as God meant humanity to rule from the beginning (Genesis 1:26–28).

With the clouds of heaven. But he is more than a man. In the Old Testament riding on the clouds is a picture used of God himself: “he makes the clouds his chariot” (Psalm 104:3). This figure is human, yet he travels as God travels, and he is brought into the very presence of the Ancient of Days.

Jesus, the Son of Man. Jesus called himself “the Son of Man” more than by any other title, and he drew it above all from this verse. At his trial, when the high priest demanded, “Are you the Christ, the Son of the Blessed?”, Jesus answered, “I am, and you will see the Son of Man seated at the right hand of Power, and coming with the clouds of heaven” (Mark 14:61–62). The high priest tore his clothes and charged him with blasphemy, for he understood the claim: to be the King of Daniel 7, both man and God. The prisoner standing bound before him was the one before whom every throne on earth will one day stand.

He came to the Ancient of Days. The direction of travel matters: from earth to heaven’s throne. Many see this fulfilled first in the ascension, when “a cloud took him out of their sight” (Acts 1:9) and he was enthroned in heaven; dying Stephen saw “the Son of Man standing at the right hand of God” (Acts 7:56). And the same Jesus will come again with the clouds: “Behold, he is coming with the clouds, and every eye will see him” (Revelation 1:7). He has already received his kingdom; at his return everyone will see it.

Dominion and glory and a kingdom. Everything the beasts grasped at is given to him. Nebuchadnezzar demanded that peoples, nations and languages bow to his image (3:4); now all peoples, nations and languages will serve the Son of Man, and his kingdom, unlike every beastly empire, “shall not pass away”.
