After his resurrection Jesus spoke as the one who had received it: “All authority in heaven and on earth has been given to me” (Matthew 28:18). That is why the church goes to all nations: the Son of Man is gathering his people from every language on earth.

Power that makes us less human. Why does God show the great empires as animals? Partly because power without God does to rulers what it did to Nebuchadnezzar: it drags them below humanity. We still admire the beast, following the strong leader and the side that wins, and are startled each time power turns predatory (on the suspicion of power this breeds, see the note on Matthew 20:24–25). Daniel’s vision answers both admiration and cynicism. The final, everlasting power in the universe is given to one like a son of man, the first truly humane ruler. And when Jesus took the title, he defined how he would use it: “For even the Son of Man came not to be served but to serve, and to give his life as a ransom for many” (Mark 10:45). The one to whom all dominion is given used it first to die for his subjects. That is the only kind of power that can be trusted with everything.

Where Christians differ: who is the one like a son of man? Many modern scholars, noting that the kingdom is given to “the saints” (vv. 18, 27), take him as a symbol for God’s faithful people, or as an angel such as Michael (10:21; 12:1). Older Jewish tradition often read him as the Messiah: the Talmud (Sanhedrin 98a) sets this verse beside Zechariah 9:9, saying the Messiah comes with the clouds if Israel is worthy and lowly on a donkey if not, and Rashi names him the King Messiah; many Jewish readers today take him as faithful Israel. This commentary’s view: he is the Messiah, who also represents his people, so that what is given to him is shared with them, as Jesus claimed at his trial (Mark 14:62). The readings are not rivals so much as parts of one truth: the King and his saints receive the kingdom together.
verseByVerse.note: At his trial Jesus joined this verse to Psalm 110:1, “seated at the right hand” (Mark 14:62).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 15–22 — The Saints Shall Receive the Kingdom
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The kingdom given to the son of man will be shared with God’s holy people, even though they must first suffer. Daniel is shaken and asks one of those standing by for the truth (vv. 15–16). The beasts are four kings, he is told, but the saints of the Most High will receive the kingdom and possess it for ever (vv. 17–18). Daniel presses for the meaning of the fourth beast and its horn, and he sees the horn make war on the saints and prevail, until the Ancient of Days comes, judgment is given for the saints, and they possess the kingdom (vv. 19–22).
verseByVerse.theology: The people of God may be overpowered for a time, but the kingdom is finally theirs.

verseByVerse.quote: "As for me, Daniel, my spirit within me was anxious, and the visions of my head alarmed me. I approached one of those who stood there and asked him the truth concerning all this. So he told me and made known to me the interpretation of the things. 'These four great beasts are four kings who shall arise out of the earth. But the saints of the Most High shall receive the kingdom and possess the kingdom forever, forever and ever.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Shaken by the vision, Daniel asks for its meaning and is told that the beasts are earthly kings, but the kingdom will be given for ever to God’s holy people.

My spirit within me was anxious. The ESV notes that “within me” is literally “within its sheath”, a picture of the body holding the spirit as a sheath holds a sword. Seeing the future did not make Daniel proud or excited; it made him tremble. Prophecy is not given to satisfy curiosity but to prepare God’s people.

Asked him the truth concerning all this. Daniel does what every reader of prophecy should do: he asks for the true meaning, and receives it from heaven. We too need God’s own interpretation, and we have it, in the rest of Scripture.

Who shall arise out of the earth. The beasts came up from the sea (v. 3); here they arise out of the earth. Both images make the same point: these kingdoms have a purely earthly origin, unlike the son of man who comes with the clouds. The kings stand for their kingdoms (v. 23).

The saints of the Most High shall receive the kingdom. The saints are God’s holy people, set apart to belong to him. The kingdom given to the son of man (v. 14) is also given to his people (see the note on vv. 13–14). The King shares his reign: “The one who conquers, I will grant him to sit with me on my throne, as I also conquered and sat down with my Father on his throne” (Revelation 3:21); “if we endure, we will also reign with him” (2 Timothy 2:12). And Jesus told his small, weak band of followers, “Fear not, little flock, for it is your Father’s good pleasure to give you the kingdom” (Luke 12:32).

verseByVerse.quote: "Then I desired to know the truth about the fourth beast, which was different from all the rest, exceedingly terrifying, with its teeth of iron and claws of bronze, and which devoured and broke in pieces and stamped what was left with its feet, and about the ten horns that were on its head, and the other horn that came up and before which three of them fell, the horn that had eyes and a mouth that spoke great things, and that seemed greater than its companions. As I looked, this horn made war with the saints and prevailed over them, until the Ancient of Days came, and judgment was given for the saints of the Most High, and the time came when the saints possessed the kingdom.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Daniel sees that the horn will make war on the saints and defeat them, but only until the Ancient of Days comes and the court rules in their favour. God’s people may lose for a time; they will not lose in the end.

The truth about the fourth beast. Daniel is most troubled by the fourth beast and its horn, and the retelling adds details: claws of bronze, and a horn that “seemed greater than its companions”.

This horn made war with the saints and prevailed over them. The first description did not mention this. God’s people will not always win in this world; for a time they will be defeated, persecuted and killed. Revelation says the same of the beast: “it was allowed to make war on the saints and to conquer them” (Revelation 13:7). Christians should not be shocked when faithfulness leads to suffering. It was foretold.

Until the Ancient of Days came. The key word is “until”. The horn’s victory has an end date. Then the court rules for the persecuted, and the kingdom the horn tried to seize is handed to the people it oppressed. Paul reminds believers of their future: “do you not know that the saints will judge the world?” (1 Corinthians 6:2).

Uncertain wording. “Judgment was given for the saints” could also be read “judgment was given to the saints”: either the court decided in their favour, or they were given the right to judge. Both are true elsewhere in Scripture (Revelation 20:4; 1 Corinthians 6:2), and the context, a court vindicating the oppressed, favours “for”.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 23–28 — Time, Times, and Half a Time
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The last enemy’s time is fixed and short, and the kingdom will be given to the saints for ever. The angel explains that the fourth kingdom will devour the whole earth; ten kings will come from it, and then another who will put down three, speak against the Most High, wear out the saints and try to change the times and the law, for a time, times, and half a time (vv. 23–25). Then the court will sit, his dominion will be destroyed, and the kingdom and greatness of all kingdoms will be given to the people of the saints (vv. 26–27). Daniel is left pale and troubled, and keeps the matter in his heart (v. 28).
verseByVerse.theology: The persecution of God's people is real but limited, and God's judgment and kingdom are certain.

verseByVerse.quote: "Thus he said: 'As for the fourth beast, there shall be a fourth kingdom on earth, which shall be different from all the kingdoms, and it shall devour the whole earth, and trample it down, and break it to pieces. As for the ten horns, out of this kingdom ten kings shall arise, and another shall arise after them; he shall be different from the former ones, and shall put down three kings. He shall speak words against the Most High, and shall wear out the saints of the Most High, and shall think to change the times and the law; and they shall be given into his hand for a time, times, and half a time.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The angel explains that from the fourth kingdom will come a final ruler who blasphemes God, wears down his people and tries to overturn God’s order, but only for a limited time that God has set.

Ten kings shall arise. Some take the ten horns as ten literal rulers of a final world order; others take ten as a round number for the full set of powers that come from the fourth kingdom. Revelation also speaks of ten horns as “ten kings who have not yet received royal power”, ruling “together with the beast” (Revelation 17:12).

He shall speak words against the Most High. Here are the marks of the final enemy. He will exalt himself against God. He will “wear out the saints”, not always by one violent blow, but by constant, grinding pressure. And he will “think to change the times and the law”, trying to overturn God’s order: the sacred calendar, the worship of God and the moral law itself. Every age has seen rulers who tried to redefine what is good, erase the memory of God from public life and wear believers down until they give up.

They shall be given into his hand. But his power is given, for a set period. The persecution is real, but it is measured, limited and controlled by God. Revelation counts the same period as “a time, and times, and half a time” (Revelation 12:14), and as forty-two months and 1,260 days (Revelation 11:2–3; 12:6), and applies it to the church’s whole time of witness in the world.

Where Christians differ: how long is “a time, times, and half a time”? Most take it as one year, two years and half a year: three and a half. Some Christians, especially dispensationalists, take it as a literal three and a half years at the very end of history. Many others, including many in the Reformed tradition, take it as a symbolic number for a limited period of persecution: three and a half is half of seven, the number of completeness, so the enemy’s time is broken off halfway. This commentary’s view: the symbolic reading, in keeping with its amillennial view (that the thousand years of Revelation 20 picture the whole age between Christ’s first and second comings), while honouring those who differ. Either way the comfort is the same: God has fixed the end of it.

Uncertain wording. The word for “time” does not itself mean a year; it is used of a set period of unstated length, as in “seven periods of time” (4:16). “Times” is probably two, though the form is not certain. What is clear is the shape: a period that seems to grow, and then is cut short.
verseByVerse.note: “A time, times, and half a time” makes three and a half, half of seven: a limited period of persecution, cut short by God.

verseByVerse.quote: But the court shall sit in judgment, and his dominion shall be taken away, to be consumed and destroyed to the end. And the kingdom and the dominion and the greatness of the kingdoms under the whole heaven shall be given to the people of the saints of the Most High; his kingdom shall be an everlasting kingdom, and all dominions shall serve and obey him.' "Here is the end of the matter. As for me, Daniel, my thoughts greatly alarmed me, and my color changed, but I kept the matter in my heart."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The heavenly court will sit, the enemy will be destroyed for ever, and the kingdom of all the earth will be given to God’s holy people; Daniel is left shaken, and keeps it in his heart.

But the court shall sit in judgment. The angel returns, as the vision did, to the court. However loud the horn becomes, however long the saints are worn down, a day of judgment is coming, and his dominion will be destroyed to the end. He will never rise again.

The greatness of the kingdoms under the whole heaven. Everything the beasts ever possessed will be given to God’s people. The kingdom belongs to God and his King, and he shares it with his people: “and they will reign forever and ever” (Revelation 22:5).

I kept the matter in my heart. Daniel does not come away with a chart of dates. He comes away shaken, pale and thoughtful, treasuring and pondering what he has seen, as Mary would do with the words spoken about her Son: “Mary treasured up all these things, pondering them in her heart” (Luke 2:19).

The right response to prophecy. Its purpose is not to feed speculation about which world leader is the little horn, but to steady God’s people. The beasts are real, and they may prevail for a while. But the court is already seated, the Son of Man has already received the kingdom, and the saints will possess it for ever. When the news seems full of beasts, Christians can lift their eyes to the throne.

Uncertain wording. The second half of verse 27 can be read “his kingdom shall be an everlasting kingdom, and all dominions shall serve and obey him”, or “their kingdom … them” (ESV note). The Aramaic pronoun can refer to the Most High or to his people. Both readings are true together: the kingdom is God’s, and he gives it to his saints.

7.title: One Like a Son of Man
7.overview:
Where we are. Chapter 7 steps back to “the first year of Belshazzar” (v. 1), before the feast of chapter 5, and the book turns from stories about Daniel to visions told by Daniel himself. Still in Aramaic, it is the hinge of the book: it closes the section begun in chapter 2 and shows the statue’s four kingdoms as heaven sees them.

The message. The empires of this world, however glorious they look, are beasts in God’s sight, and they rise, rage and fall only as he allows. Above them the Ancient of Days sits in judgment, and he gives an everlasting kingdom to one like a son of man, who shares it with his suffering people. The beast may wear out the saints for a while, but the court will sit, and the kingdom will be theirs.

Why it was said. Daniel’s people had lost their land and king, and would watch empire after empire rise over them, up to a persecutor who tried to stamp out their faith (see the introduction). They needed to know that history is not a meaningless storm: there is a throne above it, a limit on its cruelty and a King at its end.

How the chapter makes its case. Four beasts rise from the stormy sea, the fourth with iron teeth and a boastful little horn (vv. 1–8). Then heaven’s court sits: the Ancient of Days takes his throne, the beast is destroyed, and one like a son of man comes with the clouds to receive an everlasting kingdom (vv. 9–14). Daniel is told that the saints will receive the kingdom, though the horn makes war on them (vv. 15–22), and that the horn will wear them out for “a time, times, and half a time”, until the court sits and the kingdom is theirs (vv. 23–28).

Where it leads. To Christ directly, by promise. Jesus took “the Son of Man” as his own favourite name, and at his trial he claimed this vision: “you will see the Son of Man seated at the right hand of Power, and coming with the clouds of heaven” (Mark 14:62). He received the kingdom when he rose and ascended, “All authority in heaven and on earth has been given to me” (Matthew 28:18), and he will come with the clouds for every eye to see (Revelation 1:7). The saints receive the kingdom because they belong to him.

For us. When the news is full of beasts, lift your eyes to the throne. The suffering of God’s people is real but measured, and the kingdom is promised not to the strong but to those who belong to the Son of Man. Read prophecy as Daniel did: not to build charts, but to be steadied, and to keep the matter in your heart.
7.theology:
God rules over the turmoil of history; the empires of the world, however glorious they appear, are beastly in God's sight and hold power only as it is given to them (vv. 2-7).

The Ancient of Days is the eternal Judge who records every deed; the court will sit and the proud will be destroyed (vv. 9-12, 26; Ps 2:4; Rev 20:12).

The one like a son of man, coming with the clouds and receiving an everlasting kingdom, is Jesus Christ, who shares the glory of God, has received all authority and will come again (vv. 13-14; Mark 14:61-62; Acts 1:9; 7:56; Matt 28:18; Rev 1:7, 13-14).

The saints share the kingdom of their King and will reign with him forever (vv. 18, 22, 27; Luke 12:32; Rev 3:21; 22:5; 2 Tim 2:12; 1 Cor 6:2).

A final enemy will blaspheme God and persecute his people, foreshadowed by many antichrists, but his time is limited and his defeat certain (vv. 8, 21, 24-26; 2 Thess 2:3-4; 1 John 2:18; Rev 13:5-7).

Prophecy is given not to feed speculation but to steady God's people in suffering (vv. 15, 28).
7.examples: When the news is full of beasts, war, tyranny and believers worn down by grinding pressure, Daniel 7 tells us where to look. The court is seated, the books are open, and the Son of Man already holds the kingdom. A Christian imprisoned for the faith, or simply mocked at work, can know that the horn's time is measured and that the kingdom is promised to the saints.

keyVerse.quote: I saw in the night visions, and behold, with the clouds of heaven there came one like a son of man, and he came to the Ancient of Days and was presented before him. And to him was given dominion and glory and a kingdom, that all peoples, nations, and languages should serve him; his dominion is an everlasting dominion, which shall not pass away, and his kingdom one that shall not be destroyed.
keyVerse.note: This is the turning point of the vision and one of the great promises of the Old Testament. After the beastly empires comes a human King who travels with the clouds as God does and receives a kingdom that will never end. Jesus claimed these words at his trial (Mark 14:62), and they are fulfilled in his ascension, his present reign and his coming again.

7.reflection:
Daniel sees the great empires of history as beasts (vv. 2–8). What does this vision teach about how God views worldly power? Where are we tempted to admire or fear the “beasts” of our own day?

While the horn is boasting on earth, the Ancient of Days takes his seat and the books are opened (vv. 9–11). How does knowing that God sees and records every injustice help believers who are suffering or watching others suffer?

Jesus applied verses 13–14 to himself at his trial (Mark 14:62). What does this passage add to your understanding of who Jesus is and what he has received? How does Mark 10:45 show the way he uses his power?

The saints are “worn out” for a time, but will receive the kingdom (vv. 21–22, 25–27). How should this shape the way we face pressure and opposition for our faith? Why do you think Daniel’s response was to keep the matter in his heart rather than to calculate dates?

8.text: <sup>1</sup>In the third year of the reign of King Belshazzar a vision appeared to me, Daniel, after that which appeared to me at the first.<sup>2</sup>And I saw in the vision; and when I saw, I was in Susa the citadel, which is in the province of Elam. And I saw in the vision, and I was at the Ulai canal.<sup>3</sup>I raised my eyes and saw, and behold, a ram standing on the bank of the canal. It had two horns, and both horns were high, but one was higher than the other, and the higher one came up last.<sup>4</sup>I saw the ram charging westward and northward and southward. No beast could stand before him, and there was no one who could rescue from his power. He did as he pleased and became great.<sup>5</sup>As I was considering, behold, a male goat came from the west across the face of the whole earth, without touching the ground. And the goat had a conspicuous horn between his eyes.<sup>6</sup>He came to the ram with the two horns, which I had seen standing on the bank of the canal, and he ran at him in his powerful wrath.<sup>7</sup>I saw him come close to the ram, and he was enraged against him and struck the ram and broke his two horns. And the ram had no power to stand before him, but he cast him down to the ground and trampled on him. And there was no one who could rescue the ram from his power.<sup>8</sup>Then the goat became exceedingly great, but when he was strong, the great horn was broken, and instead of it there came up four conspicuous horns toward the four winds of heaven.<sup>9</sup>Out of one of them came a little horn, which grew exceedingly great toward the south, toward the east, and toward the glorious land.<sup>10</sup>It grew great, even to the host of heaven. And some of the host and some of the stars it threw down to the ground and trampled on them.<sup>11</sup>It became great, even as great as the Prince of the host. And the regular burnt offering was taken away from him, and the place of his sanctuary was overthrown.<sup>12</sup>And a host will be given over to it together with the regular burnt offering because of transgression, and it will throw truth to the ground, and it will act and prosper.<sup>13</sup>Then I heard a holy one speaking, and another holy one said to the one who spoke, "For how long is the vision concerning the regular burnt offering, the transgression that makes desolate, and the giving over of the sanctuary and host to be trampled underfoot?"<sup>14</sup>And he said to me, "For 2,300 evenings and mornings. Then the sanctuary shall be restored to its rightful state."<sup>15</sup>When I, Daniel, had seen the vision, I sought to understand it. And behold, there stood before me one having the appearance of a man.<sup>16</sup>And I heard a man's voice between the banks of the Ulai, and it called, "Gabriel, make this man understand the vision."<sup>17</sup>So he came near where I stood. And when he came, I was frightened and fell on my face. But he said to me, "Understand, O son of man, that the vision is for the time of the end."<sup>18</sup>And when he had spoken to me, I fell into a deep sleep with my face to the ground. But he touched me and made me stand up.<sup>19</sup>He said, "Behold, I will make known to you what shall be at the latter end of the indignation, for it refers to the appointed time of the end.<sup>20</sup>As for the ram that you saw with the two horns, these are the kings of Media and Persia.<sup>21</sup>And the goat is the king of Greece. And the great horn between his eyes is the first king.<sup>22</sup>As for the horn that was broken, in place of which four others arose, four kingdoms shall arise from his nation, but not with his power.<sup>23</sup>And at the latter end of their kingdom, when the transgressors have reached their limit, a king of bold face, one who understands riddles, shall arise.<sup>24</sup>His power shall be great— but not by his own power; and he shall cause fearful destruction and shall succeed in what he does, and destroy mighty men and the people who are the saints.<sup>25</sup>By his cunning he shall make deceit prosper under his hand, and in his own mind he shall become great. Without warning he shall destroy many. And he shall even rise up against the Prince of princes, and he shall be broken—but by no human hand.<sup>26</sup>The vision of the evenings and the mornings that has been told is true, but seal up the vision, for it refers to many days from now."<sup>27</sup>And I, Daniel, was overcome and lay sick for some days. Then I rose and went about the king's business, but I was appalled by the vision and did not understand it.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–14 — The Vision at the Ulai
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God sees the empires coming long before they arrive, and he sets the limit of the cruellest persecutor. Daniel, carried in vision to Susa, sees a two-horned ram, Media and Persia, charging wherever it pleases (vv. 1–4), until a goat from the west, Greece under Alexander, shatters it, only to have its own great horn broken at the height of its strength and replaced by four (vv. 5–8). From one of these grows a little horn that reaches toward heaven, takes away the daily offering, overthrows the sanctuary and throws truth to the ground (vv. 9–12). Then a holy one asks the sufferers’ question, “For how long?”, and the answer is a number: 2,300 evenings and mornings, and then the sanctuary will be restored (vv. 13–14).
verseByVerse.theology: Empires rise and fall at God's word, and even the desecration of his sanctuary has a limit he has fixed.

verseByVerse.quote: In the third year of the reign of King Belshazzar a vision appeared to me, Daniel, after that which appeared to me at the first. And I saw in the vision; and when I saw, I was in Susa the citadel, which is in the province of Elam. And I saw in the vision, and I was at the Ulai canal.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Two years after his first vision, Daniel is carried in a vision to Susa, the future heart of Persian power, to be shown what lies ahead for the empires after Babylon.

In the third year of the reign of King Belshazzar. This vision came two years after chapter 7, while Belshazzar still ruled and before Babylon fell. From here the book is in Hebrew again (see the introduction), and its focus narrows to God’s own people and his sanctuary.

Susa the citadel. Daniel was taken in the vision to Susa, some two hundred miles east of Babylon, which would soon become a Persian capital. Esther lived there, in “Susa, the citadel” (Esther 1:2), and Nehemiah served the Persian king there (Nehemiah 1:1). God set the scene of the vision in the future centre of the next world power.
verseByVerse.note: Susa lay in Elam, in what is now south-western Iran.

verseByVerse.quote: I raised my eyes and saw, and behold, a ram standing on the bank of the canal. It had two horns, and both horns were high, but one was higher than the other, and the higher one came up last. I saw the ram charging westward and northward and southward. No beast could stand before him, and there was no one who could rescue from his power. He did as he pleased and became great.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The ram is the empire of the Medes and Persians, which for two centuries did as it pleased because no one could stop it.

A ram standing on the bank of the canal. We do not have to guess what the ram means. Gabriel says it plainly: “these are the kings of Media and Persia” (v. 20). The two horns are two peoples united in one empire. The Medes were the stronger partner at first, but Persia “came up last” and grew “higher”, until under Cyrus it dominated the partnership. This matches the bear “raised up on one side” in 7:5.

He did as he pleased and became great. That is the recurring sin of empires in Daniel: they use their power as if they answered to no one. The phrase is also a warning, for in this book those who do as they please are always about to meet the God who “does according to his will” (4:35).
verseByVerse.note: The ram is Media-Persia (v. 20).

verseByVerse.quote: As I was considering, behold, a male goat came from the west across the face of the whole earth, without touching the ground. And the goat had a conspicuous horn between his eyes. He came to the ram with the two horns, which I had seen standing on the bank of the canal, and he ran at him in his powerful wrath. I saw him come close to the ram, and he was enraged against him and struck the ram and broke his two horns. And the ram had no power to stand before him, but he cast him down to the ground and trampled on him. And there was no one who could rescue the ram from his power. Then the goat became exceedingly great, but when he was strong, the great horn was broken, and instead of it there came up four conspicuous horns toward the four winds of heaven.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Greece under Alexander the Great overruns Persia with astonishing speed, but at the height of his power the conqueror is broken and his empire split four ways.

A male goat came from the west. The goat charges in so fast that its feet do not seem to touch the ground. Gabriel explains: “the goat is the king of Greece. And the great horn between his eyes is the first king” (v. 21). (There the ESV notes that the Hebrew may mean ‘the shaggy goat’.) Alexander the Great crossed from Greece into Asia in 334 BC, and within about three years he had broken the power of the Persian empire.

There was no one who could rescue the ram from his power. The words of verse 4 are turned back on the ram. Once no one could rescue anyone from the ram; now no one can rescue the ram.

When he was strong, the great horn was broken. At the very height of his power, in 323 BC, Alexander died suddenly in Babylon, only about thirty-two years old. He had conquered the known world and could not conquer death. His empire was eventually divided among his generals into four main kingdoms, “toward the four winds of heaven”, as the leopard of chapter 7 had four heads. “Pride goes before destruction” (Proverbs 16:18).
verseByVerse.note: The goat is Greece; its great horn, Alexander the Great, who died young in 323 BC and whose empire split four ways.

verseByVerse.quote: Out of one of them came a little horn, which grew exceedingly great toward the south, toward the east, and toward the glorious land. It grew great, even to the host of heaven. And some of the host and some of the stars it threw down to the ground and trampled on them. It became great, even as great as the Prince of the host. And the regular burnt offering was taken away from him, and the place of his sanctuary was overthrown. And a host will be given over to it together with the regular burnt offering because of transgression, and it will throw truth to the ground, and it will act and prosper.
verseByVerse.commentary:
From one of the four Greek kingdoms comes a king who attacks God’s land, people and worship as if he were storming heaven itself, and for a time he succeeds.

Out of one of them came a little horn. Now the vision narrows to one ruler. This little horn grows out of one of the four Greek kingdoms. It is not the horn of chapter 7, which came from the fourth beast; this one comes from Greece.

Antiochus IV Epiphanes. There is wide agreement about who this little horn is: Antiochus IV, a king of the Seleucid dynasty, which ruled Syria and the lands to the east. He reigned from 175 to 164 BC and called himself Epiphanes, meaning ‘God made manifest’. He campaigned “toward the south” (Egypt), “toward the east” (Persia) and “toward the glorious land”, the land of Israel, which Daniel loved.

Even to the host of heaven. The horn’s pride reaches toward heaven itself. The host and the stars are probably a picture of God’s people, who are elsewhere in Daniel compared to stars (12:3), together with the heavenly armies who stand behind them. Antiochus attacked the faithful Jews as if he were attacking heaven, and in a sense he was. To persecute God’s people is to make war on God.

The Prince of the host. This is God himself, the commander of heaven’s armies, and the horn sets itself up as his equal. It strikes at the heart of Israel’s worship. “The regular burnt offering” was the lamb offered every morning and evening in the temple (Exodus 29:38–42). In 167 BC Antiochus stopped these sacrifices, set up pagan worship in God’s temple and forbade the Jews, on pain of death, to keep the Sabbath, circumcise their sons or own the Scriptures. The Jewish history book known as 1 Maccabees records these horrors.

Because of transgression. All this happens “because of transgression”. Either Israel’s own sin opened the door to this judgment, or the horn’s rebellion is in view; in fact both were true, for many Jews of that time were eagerly abandoning God’s law for Greek ways. And the horn “will throw truth to the ground”. Tyranny always attacks truth, because God’s truth exposes its lies. For a time “it will act and prosper”: God’s people must be ready for evil to succeed for a season.

The king who wanted to be seen as a god. Antiochus had his title stamped on his coins, and the historian Polybius records that some of his subjects punned on it and called him Epimanes, ‘the madman’. We do not put our faces on coins, but the hunger behind the title is familiar. To be seen, admired, recognised as remarkable: a great deal of modern life, from the personal brand to the carefully chosen photograph, is an effort to make ourselves manifest. It is exhausting, because an image has to be kept up, and the self behind it lives in fear of being found out. The irony is that God really has made himself manifest, and he did it the opposite way. Paul uses a form of the same Greek word when he writes that “the grace of God has appeared” (Titus 2:11): God appeared in a manger, among the poor, and was finally put on display on a cross. The true God made manifest hid his glory in order to come near us. And he frees us from the work of making ourselves seen, because in him we are already fully seen, fully known and loved.

Uncertain wording. The Hebrew of verses 10–12 is among the hardest in the book, and translations differ. The ESV notes that verse 10 may mean ‘the host, that is, some of the stars’, making the host and the stars one and the same, and that “because of transgression” in verse 12 may mean ‘in an act of rebellion’. It is also unclear whether “a host will be given over to it” means God’s people handed over to the horn or an army given to it. The overall sense is not in doubt: for a time the horn overpowers God’s people and stops their worship, and it does so only because it is allowed to.
verseByVerse.note: The little horn is usually identified as Antiochus IV Epiphanes, who desecrated the temple in 167 BC.

verseByVerse.quote: Then I heard a holy one speaking, and another holy one said to the one who spoke, "For how long is the vision concerning the regular burnt offering, the transgression that makes desolate, and the giving over of the sanctuary and host to be trampled underfoot?" And he said to me, "For 2,300 evenings and mornings. Then the sanctuary shall be restored to its rightful state."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Heaven itself asks how long the desecration will last, and the answer is a number: God has counted the days, and then the sanctuary will be restored.

For how long is the vision? Even angels ask the question God’s suffering people ask. It is the cry of the psalms, “How long, O God, is the foe to scoff?” (Psalm 74:10), and of the martyrs in Revelation, “how long before you will judge and avenge our blood” (Revelation 6:10)? The answer is a number, and a number means a limit. God has counted the days of the desecration.

The transgression that makes desolate. This phrase introduces an idea that returns in 9:27, 11:31 and 12:11: an outrage against God so terrible that it leaves his sanctuary desolate. Jesus himself took up the language when he warned of “the abomination of desolation spoken of by the prophet Daniel” (Matthew 24:15).

For 2,300 evenings and mornings. There are two main readings. Some take it as 2,300 days, a little over six years, perhaps counting from the first attacks on the faithful to the end of Antiochus’s persecution. Others note that the temple had an evening and a morning offering each day, so 2,300 offerings would be 1,150 days, a little over three years. That is close to the time between the desecration of the temple in 167 BC and its cleansing and rededication by faithful Jews in December 164 BC, which was exactly three years by the Jewish calendar (1 Maccabees 1:54; 4:52). The second reading fits well, since the evening and morning offerings have just been named as taken away (v. 11), though 1,150 days runs about two months beyond three years, and no reading fits every date exactly. Either way, God set a date, and the sanctuary was restored.

The sanctuary shall be restored to its rightful state. The Jews celebrated that rededication every year afterwards with the Feast of Dedication, known today as Hanukkah. John tells us that Jesus was in the temple at that very feast: “At that time the Feast of Dedication took place at Jerusalem. It was winter, and Jesus was walking in the temple” (John 10:22–23). There, while the people remembered the cleansing of the temple, Jesus spoke of himself as the one “whom the Father consecrated and sent into the world” (John 10:36). The true temple, the place where God dwells with man, was walking among them: “he was speaking about the temple of his body” (John 2:21).

Where Christians differ. Seventh-day Adventists have read the 2,300 evenings and mornings as 2,300 years, ending in 1844, when, they teach, Christ began a work of judgment in the heavenly sanctuary.

This commentary’s view. The text speaks of evenings and mornings, not years; the vision is for “the time of the end” of the Greek kingdom (vv. 17, 21–23), and the sanctuary here is the temple Antiochus defiled. And Hebrews teaches that Christ entered the heavenly holy places once for all at his ascension (Hebrews 9:12, 24), not in 1844.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: What God reveals about the future he also explains, and the explanation ends with the persecutor broken by God’s own hand. Gabriel, sent at the command of a voice above the Ulai, tells the terrified Daniel that the vision is for the appointed time of the end (vv. 15–19). He names the ram as Media and Persia and the goat as Greece, with its first great king and four lesser kingdoms after him (vv. 20–22). Then comes a bold and cunning king whose power is not his own: he will destroy the saints and rise against the Prince of princes, and be broken by no human hand (vv. 23–25). The vision is sealed for many days, and Daniel, sick and appalled, gets up and goes back to the king’s business (vv. 26–27).
verseByVerse.theology: God tells his people in advance what they will suffer, so that when it comes they will know he still rules.

verseByVerse.quote: When I, Daniel, had seen the vision, I sought to understand it. And behold, there stood before me one having the appearance of a man. And I heard a man's voice between the banks of the Ulai, and it called, "Gabriel, make this man understand the vision." So he came near where I stood. And when he came, I was frightened and fell on my face. But he said to me, "Understand, O son of man, that the vision is for the time of the end." And when he had spoken to me, I fell into a deep sleep with my face to the ground. But he touched me and made me stand up. He said, "Behold, I will make known to you what shall be at the latter end of the indignation, for it refers to the appointed time of the end.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Gabriel is sent to make Daniel understand, and his first word is that the vision concerns the end God has appointed for his people’s suffering.

Gabriel, make this man understand the vision. This is the first time an angel is named in the Bible. Five centuries later the same Gabriel appeared to Zechariah and to Mary: “I am Gabriel. I stand in the presence of God” (Luke 1:19). The messenger who explained the rise and fall of empires to Daniel announced the birth of the King whose kingdom has no end (Luke 1:26–33).

A man’s voice between the banks of the Ulai. Someone with authority to command Gabriel gives the order. The book does not say who he is, but many have connected him with the man clothed in linen who stands above the waters of the stream in 12:6–7.

O son of man. Gabriel calls Daniel “son of man”, as God addressed Ezekiel (Ezekiel 2:1). Here it simply means ‘mortal man’, a reminder of how small Daniel is before the messengers of God.

The vision is for the time of the end. In this chapter the explanation centres on “the latter end of the indignation”, the period of God’s anger against his people’s sin, which came to its climax under Antiochus. And that end is “appointed”: God has fixed it. But the vision also looks beyond him. The persecutor of chapter 8 and the horn of chapter 7 share the same marks: pride, blasphemy and war on God’s people and worship. Antiochus is a preview of a greater enemy who will arise at the end of history (11:36–45), and what happened under him is a pattern of what the church must expect before Christ returns.
verseByVerse.note: Only two angels are named in the Old Testament, Gabriel and Michael (10:13), both in Daniel.

verseByVerse.quote: As for the ram that you saw with the two horns, these are the kings of Media and Persia. And the goat is the king of Greece. And the great horn between his eyes is the first king. As for the horn that was broken, in place of which four others arose, four kingdoms shall arise from his nation, but not with his power.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Gabriel names the empires outright: Media and Persia, then Greece, with its first great king and four lesser kingdoms after him.

The kings of Media and Persia. Few prophecies in the Bible are so specific: the vision describes nearly four centuries of history before it happened. This precision is the main reason many scholars think the book was written after the events, about 165 BC. This commentary holds that God, who knows the end from the beginning, gave Daniel these things in advance, while granting that the date of the book is debated (see the introduction).

Light on chapters 2 and 7. Here Media and Persia are one animal, and Greece comes next. That is a main reason this commentary reads the silver kingdom and the bear as Medo-Persia, the bronze and the leopard as Greece, and the fourth kingdom as Rome (see 2:39–40).

verseByVerse.quote: And at the latter end of their kingdom, when the transgressors have reached their limit, a king of bold face, one who understands riddles, shall arise. His power shall be great— but not by his own power; and he shall cause fearful destruction and shall succeed in what he does, and destroy mighty men and the people who are the saints. By his cunning he shall make deceit prosper under his hand, and in his own mind he shall become great. Without warning he shall destroy many. And he shall even rise up against the Prince of princes, and he shall be broken—but by no human hand.
verseByVerse.commentary:
A shameless and cunning king will rise with borrowed power, destroy many of God’s people and defy God himself, and then God alone will break him.

When the transgressors have reached their limit. God allows sin to go on only up to a limit he has set, and then he acts. The “king of bold face” is shameless and hard. He “understands riddles”, meaning he is clever at scheming and double-dealing. Antiochus was famous for his cunning.

But not by his own power. However frightening he becomes, his strength is given to him. He is a tool in a hand larger than his own. He will destroy “the people who are the saints”: Daniel is not promised that God’s people will be spared, only that God is still in control.

By his cunning. His weapons are cunning and deceit, and he strikes without warning. “In his own mind he shall become great”, the same inward pride that brought down Nebuchadnezzar. At last he goes too far and rises “against the Prince of princes”, God himself.

By no human hand. Then comes his end. He will be broken “by no human hand”, the very words used in 2:34 of the stone that shatters the statue. Antiochus was not killed in battle; he died of a sudden illness while campaigning in the east in 164 BC. God himself removed him.

The Prince of princes. The Prince of princes has one final answer to every tyrant: “They will make war on the Lamb, and the Lamb will conquer them, for he is Lord of lords and King of kings” (Revelation 17:14). The rulers of the earth once took counsel together against God’s Anointed, Jesus, and crucified him. But they did only “whatever your hand and your plan had predestined to take place” (Acts 4:28), and God raised him from the dead.

verseByVerse.quote: The vision of the evenings and the mornings that has been told is true, but seal up the vision, for it refers to many days from now." And I, Daniel, was overcome and lay sick for some days. Then I rose and went about the king's business, but I was appalled by the vision and did not understand it.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The vision is true and must be kept safe for a distant day; the prophet who sees it is crushed by it, yet he gets up and goes back to work.

Seal up the vision. This does not mean hide it. It means preserve it safely, like a legal document sealed for the future. The events were “many days from now”, nearly four hundred years away. When they came, the faithful Jews who suffered under Antiochus could open Daniel and know that God had foreseen every step of their suffering and had set its limit. “For whatever was written in former days was written for our instruction, that through endurance and through the encouragement of the Scriptures we might have hope” (Romans 15:4).

I, Daniel, was overcome and lay sick for some days. He had seen the future suffering of his people and the desecration of God’s sanctuary, and it made him ill.

I rose and went about the king’s business. And yet, when he recovered, he went back to work. Knowing the future did not make him quit and wait for the end. Christians, too, are to serve faithfully in the present. They do not need to work out a timetable of the future, because the God who holds the future holds them.

Did not understand it. Even the prophet did not grasp everything he saw. Peter says that the prophets “searched and inquired carefully” about what they foretold, and that “they were serving not themselves but you” (1 Peter 1:10, 12). We live after these events. We can see how they came true, and see in them the pattern of the final conflict before Christ returns. Most of all, we know the Prince against whom every little horn rises, and we know that he has already won.

8.title: The Ram and the Goat
8.overview:
Where we are. Two years after the vision of chapter 7, still in Belshazzar’s reign, Daniel sees a second vision. The book turns from Aramaic back to Hebrew, and the view of four world empires narrows to two, Persia and Greece, and then to one king who will attack God’s people and his sanctuary.

The message. God knows every empire before it rises, he sets the limit of every persecutor, and he breaks the proud by no human hand. Even when his people’s worship is trampled and truth is thrown to the ground, their suffering has a number on it, and the sanctuary will be restored.

Why it was said. Daniel’s first hearers were exiles whose temple lay in ruins (see the introduction). The vision looks further, to faithful Jews under the Greek king Antiochus IV nearly four centuries later, so that people under pressure would know that God had seen their suffering coming and had already set its end.

How the chapter makes its case. A two-horned ram charges where it pleases until a goat from the west smashes it; but at the height of its strength the goat’s great horn is broken and four take its place (vv. 1–8). From one of these grows a little horn that reaches toward heaven, takes away the daily offering and throws truth to the ground, and when a holy one asks “For how long?”, the answer is a number: 2,300 evenings and mornings (vv. 9–14). Gabriel explains that the ram is Media and Persia and the goat is Greece (vv. 15–22). A bold and cunning king will destroy the saints and rise against the Prince of princes, and God himself will break him (vv. 23–25). Daniel, sick at heart, then goes back to work (vv. 26–27).

Where it leads. To Christ chiefly by pattern and by the character of God. Antiochus, who called himself “God made manifest”, is a pattern of every proud power that sets itself against God and his people, and of the final enemy whom Christ will destroy at his coming (see 11:36–45). The temple Antiochus defiled was cleansed and remembered every winter at the Feast of Dedication, and at that feast Jesus walked in the temple and spoke of himself as the one the Father consecrated (John 10:22–36): the true temple was among them. And the true God made manifest came the opposite way from Antiochus, in a manger and on a cross.

For us. Expect evil to “act and prosper” for a season (v. 12), and do not be shaken by it: every persecutor of Christ’s people has a limit set in heaven. Let what you know of the future send you back, like Daniel, to faithful work, resting in the Prince who has already won.
8.theology:
God knows and announces the rise and fall of empires long before they happen (vv. 3-8, 20-22; Rom 15:4).

Pride and unchecked power end in ruin; the greatest conquerors are broken at God's word (vv. 4, 7-8, 25; Prov 16:18).

To attack God's people and worship is to make war on God, and God permits such evil only for a fixed and limited time (vv. 10-14, 24; Ps 74:10; Rev 6:10).

The desecrations of history, like Antiochus's, foreshadow the final enemy of God and his people (vv. 17, 19; Matt 24:15).

The restored sanctuary points to Christ, the true temple consecrated by the Father, whose single sacrifice fulfils the regular offerings (vv. 11-14; John 2:19-21; 10:22, 36; Heb 10:11-12).

Every enemy who rises against the Prince of princes is broken by God, and Christ the Lamb conquers (v. 25; Rev 17:14; Acts 4:26-28).

Prophecy is given to steady God's people, and they serve faithfully in the present while trusting God with what they do not understand (v. 27; 1 Pet 1:10-12).
8.examples: Daniel 8 was written for believers who would one day watch their faith outlawed and their worship stopped. When they suffered under Antiochus, they could open this chapter and see that God had foreseen every step and set its end. Christians who face hostile rulers now can read it the same way, and then, like Daniel, get up and go back to their work.

keyVerse.quote: And he said to me, “For 2,300 evenings and mornings. Then the sanctuary shall be restored to its rightful state.”
keyVerse.note: This verse answers the cry of God’s suffering people, “For how long?”, with a number, and a number means a limit. The persecutor will act and prosper for a season, but God has counted every day of it, and after them the sanctuary will be put right. It is the chapter’s comfort in one sentence: evil has an end, and God has already set it.

8.reflection:
Persia “did as he pleased and became great” (v. 4), and Alexander was broken “when he was strong” (v. 8). Where do you see people or powers acting today as if they answer to no one? How does this chapter change the way you see them, and your own ambitions?

The little horn would “throw truth to the ground” and “act and prosper” for a time (v. 12). How should Christians respond when evil seems to succeed and truth is mocked? What does the holy one’s question “For how long?” (v. 13) teach us about bringing that to God?

Antiochus called himself ‘God made manifest’. How does the way God actually made himself known in Jesus, in a manger and on a cross, free us from the work of making ourselves seen?

Daniel was overwhelmed by the vision, yet he “rose and went about the king’s business” (v. 27). How should what we know about the future shape our ordinary work this week?

9.text: <sup>1</sup>In the first year of Darius the son of Ahasuerus, by descent a Mede, who was made king over the realm of the Chaldeans—<sup>2</sup>in the first year of his reign, I, Daniel, perceived in the books the number of years that, according to the word of the LORD to Jeremiah the prophet, must pass before the end of the desolations of Jerusalem, namely, seventy years.<sup>3</sup>Then I turned my face to the Lord God, seeking him by prayer and pleas for mercy with fasting and sackcloth and ashes.<sup>4</sup>I prayed to the LORD my God and made confession, saying, "O Lord, the great and awesome God, who keeps covenant and steadfast love with those who love him and keep his commandments,<sup>5</sup>we have sinned and done wrong and acted wickedly and rebelled, turning aside from your commandments and rules.<sup>6</sup>We have not listened to your servants the prophets, who spoke in your name to our kings, our princes, and our fathers, and to all the people of the land.<sup>7</sup>To you, O Lord, belongs righteousness, but to us open shame, as at this day, to the men of Judah, to the inhabitants of Jerusalem, and to all Israel, those who are near and those who are far away, in all the lands to which you have driven them, because of the treachery that they have committed against you.<sup>8</sup>To us, O LORD, belongs open shame, to our kings, to our princes, and to our fathers, because we have sinned against you.<sup>9</sup>To the Lord our God belong mercy and forgiveness, for we have rebelled against him<sup>10</sup>and have not obeyed the voice of the LORD our God by walking in his laws, which he set before us by his servants the prophets.<sup>11</sup>All Israel has transgressed your law and turned aside, refusing to obey your voice. And the curse and oath that are written in the Law of Moses the servant of God have been poured out upon us, because we have sinned against him.<sup>12</sup>He has confirmed his words, which he spoke against us and against our rulers who ruled us, by bringing upon us a great calamity. For under the whole heaven there has not been done anything like what has been done against Jerusalem.<sup>13</sup>As it is written in the Law of Moses, all this calamity has come upon us; yet we have not entreated the favor of the LORD our God, turning from our iniquities and gaining insight by your truth.<sup>14</sup>Therefore the LORD has kept ready the calamity and has brought it upon us, for the LORD our God is righteous in all the works that he has done, and we have not obeyed his voice.<sup>15</sup>And now, O Lord our God, who brought your people out of the land of Egypt with a mighty hand, and have made a name for yourself, as at this day, we have sinned, we have done wickedly.<sup>16</sup>"O Lord, according to all your righteous acts, let your anger and your wrath turn away from your city Jerusalem, your holy hill, because for our sins, and for the iniquities of our fathers, Jerusalem and your people have become a byword among all who are around us.<sup>17</sup>Now therefore, O our God, listen to the prayer of your servant and to his pleas for mercy, and for your own sake, O Lord, make your face to shine upon your sanctuary, which is desolate.<sup>18</sup>O my God, incline your ear and hear. Open your eyes and see our desolations, and the city that is called by your name. For we do not present our pleas before you because of our righteousness, but because of your great mercy.<sup>19</sup>O Lord, hear; O Lord, forgive. O Lord, pay attention and act. Delay not, for your own sake, O my God, because your city and your people are called by your name."<sup>20</sup>While I was speaking and praying, confessing my sin and the sin of my people Israel, and presenting my plea before the LORD my God for the holy hill of my God,<sup>21</sup>while I was speaking in prayer, the man Gabriel, whom I had seen in the vision at the first, came to me in swift flight at the time of the evening sacrifice.<sup>22</sup>He made me understand, speaking with me and saying, "O Daniel, I have now come out to give you insight and understanding.<sup>23</sup>At the beginning of your pleas for mercy a word went out, and I have come to tell it to you, for you are greatly loved. Therefore consider the word and understand the vision.<sup>24</sup>"Seventy weeks are decreed about your people and your holy city, to finish the transgression, to put an end to sin, and to atone for iniquity, to bring in everlasting righteousness, to seal both vision and prophet, and to anoint a most holy place.<sup>25</sup>Know therefore and understand that from the going out of the word to restore and build Jerusalem to the coming of an anointed one, a prince, there shall be seven weeks. And for sixty-two weeks it shall be built again with squares and moat, but in a troubled time.<sup>26</sup>And after the sixty-two weeks, an anointed one shall be cut off and shall have nothing. And the people of the prince who is to come shall destroy the city and the sanctuary. Its end shall come with a flood, and to the end there shall be war. Desolations are decreed.<sup>27</sup>And he shall make a strong covenant with many for one week, and for half of the week he shall put an end to sacrifice and offering. And on the wing of abominations shall come one who makes desolate, until the decreed end is poured out on the desolator."

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God’s promises do not make prayer unnecessary; they make it urgent and confident. It is 539 or 538 BC. Babylon has fallen, and the aged Daniel, a captive since 605 BC, is reading the scroll of Jeremiah, his older contemporary (v. 1). There he finds the word of the LORD that Jerusalem’s desolations would last seventy years, and he realises that the time is almost up (v. 2). Instead of sitting back to wait, he turns to God in prayer, for the same prophecy had promised that when the exiles called on God, he would hear them. These two verses set the scene for the prayer that follows.
verseByVerse.theology: God's promises in Scripture move his people to pray.

verseByVerse.quote: In the first year of Darius the son of Ahasuerus, by descent a Mede, who was made king over the realm of the Chaldeans— in the first year of his reign, I, Daniel, perceived in the books the number of years that, according to the word of the LORD to Jeremiah the prophet, must pass before the end of the desolations of Jerusalem, namely, seventy years.
verseByVerse.commentary:
As Babylon falls, the aged Daniel reads in Jeremiah that the seventy years of exile are nearly over, and the promise sends him to prayer.

In the first year of Darius. The date is 539 or 538 BC. Babylon has just fallen, as chapter 5 described. Daniel is now an old man, probably over eighty, who has lived through the whole of Babylon’s empire and seen it collapse in a single night. (Who Darius the Mede was is debated: perhaps another title for Cyrus, perhaps the governor Cyrus set over Babylon; see 5:31.)

I, Daniel, perceived in the books. The books were the Scriptures available to him, including Jeremiah, his older contemporary, who had written: “When seventy years are completed for Babylon, I will visit you, and I will fulfill to you my promise and bring you back to this place” (Jeremiah 29:10). Daniel had been taken captive in 605 BC. Now Babylon had fallen. He did the arithmetic: the seventy years were almost over.

Seventy years. Chronicles explains why the exile lasted seventy years. The land had to make up for the Sabbath years Israel had failed to keep: “All the days that it lay desolate it kept Sabbath, to fulfill seventy years” (2 Chronicles 36:21). That detail will matter when we come to the seventy ‘weeks’ at the end of the chapter.

Promises that prompt prayer. Finding the promise about to be fulfilled, Daniel did not sit back and wait. He prayed. God’s sovereign promises never make prayer unnecessary; they make it confident. Jeremiah’s own prophecy said so: “Then you will call upon me and come and pray to me, and I will hear you” (Jeremiah 29:12). The Bible’s promises are meant to be turned into prayers, and the Spirit himself helps believers to pray them (Romans 8:26).
verseByVerse.note: Daniel reads Jeremiah’s prophecy of seventy years of exile.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The only plea a sinner can bring to God is his great mercy. Daniel begins with God, great and awesome, who keeps covenant and steadfast love, and then confesses without excuse that Israel has sinned, rebelled and refused to listen to the prophets (vv. 3–6). Righteousness belongs to God and open shame to his people, yet mercy and forgiveness belong to God too (vv. 7–10). Every curse written in the Law of Moses has fallen, and God was right in all of it (vv. 11–14). Then confession turns to petition: remember the exodus, turn your anger from your city, and act, not because of our righteousness but for your own sake and your own name (vv. 15–19).
verseByVerse.theology: True prayer confesses sin honestly and pleads only God's mercy and the honor of his name.

verseByVerse.quote: Then I turned my face to the Lord God, seeking him by prayer and pleas for mercy with fasting and sackcloth and ashes. I prayed to the LORD my God and made confession, saying, "O Lord, the great and awesome God, who keeps covenant and steadfast love with those who love him and keep his commandments, we have sinned and done wrong and acted wickedly and rebelled, turning aside from your commandments and rules. We have not listened to your servants the prophets, who spoke in your name to our kings, our princes, and our fathers, and to all the people of the land.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Daniel turns to God with his whole being, beginning with God’s faithful love and then confessing his people’s sin without excuse, as one of them.

Fasting and sackcloth and ashes. Fasting, rough sackcloth and ashes on the head were signs of mourning and humility (see mourning customs). Daniel’s whole body joined in his prayer, expressing sorrow over sin.

The great and awesome God. Daniel begins with God, not with his own needs. God is “great and awesome”, and he “keeps covenant and steadfast love”. Before Daniel speaks of Israel’s unfaithfulness, he remembers God’s faithfulness. That is where every prayer of confession must begin, or confession turns into despair.

What steadfast love means here. The Hebrew word is hesed: love that has bound itself by promise and stays bound. Daniel joins it to covenant, because the covenant is where God put that love in writing. Notice what this does to confession. We hold back from admitting our sin fully because we half believe that love depends on our record, and that the whole truth would end it. Daniel can name every failure without excuse because God’s love never rested on Israel’s record. And we know how far that love would go: “God shows his love for us in that while we were still sinners, Christ died for us” (Romans 5:8). So when you confess this week, begin where Daniel began: not with how badly you have done, but with the love that has promised not to let you go. See Steadfast love in the Theological Dictionary.

We have sinned and done wrong. The confession piles up words for sin and makes no excuses. And the pronoun is we. Daniel is the most faithful man in the book; his enemies searched his life and found no fault (6:4). Yet he does not pray ‘they have sinned’. He stands with his people and confesses their sin as his own, as Ezra and Nehemiah later prayed (Ezra 9:6; Nehemiah 1:6). God’s law had promised that if his exiled people would “confess their iniquity and the iniquity of their fathers”, he would “remember my covenant” (Leviticus 26:40, 42). Daniel is doing exactly what God asked.

We have not listened to your servants the prophets. At the root of Israel’s disaster was a refusal to listen. God had spoken again and again through the prophets, to kings and to ordinary people, and they would not hear. That is still the root of spiritual ruin: not a lack of God’s word, but a refusal to listen to it.

Pointing to Christ. In this Daniel points us to Christ, who went much further. Daniel identified with sinners and confessed sins he shared. Jesus, who had no sin at all, took the sins of his people upon himself: “he bore the sin of many, and makes intercession for the transgressors” (Isaiah 53:12).

Why confess sins you did not commit? To a modern ear Daniel’s we can sound strange, even unjust. Surely each of us answers for our own choices and no one else’s. Yet we are not consistent about this. The same people who insist they are responsible only for themselves also feel, often keenly, that they belong to histories they did not choose: families, churches, institutions and nations whose wrongs they inherit and whose names they carry. So we lurch between two poses: indifference (that was nothing to do with me) and a kind of guilt that is quicker to accuse others than to kneel. Daniel does neither. He does not pretend to be untouched by his people’s sin, and he does not stand above it to denounce it. He kneels inside it, says we, and carries all of it, his own share and theirs, to the only place where guilt can actually be dealt with: the mercy of God (v. 9). Christians can pray like that without despair, because the sinless one has already carried what they confess.

verseByVerse.quote: To you, O Lord, belongs righteousness, but to us open shame, as at this day, to the men of Judah, to the inhabitants of Jerusalem, and to all Israel, those who are near and those who are far away, in all the lands to which you have driven them, because of the treachery that they have committed against you. To us, O LORD, belongs open shame, to our kings, to our princes, and to our fathers, because we have sinned against you. To the Lord our God belong mercy and forgiveness, for we have rebelled against him and have not obeyed the voice of the LORD our God by walking in his laws, which he set before us by his servants the prophets.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God was right to send the exile and Israel has nothing to plead but shame; yet mercy and forgiveness belong to God, and that is Daniel’s hope.

To you, O Lord, belongs righteousness. Daniel sets two things side by side: “To you, O Lord, belongs righteousness, but to us open shame”. God was right to send the exile, and Israel had no complaint to make. The scattered people, near and far away, were living proof that God had kept his word.

Genuine repentance. This is the heart of genuine repentance. It does not say, ‘God, why did you do this to me?’ It says, ‘God, you are just, and the fault is mine.’ The tax collector in Jesus’ parable prayed only, “God, be merciful to me, a sinner!” (Luke 18:13), and he went home justified.

To the Lord our God belong mercy and forgiveness. Here is the turn in the prayer. God has righteousness, and he also has mercy and forgiveness. Israel has only shame, and yet Daniel dares to hope, because mercy belongs to God. He even gives the reason: “for we have rebelled”. He does not say God should forgive because Israel deserves it; he appeals to mercy precisely because they do not. Only those who have no defence to offer need mercy.

verseByVerse.quote: All Israel has transgressed your law and turned aside, refusing to obey your voice. And the curse and oath that are written in the Law of Moses the servant of God have been poured out upon us, because we have sinned against him. He has confirmed his words, which he spoke against us and against our rulers who ruled us, by bringing upon us a great calamity. For under the whole heaven there has not been done anything like what has been done against Jerusalem. As it is written in the Law of Moses, all this calamity has come upon us; yet we have not entreated the favor of the LORD our God, turning from our iniquities and gaining insight by your truth. Therefore the LORD has kept ready the calamity and has brought it upon us, for the LORD our God is righteous in all the works that he has done, and we have not obeyed his voice.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The exile was exactly what the Law of Moses had warned, so it proves that God keeps his word, and Daniel declares him righteous in all of it.

The curse and oath that are written in the Law of Moses. The Law had set before Israel blessings for obedience and curses for disobedience, including defeat by enemies and exile from the land (Leviticus 26; Deuteronomy 28). Everything that had happened was written in advance. The exile was not a sign that God had lost control or broken his promises. It was proof that he keeps every word, including his warnings.

Anything like what has been done against Jerusalem. The destruction of Jerusalem was unique because Jerusalem was unique: it was the city God had chosen for his name. The greater the privilege, the greater the fall. (The ESV notes that “our rulers who ruled us” can be translated ‘our judges who judged us’.)

Yet we have not entreated the favor of the LORD our God. This is one of the saddest sentences in the prayer. Even after the calamity fell, the people had not turned to God. Suffering alone does not change hearts; only God’s grace does that.

The LORD our God is righteous. Again Daniel says that God is righteous (see v. 7), and he will appeal to God’s “righteous acts” in verse 16. He never accuses God. A man torn from his home as a boy insists that God was just in all of it.

verseByVerse.quote: And now, O Lord our God, who brought your people out of the land of Egypt with a mighty hand, and have made a name for yourself, as at this day, we have sinned, we have done wickedly. "O Lord, according to all your righteous acts, let your anger and your wrath turn away from your city Jerusalem, your holy hill, because for our sins, and for the iniquities of our fathers, Jerusalem and your people have become a byword among all who are around us. Now therefore, O our God, listen to the prayer of your servant and to his pleas for mercy, and for your own sake, O Lord, make your face to shine upon your sanctuary, which is desolate.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Daniel now pleads: as God once saved his people from Egypt, let him turn his anger from his ruined city and sanctuary, for the sake of his own name.

And now, O Lord our God. The prayer turns to request, and its first argument is history. God brought his people out of slavery in Egypt “with a mighty hand”, and that great rescue made his name known among the nations. Daniel is asking God to do it again: a new exodus, this time from Babylon. The God who saved before can save again.

According to all your righteous acts. Here God’s righteousness is not only his justice in punishing but also his faithfulness in saving, keeping his covenant promises. And Daniel appeals to God’s reputation. Jerusalem has become “a byword”, a joke among the nations; when God’s people are disgraced, God’s name is mocked.

Make your face to shine upon your sanctuary. This echoes the priestly blessing (Numbers 6:25). Daniel longs for God’s favour to return to his ruined temple, and the ground of his plea is “for your own sake”. (The ESV notes that the Hebrew says ‘for the Lord’s sake’.) The great hope of every sinner is not that God owes us anything, but that he will act for the honour of his own name and keep what he has promised. He will be true to himself.

verseByVerse.quote: O my God, incline your ear and hear. Open your eyes and see our desolations, and the city that is called by your name. For we do not present our pleas before you because of our righteousness, but because of your great mercy. O Lord, hear; O Lord, forgive. O Lord, pay attention and act. Delay not, for your own sake, O my God, because your city and your people are called by your name."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Daniel rests his whole plea on God’s great mercy, not on any righteousness of his people, and ends in urgent cries for God to hear, forgive and act.

Because of your great mercy. This verse is the gospel in the Old Testament: “we do not present our pleas before you because of our righteousness, but because of your great mercy”. Daniel, one of the most righteous men who ever lived, brings nothing but his need, and appeals to nothing but God’s mercy. That is how every sinner must come: not ‘accept me because I have tried hard’, but ‘accept me because you are merciful’.

Mercy and justice meet. The New Testament shows how a righteous God can be merciful to sinners without denying his justice. God put Christ forward “as a propitiation by his blood” (a sacrifice that turns God’s just anger away from the sinner), “so that he might be just and the justifier of the one who has faith in Jesus” (Romans 3:25–26). In Christ, God’s mercy and God’s righteousness meet.

O Lord, hear; O Lord, forgive. The prayer ends in short, urgent cries, a man pouring out his heart, and it ends where it began: “for your own sake”, because the city and people bear God’s name. Christians can pray this way too, for we bear the name of Christ: “Let us then with confidence draw near to the throne of grace, that we may receive mercy and find grace to help in time of need” (Hebrews 4:16).

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God hears his people sooner, and loves them more, than they dare to think. While Daniel is still speaking, confessing his own sin and his people’s, Gabriel arrives in swift flight at the hour of the evening sacrifice, the time when the lamb used to be offered in a temple that has lain in ruins for half a century (vv. 20–21). He brings two pieces of news: the answer went out at the very beginning of Daniel’s pleas, and Daniel is greatly loved (vv. 22–23). After a prayer full of sin and shame, heaven’s first word is love. Then Gabriel calls him to consider the word that follows.
verseByVerse.theology: God hears the prayers of his people from their first word, and he loves them.

verseByVerse.quote: While I was speaking and praying, confessing my sin and the sin of my people Israel, and presenting my plea before the LORD my God for the holy hill of my God, while I was speaking in prayer, the man Gabriel, whom I had seen in the vision at the first, came to me in swift flight at the time of the evening sacrifice. He made me understand, speaking with me and saying, "O Daniel, I have now come out to give you insight and understanding. At the beginning of your pleas for mercy a word went out, and I have come to tell it to you, for you are greatly loved. Therefore consider the word and understand the vision.
verseByVerse.commentary:
While Daniel is still praying, God’s answer arrives: it was sent at his first word, and it comes with the assurance that he is greatly loved.

My sin and the sin of my people Israel. Now Daniel says “my sin” as well as his people’s. The holiest man in Babylon knew he was a sinner.

At the time of the evening sacrifice. Gabriel, the angel of chapter 8, arrives at the hour of the evening sacrifice. There had been no temple and no evening sacrifice in Jerusalem for nearly fifty years, but Daniel still marked the time of day when the lamb used to be offered. His heart kept the rhythm of worship even in exile, and at that hour God answered.

At the beginning of your pleas for mercy. God answered at the beginning of Daniel’s prayer, before he had finished speaking. God is not reluctant to hear his people. Jesus said, “your Father knows what you need before you ask him” (Matthew 6:8).

For you are greatly loved. After a whole prayer of confessing sin and shame, heaven’s reply begins by telling Daniel that he is loved. That is how God receives repentant sinners. Every believer in Christ can hear the same word: we are not loved because we deserve it, but because God has set his love upon us in his Son.
verseByVerse.note: The evening sacrifice was offered in the afternoon; by New Testament times it was linked with the ninth hour.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Return from exile would not cure Israel’s deepest problem; God’s answer is an Anointed One who will be cut off to deal with sin itself. Daniel prayed about seventy years, and God answers with seventy weeks, whose goals are to end transgression, atone for iniquity and bring in everlasting righteousness (v. 24). From the word to rebuild Jerusalem, a troubled time of rebuilding leads to an anointed one, a prince (v. 25). He will be cut off and have nothing, and the city and sanctuary will again be destroyed (v. 26). In the final week a strong covenant is made with many, sacrifice ends, and the desolator meets his decreed end (v. 27). Christians read the details differently; this commentary finds them fulfilled in Christ’s death and Jerusalem’s fall.
verseByVerse.theology: God has decreed the time of the Messiah, who would be cut off to atone for sin and bring in everlasting righteousness.

verseByVerse.quote: "Seventy weeks are decreed about your people and your holy city, to finish the transgression, to put an end to sin, and to atone for iniquity, to bring in everlasting righteousness, to seal both vision and prophet, and to anoint a most holy place.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God answers Daniel’s seventy years with seventy weeks, a decreed period that will end not merely in a return from exile but in sin dealt with and everlasting righteousness brought in.

Seventy weeks. Daniel had been thinking about Jeremiah’s seventy years; God answers with seventy weeks. The word means ‘sevens’, and most interpreters understand seventy sevens of years, that is, 490 years. Remember 2 Chronicles 36:21: the seventy years of exile made up for missed Sabbath years, which came every seventh year. Now God announces seventy times seven. The exile was nearly over, but a far greater problem remained. Seventy years in Babylon had not solved Israel’s sin. A longer period, fixed by God, would lead to the real solution.

Decreed about your people and your holy city. God has set the timetable, and its goal comes in six phrases. The first three deal with sin: “to finish the transgression, to put an end to sin, and to atone for iniquity”. The last three describe what God will bring in: “everlasting righteousness”, the sealing of “vision and prophet” (confirming what the prophets foretold by bringing it to pass), and the anointing of “a most holy place”.

Who could possibly do this? The temple sacrifices never put an end to sin, and no return from exile brought in everlasting righteousness. These goals describe the work of Jesus Christ. He came “to put away sin by the sacrifice of himself” (Hebrews 9:26). He entered the holy places “by means of his own blood, thus securing an eternal redemption” (Hebrews 9:12). He is the fulfilment of all the prophets (Luke 24:44). And since the ESV notes that “a most holy place” could also be ‘a most holy thing, or one’, many see here the anointing of Christ himself, the true temple, whom God anointed “with the Holy Spirit and with power” (Acts 10:38).

How Jewish readers take it. Jewish interpreters usually read the seventy weeks as reaching from the destruction of the first temple to that of the second (a rabbinic count), and take the anointed ones of verses 25 and 26 as a Persian king, high priests or Judean rulers rather than the Messiah; the end of sacrifice is the fall of the temple in AD 70. So both readings agree that the weeks run up to Jerusalem’s destruction by Rome. This commentary reads the anointed one who is cut off as Jesus, because only his death meets the goals of this verse, putting away sin by the sacrifice of himself (Hebrews 9:26).
verseByVerse.note: “Seventy weeks” is literally “seventy sevens.” Interpreters differ on how to count them; most Christian readers see their goal in Christ’s atoning work.

verseByVerse.quote: Know therefore and understand that from the going out of the word to restore and build Jerusalem to the coming of an anointed one, a prince, there shall be seven weeks. And for sixty-two weeks it shall be built again with squares and moat, but in a troubled time.
verseByVerse.commentary:
From the word to rebuild Jerusalem, through a long and troubled time of rebuilding, the count runs to the coming of an anointed one, a prince.

Three periods. The seventy weeks are divided into seven weeks, sixty-two weeks and one final week (v. 27). The count begins with “the going out of the word to restore and build Jerusalem” and runs to “an anointed one, a prince”. Anointed one is what the title Messiah means, and Christ is the same title in Greek. When Andrew met Jesus he said, “We have found the Messiah” (which means Christ) (John 1:41).
