The word was used of kings and priests who were anointed for their office, and above all of the promised King.

Which word to restore and build Jerusalem starts the count? Several decrees were issued by Persian kings. Cyrus allowed the Jews to return and rebuild the temple in 538 BC (Ezra 1:2–3). Artaxerxes sent Ezra to Jerusalem with broad authority in 458 BC (Ezra 7:11–13). And Artaxerxes allowed Nehemiah to rebuild the city walls in 445 or 444 BC (Nehemiah 2:5). Many interpreters have noticed that if you count 483 years (sixty-nine weeks) from Ezra’s commission in 458 BC, you arrive at about AD 26 or 27, when Jesus was baptised, anointed by the Spirit and began his public ministry. Others count from Nehemiah’s commission, using a 360-day ‘prophetic year’, and arrive at the days of Jesus’ ministry and his entry into Jerusalem. Neither count is free of difficulty: the starting decree is debated, and the arithmetic should not be pressed to the day. But both lines of reckoning point to the time of Christ. The first is the simpler: it needs no special year, and it ends at the anointing of Jesus with the Spirit at his baptism, when the Anointed One appeared.

Built again with squares and moat. Meanwhile Jerusalem “shall be built again with squares and moat, but in a troubled time”. Ezra and Nehemiah describe exactly that: rebuilding against opposition and fear.

Uncertain wording. Where verse 25 should pause is uncertain. The ESV notes another way of dividing it: ‘there shall be seven weeks and sixty-two weeks. It shall be built again’. On that reading the anointed one comes after sixty-nine weeks (483 years). This commentary takes that reading, and the counts above assume it. The accent marks added to the Hebrew by medieval scribes put a pause after the seven weeks; the KJV and many older translations read the two periods together. The KJV’s ‘unto the Messiah the Prince’ reads as a title; the Hebrew has no ‘the’, hence the ESV’s “an anointed one”.

verseByVerse.quote: And after the sixty-two weeks, an anointed one shall be cut off and shall have nothing. And the people of the prince who is to come shall destroy the city and the sanctuary. Its end shall come with a flood, and to the end there shall be war. Desolations are decreed.
verseByVerse.commentary:
After the sixty-two weeks the anointed one will be killed and left with nothing, and afterwards the city and sanctuary will be destroyed once more.

An anointed one shall be cut off. After the long wait, the anointed one comes, and then he is “cut off”, a phrase used of being killed. The Messiah would not come to be served but to die. He “shall have nothing”, dying apparently without kingdom, followers or success.

The death of Jesus. Christians have long seen here the death of Jesus. Isaiah had said of the suffering Servant, “who considered that he was cut off out of the land of the living, stricken for the transgression of my people?” (Isaiah 53:8). When Jesus hung on the cross, abandoned by his disciples, stripped of his clothes and mocked as a failed king, he truly had nothing. But by being cut off, he accomplished the very things verse 24 promised.

Shall destroy the city and the sanctuary. Jerusalem and its rebuilt temple will be destroyed again. Jesus wept over the city and foretold it: “they will not leave one stone upon another in you, because you did not know the time of your visitation” (Luke 19:44). In AD 70, about forty years after the crucifixion, Roman armies under the general Titus did exactly that. The city that rejected its Messiah lost its temple, and the temple has never been rebuilt.

Uncertain wording. “Shall have nothing” renders a terse Hebrew phrase, literally ‘and nothing to him’, which the ESV follows; the KJV reads ‘but not for himself’. The ESV also notes that “Its end” can be read ‘His end’.
verseByVerse.note: On the traditional Christian reading, the anointed one cut off is Jesus in his death, and the destruction that follows is Jerusalem’s fall in AD 70.

verseByVerse.quote: And he shall make a strong covenant with many for one week, and for half of the week he shall put an end to sacrifice and offering. And on the wing of abominations shall come one who makes desolate, until the decreed end is poured out on the desolator."
verseByVerse.commentary:
In the final week a strong covenant is made with many and sacrifice is brought to an end, and the one who makes desolate will himself meet the end God has decreed.

For one week. The final week is the hardest part of the passage, and here Christians differ most. The key question is who “he” is at the start of the verse (see below).

Where the chapter began. Think of where this chapter began. Daniel was praying about seventy years and a ruined city. God answered with the promise of a far greater deliverance: not only the return of exiles to Jerusalem, but the coming of the Anointed One who would deal with sin itself. “But when the fullness of time had come, God sent forth his Son” (Galatians 4:4). And when Jesus began to preach, his first words were, “The time is fulfilled” (Mark 1:15).

Where Christians differ. There are three main answers. The first is the Messiah. Many in the Reformed tradition, and many Christians before them, take “he” to be the anointed one of verses 25–26. Jesus is then the one who makes a strong covenant with many, through his blood: “this is my blood of the covenant, which is poured out for many for the forgiveness of sins” (Matthew 26:28). By his death, partway through that final week, he puts an end to sacrifice and offering: after his once-for-all sacrifice the temple offerings had no more purpose, and within a generation they ceased for ever. The one who makes desolate is then the Roman power that came against Jerusalem, and God’s judgment will finally fall on the desolator too. Jesus spoke of “the abomination of desolation spoken of by the prophet Daniel” and linked it with the coming destruction of Jerusalem (Matthew 24:15; Luke 21:20).

A future ruler. Many other Christians, especially dispensationalists (who read God’s dealings with Israel and with the church as separate stages of history), take “he” to be “the prince who is to come” of verse 26, a future antichrist. On this reading the first sixty-nine weeks ended with Christ’s first coming, and then comes a gap, the present church age, not counted in the prophecy. The seventieth week is still future: seven years at the end of history, when the antichrist will make a treaty with Israel, break it halfway through, stop the temple sacrifices and set up an abomination, before Christ returns to destroy him. Its reasons deserve a hearing: the prince who is to come is the nearest person named before “he”; Jesus spoke of the abomination of desolation as still to come in his day (Matthew 24:15); and the goals of verse 24 are not yet seen in full in the world.

The second century. Most critical scholars, who date the book’s visions to about 165 BC, find the whole prophecy in the second century BC. The anointed one cut off is the high priest Onias III, murdered about 171 BC; the prince who is to come is Antiochus IV (see chapter 8); the last half-week is the roughly three years in which he stopped the sacrifices and set up a pagan altar in the temple (11:31); and the most holy place is anointed when the temple is rededicated in 164 BC. Its strength is that chapters 8 and 11 describe Antiochus in similar words. Its weaknesses: 490 years from the exile overshoot the 160s BC by decades, and atonement and everlasting righteousness did not arrive in 164 BC. Some interpreters, again, take the numbers symbolically, as a complete period stretching from the return from exile to the end of all things.

This commentary’s view. This commentary follows the first reading, because it best explains the six great goals of verse 24, needs no gap that the text itself does not mention, and fits the way the New Testament speaks of Christ’s covenant and sacrifice and of Jerusalem’s fall. But faithful Christians hold the other views, and we should hold our differences with humility. Nor should anyone use these weeks to set a date for Christ’s return: of that day, Jesus said, no one knows (Matthew 24:36). All Christians can agree on the most important thing: God decreed the time of the Messiah, who would be cut off, and through his death sin would be atoned for and everlasting righteousness brought in.

Uncertain wording. “On the wing of abominations” is one of the most obscure phrases in the book, and translations differ widely. ‘Wing’ may mean a pinnacle or corner of the temple, or the outspread reach of the desolating power. What is clear is that a desolating outrage comes, and that it too has a “decreed end”.

9.title: Seventy Weeks
9.overview:
Where we are. It is the first year of Darius the Mede, 539 or 538 BC. Babylon has fallen in a single night (chapter 5), Daniel is now an old man, and the seventy years of exile foretold by Jeremiah are almost complete. Between two visions stands one of the great prayers of the Bible.

The message. God keeps his word, his warnings and his promises alike, and the only ground on which sinners can ask him for anything is his great mercy. Daniel brings nothing but confession and need; God answers before he has finished, tells him he is greatly loved, and reveals that the deeper exile, sin itself, will be dealt with by an Anointed One who is cut off.

Why it was said. The exiles needed to know why the disaster had come and whether there was any way back (see the introduction). The chapter answers both: the exile was God’s just and announced judgment, and restoration rests on his mercy alone.

How the chapter makes its case. Reading Jeremiah, Daniel sees that the seventy years are nearly done (vv. 1–2). He confesses Israel’s sin without excuse and declares God righteous in every curse that has fallen (vv. 3–14), then pleads for the city and sanctuary “because of your great mercy” (vv. 15–19). Gabriel arrives at the hour of the evening sacrifice with an answer sent at the prayer’s first word (vv. 20–23). Then God answers seventy years with seventy weeks: a decreed time in which an anointed one will come and be cut off, sin will be atoned for, everlasting righteousness brought in, and the city and sanctuary destroyed once more (vv. 24–27).

Where it leads. To Christ by direct promise. The goals of verse 24, to finish transgression, put an end to sin, atone for iniquity and bring in everlasting righteousness, are what no temple sacrifice achieved and what Christ did when he came “to put away sin by the sacrifice of himself” (Hebrews 9:26). The anointed one who is cut off and has nothing is the crucified Messiah, whose covenant blood was poured out for many (Matthew 26:28). The prayer also points to him by pattern: the righteous man who confesses his people’s sin as his own foreshadows the sinless one who bore it, and Daniel’s plea to mercy alone is answered at the cross, where God is “just and the justifier of the one who has faith in Jesus” (Romans 3:26).

For us. Let God’s promises send you to prayer rather than to idle waiting. Confess honestly, without excuse and without despair, because no one comes to God on their own record; and after every honest confession, hear heaven’s word to all who are in Christ: you are greatly loved.
9.theology:
God's promises in Scripture do not make prayer unnecessary but move his people to pray with confidence (vv. 1-3; Jer 29:10-13).

True confession honors God's righteousness, owns sin without excuse, identifies with God's people and pleads only God's mercy and the honor of his name (vv. 4-19; Lev 26:40-42; Luke 18:13; Ezra 9:6; Neh 1:6).

God keeps every word he has spoken, both his warnings and his promises (vv. 11-14).

God hears his people from the first word of their prayer and receives repentant sinners as greatly loved (v. 23; Matt 6:8; Heb 4:16).

God decreed the time of the Messiah, who would be cut off to finish transgression, atone for iniquity and bring in everlasting righteousness (vv. 24-26; Isa 53:8, 12; Heb 9:12, 26; Rom 3:25-26; Gal 4:4; Mark 1:15).

Christ made the new covenant with many by his blood and ended the need for sacrifice; the city that rejected him was destroyed (vv. 26-27; Matt 26:28; Luke 19:43-44; 21:20; Matt 24:15).

Christians differ on the timing of the seventieth week and should hold their views with humility, while agreeing on the heart of the prophecy: the Messiah's atoning death (vv. 24-27).
9.examples: An old man reads Jeremiah, does the arithmetic and puts on sackcloth in conquered Babylon. The most blameless man in Babylon prays "We have sinned" and pleads nothing but God's great mercy, at the hour of a sacrifice no longer offered. The answer is sent before he has finished, and it begins, "You are greatly loved." And at the end of the chapter stands an Anointed One, cut off, having nothing, and accomplishing everything.

keyVerse.quote: O my God, incline your ear and hear. Open your eyes and see our desolations, and the city that is called by your name. For we do not present our pleas before you because of our righteousness, but because of your great mercy.
keyVerse.note: Here is the heart of Daniel’s prayer and the heart of the gospel: sinners come to God on the ground of his mercy, never on their own record. One of the most faithful men in Scripture brings nothing but his need, and God answers with the promise of an Anointed One whose death would make that mercy just.

9.reflection:
Reading God’s promise in Jeremiah sent Daniel to prayer rather than to idle waiting (vv. 2–3). Which of God’s promises could you turn into prayer this week? Why do we so often treat God’s sovereignty as a reason not to pray?

Daniel, whose enemies could find no fault in him, prays “we have sinned” (v. 5). What would it look like to confess the sins of our church, family or nation without either indifference or self-righteous accusation?

“We do not present our pleas before you because of our righteousness, but because of your great mercy” (v. 18). Where are you tempted to come to God on your own record, good or bad? How does the cross show that God’s mercy and his justice meet?

Christians read the seventy weeks in different ways, yet all can agree that an Anointed One was cut off to atone for iniquity (vv. 24–26). How does seeing Jesus here strengthen your confidence that God keeps his word, and your humility about the details?

10.text: <sup>1</sup>In the third year of Cyrus king of Persia a word was revealed to Daniel, who was named Belteshazzar. And the word was true, and it was a great conflict. And he understood the word and had understanding of the vision.<sup>2</sup>In those days I, Daniel, was mourning for three weeks.<sup>3</sup>I ate no delicacies, no meat or wine entered my mouth, nor did I anoint myself at all, for the full three weeks.<sup>4</sup>On the twenty-fourth day of the first month, as I was standing on the bank of the great river (that is, the Tigris)<sup>5</sup>I lifted up my eyes and looked, and behold, a man clothed in linen, with a belt of fine gold from Uphaz around his waist.<sup>6</sup>His body was like beryl, his face like the appearance of lightning, his eyes like flaming torches, his arms and legs like the gleam of burnished bronze, and the sound of his words like the sound of a multitude.<sup>7</sup>And I, Daniel, alone saw the vision, for the men who were with me did not see the vision, but a great trembling fell upon them, and they fled to hide themselves.<sup>8</sup>So I was left alone and saw this great vision, and no strength was left in me. My radiant appearance was fearfully changed, and I retained no strength.<sup>9</sup>Then I heard the sound of his words, and as I heard the sound of his words, I fell on my face in deep sleep with my face to the ground.<sup>10</sup>And behold, a hand touched me and set me trembling on my hands and knees.<sup>11</sup>And he said to me, "O Daniel, man greatly loved, understand the words that I speak to you, and stand upright, for now I have been sent to you." And when he had spoken this word to me, I stood up trembling.<sup>12</sup>Then he said to me, "Fear not, Daniel, for from the first day that you set your heart to understand and humbled yourself before your God, your words have been heard, and I have come because of your words.<sup>13</sup>The prince of the kingdom of Persia withstood me twenty-one days, but Michael, one of the chief princes, came to help me, for I was left there with the kings of Persia,<sup>14</sup>and came to make you understand what is to happen to your people in the latter days. For the vision is for days yet to come."<sup>15</sup>When he had spoken to me according to these words, I turned my face toward the ground and was mute.<sup>16</sup>And behold, one in the likeness of the children of man touched my lips. Then I opened my mouth and spoke. I said to him who stood before me, "O my lord, by reason of the vision pains have come upon me, and I retain no strength.<sup>17</sup>How can my lord's servant talk with my lord? For now no strength remains in me, and no breath is left in me."<sup>18</sup>Again one having the appearance of a man touched me and strengthened me.<sup>19</sup>And he said, "O man greatly loved, fear not, peace be with you; be strong and of good courage." And as he spoke to me, I was strengthened and said, "Let my lord speak, for you have strengthened me."<sup>20</sup>Then he said, "Do you know why I have come to you? But now I will return to fight against the prince of Persia; and when I go out, behold, the prince of Greece will come.<sup>21</sup>But I will tell you what is inscribed in the book of truth: there is none who contends by my side against these except Michael, your prince.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–9 — The Man Clothed in Linen
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Before Daniel hears about the conflicts to come, he is shown the glory of the Lord who rules them. In 536 BC, two years after the exiles were freed, a true word comes to the old man about a great conflict (v. 1). He has been mourning and fasting for three weeks, through the days of Passover (vv. 2–3). Then, by the Tigris, he sees a man clothed in linen, with a belt of gold, a body like a jewel, a face like lightning, eyes like torches and a voice like a multitude (vv. 4–6). His companions flee in terror without seeing anything; Daniel, left alone, loses all his strength and falls face down (vv. 7–9).
verseByVerse.theology: Behind the events of history stands a glory that overwhelms human strength.

verseByVerse.quote: In the third year of Cyrus king of Persia a word was revealed to Daniel, who was named Belteshazzar. And the word was true, and it was a great conflict. And he understood the word and had understanding of the vision. In those days I, Daniel, was mourning for three weeks. I ate no delicacies, no meat or wine entered my mouth, nor did I anoint myself at all, for the full three weeks.
verseByVerse.commentary:
After three weeks of mourning for his people, the aged Daniel, still far from Jerusalem, receives a true word about a great conflict.

The last vision. Chapters 10–12 are one long vision, the last and longest in the book: chapter 10 sets the scene, chapter 11 gives the message and chapter 12 closes it.

In the third year of Cyrus king of Persia. The date is about 536 BC. Two years earlier Cyrus had allowed the Jews to go home, “that the word of the LORD by the mouth of Jeremiah might be fulfilled” (Ezra 1:1). Many had returned to Jerusalem. Daniel, now probably in his eighties, had not; he was still in Babylon or its region. The prayer of chapter 9 had been answered, but not all of God’s people had gone home.

I, Daniel, was mourning for three weeks. Daniel does not say why he was mourning, but we know what was happening in Jerusalem. The returned exiles had begun to rebuild the temple, and their enemies “discouraged the people of Judah and made them afraid to build” (Ezra 4:4). The great return was turning into a struggle, and news of it may have broken Daniel’s heart.

I ate no delicacies. His fast was partial. He gave up delicacies, meat, wine and the oil people used to refresh their skin. This sheds light on chapter 1. There, as a young man, Daniel refused the king’s food and wine; here, as an old man, he gives up meat and wine for a special season of mourning. His refusal in chapter 1 was not about meat and wine as such. It was about eating from that king’s table.

Is this the “Daniel fast”? Daniel fasted in mourning for his people, not for his health. The New Testament sets no diet for spiritual growth, and fasting is a voluntary humbling before God, done in secret (Matthew 6:16–18). A simple diet adopted for prayer is fine; treating it as a spiritual formula is not.

Uncertain wording. “It was a great conflict” renders a very brief Hebrew phrase. The ESV notes that it could mean ‘it was about a great conflict’, and older translations took it quite differently (the KJV has ‘the time appointed was long’). The reading of most modern translations fits what follows: the vision concerns war between the kingdoms of the earth and, as this chapter shows, in the unseen world behind them.
verseByVerse.note: The third year of Cyrus was 536 BC. The Tigris (v. 4) was the great river east of Babylon.

verseByVerse.quote: On the twenty-fourth day of the first month, as I was standing on the bank of the great river (that is, the Tigris) I lifted up my eyes and looked, and behold, a man clothed in linen, with a belt of fine gold from Uphaz around his waist. His body was like beryl, his face like the appearance of lightning, his eyes like flaming torches, his arms and legs like the gleam of burnished bronze, and the sound of his words like the sound of a multitude.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Just after the Passover season, by the Tigris, Daniel sees a man clothed in linen, shining with a glory beyond anything on earth.

On the twenty-fourth day of the first month. The first month was the month of Passover and the Feast of Unleavened Bread, which ran from the fourteenth to the twenty-first day (Exodus 12:18). Daniel’s three weeks of fasting covered the very days when Israel celebrated its deliverance from Egypt. Far from Jerusalem, instead of feasting, he mourned and prayed. Three days after the feast ended, the answer came.

A man clothed in linen. Linen was the clothing of priests and of heavenly beings; the belt of fine gold signals royalty. His body shines like a precious stone, his face flashes like lightning, his eyes blaze like torches, his limbs gleam like polished bronze, and his voice sounds like the roar of a crowd.

The same figure in Revelation. Readers of Revelation will recognise this description. John saw the risen Christ with eyes “like a flame of fire”, and “his feet were like burnished bronze, refined in a furnace, and his voice was like the roar of many waters” (Revelation 1:14–15). Whether this is Christ himself or a messenger reflecting his glory, the lesson is the same: behind the great conflict stands a Lord of unimaginable majesty.

Where Christians differ. Many Christians believe the man clothed in linen was the Son of God himself, appearing before his birth in Bethlehem, because John sees the same glory in the risen Christ. Others believe he was a mighty angel, noting that the one who speaks to Daniel in verses 11–14 had to be helped by Michael against the prince of Persia, which seems unlike the Son of God. Some suggest that the glorious figure of verses 5–6 and the messenger of verses 10–21 are two different beings.

This commentary’s view. The text does not settle the question, but this commentary judges the best reading to be that the glorious figure of verses 5–6 is the Son of God before he became man, and that the angel who speaks to Daniel in verses 10–21 is another, a messenger who needs Michael’s help.

Uncertain wording. Two details cannot be pinned down. Uphaz, named for its gold here and in Jeremiah 10:9, is an unknown place; some think it is another name for Ophir, famous for its gold. And the stone translated “beryl” (Hebrew tarshish) cannot be identified with certainty; it was some gleaming precious stone.

verseByVerse.quote: And I, Daniel, alone saw the vision, for the men who were with me did not see the vision, but a great trembling fell upon them, and they fled to hide themselves. So I was left alone and saw this great vision, and no strength was left in me. My radiant appearance was fearfully changed, and I retained no strength. Then I heard the sound of his words, and as I heard the sound of his words, I fell on my face in deep sleep with my face to the ground.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Daniel alone sees the vision; his companions flee in terror, and before such glory his own strength and dignity collapse.

The men who were with me did not see the vision. Daniel’s companions saw nothing, but they felt something, and they ran. The same happened when the risen Jesus met Saul on the road to Damascus: “The men who were traveling with him stood speechless, hearing the voice but seeing no one” (Acts 9:7). God’s presence can be real and terrifying even to those who do not see it.

So I was left alone. Daniel’s strength drains away. The ESV notes that the Hebrew says ‘My splendor was changed to ruin’. Whatever dignity and health he had as a great official of the empire collapsed in a moment. Before true glory, human glory disappears. Isaiah said the same when he saw the LORD: “Woe is me! For I am lost” (Isaiah 6:5).

I fell on my face in deep sleep. Daniel collapses face down, overwhelmed into a kind of faint. People imagine meeting God with comfort and excitement; the Bible shows them falling down. We need to recover a sense of God’s holiness. The one we worship is not a friendly idea but the glorious Lord of heaven.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 10–21 — Fear Not, Man Greatly Loved
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The God whose glory knocks his servants down lifts them up again by his touch and his word. A hand sets the trembling Daniel on his knees, and a voice calls him “man greatly loved” and tells him that his prayer was heard from the first day (vv. 10–12). The answer was delayed because the prince of the kingdom of Persia, an unseen power, resisted God’s messenger for twenty-one days until Michael came to help (vv. 13–14). Twice more Daniel is touched: his lips are opened, and he is strengthened with peace (vv. 15–19). The messenger must return to the fight, with the prince of Greece still to come; but what will happen is already written in the book of truth, and Michael stands with Daniel’s people (vv. 20–21).
verseByVerse.theology: Prayer is heard at once, even when the answer is delayed by a spiritual conflict God's people cannot see.

verseByVerse.quote: And behold, a hand touched me and set me trembling on my hands and knees. And he said to me, "O Daniel, man greatly loved, understand the words that I speak to you, and stand upright, for now I have been sent to you." And when he had spoken this word to me, I stood up trembling. Then he said to me, "Fear not, Daniel, for from the first day that you set your heart to understand and humbled yourself before your God, your words have been heard, and I have come because of your words.
verseByVerse.commentary:
A touch and a word lift Daniel up: he is greatly loved, and his humble prayer was heard from the first day.

A hand touched me. Step by step Daniel is raised. A hand lifts him to his hands and knees; then a word lifts him to his feet. And the first thing he hears, as in 9:23, is that he is “greatly loved”. When the disciples fell on their faces at the transfiguration, “Jesus came and touched them, saying, ‘Rise, and have no fear’” (Matthew 17:7). The God whose glory knocks us down is the God whose love lifts us up.

Your words have been heard. Daniel’s prayer was heard “from the first day”. God did not wait three weeks to listen; the answer was slow to arrive, but God had been listening from the start.

Humbled yourself before your God. The kind of prayer that was heard matters. Daniel set his heart to understand, seeking God’s truth, and he humbled himself before his God. God is near to those who seek him humbly: “The LORD is near to the brokenhearted and saves the crushed in spirit” (Psalm 34:18).

verseByVerse.quote: The prince of the kingdom of Persia withstood me twenty-one days, but Michael, one of the chief princes, came to help me, for I was left there with the kings of Persia, and came to make you understand what is to happen to your people in the latter days. For the vision is for days yet to come."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The answer was delayed because an evil power behind Persia resisted God’s messenger until Michael came to help: history has an unseen side.

The prince of the kingdom of Persia. Here the curtain is pulled back on something the Bible rarely shows. This prince cannot be the human king of Persia, for no human king could hold back an angel from heaven. He is a spiritual being, an evil power working behind the empire of Persia. Against him comes “Michael, one of the chief princes”, a great angel. The New Testament calls him “the archangel Michael” (Jude 9), and Revelation shows “Michael and his angels fighting against the dragon” (Revelation 12:7).

What is to happen to your people in the latter days. The visit is to explain the future of Daniel’s people, the message of chapters 11 and 12.

What does this mean for us? Paul says, “we do not wrestle against flesh and blood, but against the rulers, against the authorities, against the cosmic powers over this present darkness, against the spiritual forces of evil in the heavenly places” (Ephesians 6:12). The conflicts of history are not only political. There are spiritual powers at work behind nations and cultures, opposing God’s purposes and God’s people.

Not beyond Scripture. We must not go beyond what the Bible says. Scripture gives very few details about these powers, and it never tells us to identify them, map them or speak to them. It tells us to pray, as Daniel did. And it tells us that Christ has already won the decisive victory: “He disarmed the rulers and authorities and put them to open shame, by triumphing over them in him” (Colossians 2:15).

Why did the answer take three weeks? Because the prince of Persia resisted God’s messenger for twenty-one days, exactly the length of Daniel’s fast. Was God struggling to get through? No. The messenger was hindered, not God; the answer came at the time God appointed, and the hindrance was overcome by God’s servant Michael. The delay was real, but it was never outside God’s rule. So a slow answer is no reason to stop praying. Daniel kept seeking God for the full three weeks, and Jesus told his disciples “that they ought always to pray and not lose heart” (Luke 18:1).

Uncertain wording. “For I was left there with the kings of Persia” is a compressed phrase whose exact sense is uncertain. It probably means that the messenger had been held there, contending with the powers behind Persia, until Michael came to relieve him and set him free to come to Daniel.
verseByVerse.note: Michael is the archangel who guards Israel.

verseByVerse.quote: When he had spoken to me according to these words, I turned my face toward the ground and was mute. And behold, one in the likeness of the children of man touched my lips. Then I opened my mouth and spoke. I said to him who stood before me, "O my lord, by reason of the vision pains have come upon me, and I retain no strength. How can my lord's servant talk with my lord? For now no strength remains in me, and no breath is left in me."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Speechless again, Daniel is touched on the lips and confesses that he has no strength left.

One in the likeness of the children of man touched my lips. Once again Daniel is overwhelmed and cannot speak. A touch opens his lips, as a seraph (one of the heavenly beings at God’s throne) touched Isaiah’s lips before he was sent to speak (Isaiah 6:7). The messenger has “the likeness of the children of man”: he comes in a form Daniel can bear.

No strength remains in me. Daniel is honest about his weakness: no strength, no breath. He does not pretend to be a spiritual hero. And that is exactly the kind of person God strengthens: “My power is made perfect in weakness” (2 Corinthians 12:9).

verseByVerse.quote: Again one having the appearance of a man touched me and strengthened me. And he said, "O man greatly loved, fear not, peace be with you; be strong and of good courage." And as he spoke to me, I was strengthened and said, "Let my lord speak, for you have strengthened me."
verseByVerse.commentary:
A third touch and a word of peace give Daniel strength, and, strengthened by that word, he is ready to listen.

Fear not, peace be with you; be strong and of good courage. A third touch, and a word of peace. These words gather up the encouragement God had given his servants for centuries. Joshua heard, “Be strong and courageous. Do not be frightened” (Joshua 1:9). And the risen Jesus would stand among his frightened disciples and say, “Peace be with you” (John 20:19).

As he spoke to me, I was strengthened. Daniel was not strengthened by trying harder. God’s word itself gave him strength, and that is still how God strengthens his people. Daniel’s response is the right one: “Let my lord speak”. Once God had given him strength, he was ready to listen.

verseByVerse.quote: Then he said, "Do you know why I have come to you? But now I will return to fight against the prince of Persia; and when I go out, behold, the prince of Greece will come. But I will tell you what is inscribed in the book of truth: there is none who contends by my side against these except Michael, your prince.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The unseen conflict goes on as empires rise and fall, but its outcome is written in God’s book, and God’s people have a champion.

The prince of Greece will come. The messenger must go back to the fight, for the spiritual power behind Persia is still resisting. And after Persia, “the prince of Greece will come”. As the kingdoms of the earth rise and fall, the unseen conflict moves on with them. Chapter 11 will show the earthly side of the same struggle.

The book of truth. This is God’s own record of what will happen. The future is not uncertain to God; it is already written in his book. The psalmist says, “in your book were written, every one of them, the days that were formed for me” (Psalm 139:16).

Michael, your prince. Michael is the angel who has charge of Daniel’s people (12:1). God’s people are not alone in the conflict. When Elisha’s servant was afraid, he heard, “those who are with us are more than those who are with them”, and was shown that “the mountain was full of horses and chariots of fire all around Elisha” (2 Kings 6:16–17).

Greater comfort in Christ. For the Christian the comfort is even greater. We are not only protected by angels; we belong to Christ, who has triumphed over every power. “Little children, you are from God and have overcome them, for he who is in you is greater than he who is in the world” (1 John 4:4). Nothing in this unseen war, “nor angels nor rulers … nor powers”, “will be able to separate us from the love of God in Christ Jesus our Lord” (Romans 8:38–39).

10.title: A Great Conflict
10.overview:
Where we are. Chapters 10–12 are one long final vision, and chapter 10 sets its scene. It is the third year of Cyrus, about 536 BC. The exiles have been free to go home for two years and many have gone, but Daniel, now in his eighties, is still in the east, and the rebuilding in Jerusalem is meeting stubborn opposition.

The message. Behind the wars of nations there is an unseen war, but it is not an equal fight, and God’s people are not forgotten in it. The Lord of overwhelming glory hears humble prayer from the first day, sends his help even when it seems delayed, and lifts up and strengthens the weak by his touch and his word: “O man greatly loved, fear not”.

Why it was said. The returned exiles were few, discouraged and opposed (Ezra 4:4), and the faithful still scattered through the empire could wonder whether their prayers reached God at all (see the introduction). This chapter shows them the real battle and the real God.

How the chapter makes its case. After three weeks of mourning and fasting, Daniel sees by the Tigris a man clothed in linen, blazing with glory, and falls to the ground drained of strength while his companions flee (vv. 1–9). A hand lifts him to his knees, and a voice tells him that he is greatly loved and that his prayer was heard from the first day, though the messenger was withstood twenty-one days by the prince of Persia until Michael came to help (vv. 10–14). Twice more Daniel is touched and given speech and strength (vv. 15–19), and he learns that the conflict goes on, with the prince of Greece still to come and Michael standing for God’s people (vv. 20–21).

Where it leads. To Christ by the revelation of his glory and his victory. This commentary takes the glorious man of verses 5–6 as the Son of God before his incarnation, for John saw the same eyes like fire, feet like burnished bronze and mighty voice in the risen Christ (Revelation 1:14–15). And the Lord whose glory struck John down laid his right hand on him and said, “Fear not” (Revelation 1:17), as Daniel was lifted and told to fear not. The unseen powers that resisted God’s messenger were disarmed at the cross, where Christ triumphed over them (Colossians 2:15).

For us. Our struggles are not only what they seem, but the answer to the unseen war is not technique but humble, persevering prayer. A delay is not deafness, so keep praying. And when God’s holiness or the weight of the future leaves you weak, listen for his word, for it is by his speaking that his people are strengthened.
10.theology:
Mourning and humble prayer over the condition of God's people are pleasing to God (vv. 2-3, 12; Ps 34:18).

The glory of God and his messengers overwhelms human strength, and it foreshadows the glory of the risen Christ (vv. 5-9; Rev 1:13-17; Isa 6:5; Acts 9:7).

God lifts up those his glory has humbled, speaking love, peace and strength through his word (vv. 10-11, 18-19; Matt 17:6-7; Josh 1:9; John 20:19; 2 Cor 12:9).

Prayer is heard from the first day, even when the answer is delayed (v. 12; Luke 18:1).

Behind the nations are spiritual powers opposed to God, but God's angels contend for his people, and Christ has triumphed over every power (vv. 13, 20-21; Eph 6:12; Col 2:15; Jude 9; Rev 12:7; 2 Kgs 6:16-17).

The future is written in God's book of truth, and nothing can separate his people from his love (v. 21; Ps 139:16; 1 John 4:4; Rom 8:38-39).
10.examples: An old man fasts through the Passover season and sees, on the bank of the Tigris, a figure with a face like lightning; his companions see nothing and run anyway. Three touches lift the fallen man to his feet. His prayer was heard on the first day and answered three weeks later, because an evil spiritual power behind the Persian empire had resisted the messenger. And the man who could not speak says at last, "Let my lord speak, for you have strengthened me."

keyVerse.quote: And he said, “O man greatly loved, fear not, peace be with you; be strong and of good courage.” And as he spoke to me, I was strengthened and said, “Let my lord speak, for you have strengthened me.”
keyVerse.note: The chapter shows a glory that leaves Daniel without strength and an unseen war that delays God’s answer, and this verse shows how God deals with his weak servants in the middle of both. He tells them they are loved, gives them peace, and strengthens them by speaking to them, so that they are ready to hear the rest of his word.

10.reflection:
Daniel’s prayer was heard “from the first day”, yet the answer took three weeks to arrive (vv. 12–13). How does this help you when your prayers seem to go unanswered?

Verse 13 pulls back the curtain on spiritual powers behind the nations. How does knowing about this unseen conflict change the way you see the troubles of your world? Why do you think Scripture points us to prayer and to Christ’s victory rather than to techniques for fighting these powers?

Before the glorious man Daniel fell to the ground, drained of strength (vv. 8–9). What would it mean to recover a sense of God’s holiness in our worship, and how does Christ’s touch and his “fear not” keep that awe from becoming terror?

Daniel was strengthened as the messenger spoke to him (vv. 18–19). When has God strengthened you through his word, and how could you make more room to hear it?

11.text: <sup>1</sup>"And as for me, in the first year of Darius the Mede, I stood up to confirm and strengthen him.<sup>2</sup>"And now I will show you the truth. Behold, three more kings shall arise in Persia, and a fourth shall be far richer than all of them. And when he has become strong through his riches, he shall stir up all against the kingdom of Greece.<sup>3</sup>Then a mighty king shall arise, who shall rule with great dominion and do as he wills.<sup>4</sup>And as soon as he has arisen, his kingdom shall be broken and divided toward the four winds of heaven, but not to his posterity, nor according to the authority with which he ruled, for his kingdom shall be plucked up and go to others besides these.<sup>5</sup>"Then the king of the south shall be strong, but one of his princes shall be stronger than he and shall rule, and his authority shall be a great authority.<sup>6</sup>After some years they shall make an alliance, and the daughter of the king of the south shall come to the king of the north to make an agreement. But she shall not retain the strength of her arm, and he and his arm shall not endure, but she shall be given up, and her attendants, he who fathered her, and he who supported her in those times.<sup>7</sup>"And from a branch from her roots one shall arise in his place. He shall come against the army and enter the fortress of the king of the north, and he shall deal with them and shall prevail.<sup>8</sup>He shall also carry off to Egypt their gods with their metal images and their precious vessels of silver and gold, and for some years he shall refrain from attacking the king of the north.<sup>9</sup>Then the latter shall come into the realm of the king of the south but shall return to his own land.<sup>10</sup>"His sons shall wage war and assemble a multitude of great forces, which shall keep coming and overflow and pass through, and again shall carry the war as far as his fortress.<sup>11</sup>Then the king of the south, moved with rage, shall come out and fight against the king of the north. And he shall raise a great multitude, but it shall be given into his hand.<sup>12</sup>And when the multitude is taken away, his heart shall be exalted, and he shall cast down tens of thousands, but he shall not prevail.<sup>13</sup>For the king of the north shall again raise a multitude, greater than the first. And after some years he shall come on with a great army and abundant supplies.<sup>14</sup>"In those times many shall rise against the king of the south, and the violent among your own people shall lift themselves up in order to fulfill the vision, but they shall fail.<sup>15</sup>Then the king of the north shall come and throw up siegeworks and take a well-fortified city. And the forces of the south shall not stand, or even his best troops, for there shall be no strength to stand.<sup>16</sup>But he who comes against him shall do as he wills, and none shall stand before him. And he shall stand in the glorious land, with destruction in his hand.<sup>17</sup>He shall set his face to come with the strength of his whole kingdom, and he shall bring terms of an agreement and perform them. He shall give him the daughter of women to destroy the kingdom, but it shall not stand or be to his advantage.<sup>18</sup>Afterward he shall turn his face to the coastlands and shall capture many of them, but a commander shall put an end to his insolence. Indeed, he shall turn his insolence back upon him.<sup>19</sup>Then he shall turn his face back toward the fortresses of his own land, but he shall stumble and fall, and shall not be found.<sup>20</sup>"Then shall arise in his place one who shall send an exactor of tribute for the glory of the kingdom. But within a few days he shall be broken, neither in anger nor in battle.<sup>21</sup>In his place shall arise a contemptible person to whom royal majesty has not been given. He shall come in without warning and obtain the kingdom by flatteries.<sup>22</sup>Armies shall be utterly swept away before him and broken, even the prince of the covenant.<sup>23</sup>And from the time that an alliance is made with him he shall act deceitfully, and he shall become strong with a small people.<sup>24</sup>Without warning he shall come into the richest parts of the province, and he shall do what neither his fathers nor his fathers' fathers have done, scattering among them plunder, spoil, and goods. He shall devise plans against strongholds, but only for a time.<sup>25</sup>And he shall stir up his power and his heart against the king of the south with a great army. And the king of the south shall wage war with an exceedingly great and mighty army, but he shall not stand, for plots shall be devised against him.<sup>26</sup>Even those who eat his food shall break him. His army shall be swept away, and many shall fall down slain.<sup>27</sup>And as for the two kings, their hearts shall be bent on doing evil. They shall speak lies at the same table, but to no avail, for the end is yet to be at the time appointed.<sup>28</sup>And he shall return to his land with great wealth, but his heart shall be set against the holy covenant. And he shall work his will and return to his own land.<sup>29</sup>"At the time appointed he shall return and come into the south, but it shall not be this time as it was before.<sup>30</sup>For ships of Kittim shall come against him, and he shall be afraid and withdraw, and shall turn back and be enraged and take action against the holy covenant. He shall turn back and pay attention to those who forsake the holy covenant.<sup>31</sup>Forces from him shall appear and profane the temple and fortress, and shall take away the regular burnt offering. And they shall set up the abomination that makes desolate.<sup>32</sup>He shall seduce with flattery those who violate the covenant, but the people who know their God shall stand firm and take action.<sup>33</sup>And the wise among the people shall make many understand, though for some days they shall stumble by sword and flame, by captivity and plunder.<sup>34</sup>When they stumble, they shall receive a little help. And many shall join themselves to them with flattery,<sup>35</sup>and some of the wise shall stumble, so that they may be refined, purified, and made white, until the time of the end, for it still awaits the appointed time.<sup>36</sup>"And the king shall do as he wills. He shall exalt himself and magnify himself above every god, and shall speak astonishing things against the God of gods. He shall prosper till the indignation is accomplished; for what is decreed shall be done.<sup>37</sup>He shall pay no attention to the gods of his fathers, or to the one beloved by women. He shall not pay attention to any other god, for he shall magnify himself above all.<sup>38</sup>He shall honor the god of fortresses instead of these. A god whom his fathers did not know he shall honor with gold and silver, with precious stones and costly gifts.<sup>39</sup>He shall deal with the strongest fortresses with the help of a foreign god. Those who acknowledge him he shall load with honor. He shall make them rulers over many and shall divide the land for a price.<sup>40</sup>"At the time of the end, the king of the south shall attack him, but the king of the north shall rush upon him like a whirlwind, with chariots and horsemen, and with many ships. And he shall come into countries and shall overflow and pass through.<sup>41</sup>He shall come into the glorious land. And tens of thousands shall fall, but these shall be delivered out of his hand: Edom and Moab and the main part of the Ammonites.<sup>42</sup>He shall stretch out his hand against the countries, and the land of Egypt shall not escape.<sup>43</sup>He shall become ruler of the treasures of gold and of silver, and all the precious things of Egypt, and the Libyans and the Cushites shall follow in his train.<sup>44</sup>But news from the east and the north shall alarm him, and he shall go out with great fury to destroy and devote many to destruction.<sup>45</sup>And he shall pitch his palatial tents between the sea and the glorious holy mountain. Yet he shall come to his end, with none to help him.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God knows the course of empires before a single king is born. The angel who strengthened Michael (v. 1) begins to show Daniel “the truth”: after Cyrus three more Persian kings will reign, and then a fourth, far richer, whose wealth will drive him to attack Greece (v. 2). Greece will answer with a mighty king who does as he wills, but as soon as he has risen his kingdom will be broken and shared out to the four winds, not to his own descendants (vv. 3–4). In four verses two great empires come and go, exactly as God said, and none of them can keep what it has won.
verseByVerse.theology: God knows the course of empires before a single king is born.

verseByVerse.quote: "And as for me, in the first year of Darius the Mede, I stood up to confirm and strengthen him. "And now I will show you the truth. Behold, three more kings shall arise in Persia, and a fourth shall be far richer than all of them. And when he has become strong through his riches, he shall stir up all against the kingdom of Greece.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The messenger begins a long and astonishingly detailed preview of history, starting with Persia, so that Daniel’s people will know that God sees every king coming long before he arrives.

I stood up to confirm and strengthen him. The messenger of chapter 10 is still speaking (the chapter break falls in the middle of his speech). He reminds Daniel that he has been at work in the unseen conflict for some time (on “him”, see the Uncertain wording note below).

What kind of chapter this is. This is one of the most detailed prophecies of history in the Bible: more than three hundred years of wars, marriages and betrayals, told in advance. No king is named, but the events match the history so closely that readers have always been able to follow them. You need not memorise the details; the point is that God knew all of it beforehand.

Three more kings shall arise in Persia. After Cyrus came Cambyses, the short-lived Bardiya and Darius I, and then a fourth who was enormously wealthy. This fits Xerxes I (486–465 BC), who led a massive invasion of Greece in 480 BC. He is King Ahasuerus of the book of Esther, who “reigned from India to Ethiopia over 127 provinces” (Esther 1:1). His invasion failed, and the long feud between Persia and Greece set the stage for what came next.

Told beforehand. On the night before he died, Jesus told his disciples what was about to happen for the same reason: “I am telling you this now, before it takes place, that when it does take place you may believe that I am he” (John 13:19). The God who mapped the wars of the Ptolemies and Seleucids is the God who foretold his Son’s betrayal, death and rising, and kept his word to the letter.

Where Christians differ: was this written before or after the events? Because the detail grows sharper as it nears Antiochus IV in the 160s BC, most critical scholars, and some believing ones, date the book to about 165 BC. They add that verses 40–45 do not match how Antiochus died, which they take as a genuine prediction that failed, and that the book’s Hebrew and Aramaic, with three Greek names of instruments in chapter 3, fit a later time. Some also hold that detailed prediction cannot happen, though not all argue from that. This commentary’s view: Daniel received these visions in the sixth century BC, as the book presents them (8:1; 9:2; 10:2), though the date is debated (see the introduction). Jesus speaks of “the prophet Daniel” (Matthew 24:15). Copies among the Dead Sea Scrolls were made within about a century of 165 BC by a community that already treated the book as Scripture, hard to explain for a book only decades old. The Aramaic fits the official Aramaic of the Persian empire, and instrument names travelled early through trade. Verses 40–45 are not a failed guess about Antiochus but a look beyond him (see the note on vv. 36–39). And if God can tell the future, which Isaiah sets out as the very proof that he is God (Isaiah 46:9–10), detail is no difficulty: it is what the angel calls it, “the truth” (v. 2), shown beforehand.

Uncertain wording. Who “him” is in verse 1 is not certain. Since 10:21 has just named Michael as the one who contends at the messenger’s side, it is probably Michael, whom the messenger in turn supported. Some take it to mean King Darius, strengthened in the year Babylon fell. Either way the point stands: heaven was at work behind the empires.
verseByVerse.note: Chapter 11 traces in detail the wars of the “kings of the north” (the Seleucids of Syria) and “of the south” (the Ptolemies of Egypt) after Alexander.

verseByVerse.quote: Then a mighty king shall arise, who shall rule with great dominion and do as he wills. And as soon as he has arisen, his kingdom shall be broken and divided toward the four winds of heaven, but not to his posterity, nor according to the authority with which he ruled, for his kingdom shall be plucked up and go to others besides these.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Alexander the Great conquers the world and dies almost at once, and others carve up his empire: the mightiest human plans fall apart at God’s word.

Then a mighty king shall arise. This is Alexander the Great, the goat’s great horn of chapter 8 (8:5–8). More than a century after Xerxes attacked Greece, a Greek king overthrew Persia, ruled a vast empire and could “do as he wills”.

His kingdom shall be broken. “As soon as he has arisen”, he was gone: Alexander died in 323 BC, aged thirty-two. His half-brother and young son were both murdered within about fourteen years, and his generals divided his lands, “toward the four winds of heaven”. “Many are the plans in the mind of a man, but it is the purpose of the LORD that will stand” (Proverbs 19:21).

A kingdom not left to another. Alexander’s kingdom went “to others besides these”. Daniel has already been told of a kingdom that “shall never be destroyed, nor shall the kingdom be left to another people” (2:44). Christ’s kingdom has no crisis of succession: its King died, rose again and reigns for ever.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 5–20 — Kings of the North and the South
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The plans of kings rise and collapse, and God’s people live in the land between them. The kings of Egypt in the south and Syria in the north make a marriage alliance that ends in murder (vv. 5–6), invade each other’s lands and carry off each other’s gods (vv. 7–9), and raise ever larger armies, so that one proud victory is soon undone (vv. 10–13). Some of Daniel’s own people try to force the vision and fail, and the northern king takes the glorious land (vv. 14–16). His next schemes, a royal marriage and a western war, both backfire; a Roman commander humbles him and he dies plundering a temple, and his successor is soon struck down (vv. 17–20). Nothing these kings build lasts.
verseByVerse.theology: The plans of kings rise and collapse, and God's people live in the land between them.

verseByVerse.quote: "Then the king of the south shall be strong, but one of his princes shall be stronger than he and shall rule, and his authority shall be a great authority. After some years they shall make an alliance, and the daughter of the king of the south shall come to the king of the north to make an agreement. But she shall not retain the strength of her arm, and he and his arm shall not endure, but she shall be given up, and her attendants, he who fathered her, and he who supported her in those times.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The first peace between the two powers that would fight over Daniel’s land is sealed with a royal marriage, and it ends in murder: human treaties cannot secure lasting peace.

The king of the south. The prophecy now follows two of the kingdoms carved from Alexander’s empire, because they fought over the land of Israel between them. “The king of the south” means the Greek kings of Egypt, the Ptolemies; “the king of the north” means the Greek kings of Syria and the lands to the east, the Seleucids. For well over a century Judea was the prize and the battlefield in their wars.

One of his princes shall be stronger than he. The first king of the south was Ptolemy I. “One of his princes” was Seleucus I, who served for a time as a commander under Ptolemy and then built a far larger kingdom in the north.

The daughter of the king of the south. About 252 BC the Egyptian princess Berenice was married to the northern king Antiochus II, who divorced his first wife to marry her. Within a few years Antiochus was dead, and Berenice, her young son and her attendants were murdered; her father, the king of Egypt, had also died. Peace sealed with marriages and promises does not endure.

Uncertain wording. “He who fathered her” can also be read, from the same Hebrew letters, as ‘her child’, and some translations take it that way. Both fit what happened: her father died about this time, and her infant son was murdered with her.

verseByVerse.quote: "And from a branch from her roots one shall arise in his place. He shall come against the army and enter the fortress of the king of the north, and he shall deal with them and shall prevail. He shall also carry off to Egypt their gods with their metal images and their precious vessels of silver and gold, and for some years he shall refrain from attacking the king of the north. Then the latter shall come into the realm of the king of the south but shall return to his own land.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Berenice’s brother avenges her, sweeps north and carries the enemy’s gods home as plunder, while the northern king’s reply comes to nothing.

A branch from her roots. Berenice’s brother, Ptolemy III, came to the throne of Egypt. He invaded the northern kingdom to avenge his sister and won a great victory.

He shall also carry off to Egypt their gods. He returned with enormous plunder, including images of gods. Once again the gods of the nations can do nothing; they are carted off in wagons by whoever wins the latest war. Isaiah drew the contrast long before: idols have to be carried, but the living God carries his people (Isaiah 46:1–4).

But shall return to his own land. The northern king, Seleucus II, later struck back at Egypt but failed and went home.

verseByVerse.quote: "His sons shall wage war and assemble a multitude of great forces, which shall keep coming and overflow and pass through, and again shall carry the war as far as his fortress. Then the king of the south, moved with rage, shall come out and fight against the king of the north. And he shall raise a great multitude, but it shall be given into his hand. And when the multitude is taken away, his heart shall be exalted, and he shall cast down tens of thousands, but he shall not prevail. For the king of the north shall again raise a multitude, greater than the first. And after some years he shall come on with a great army and abundant supplies.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The wars swing back and forth: a proud Egyptian victory is wasted, and the beaten northern king returns stronger than before.

His sons shall wage war. The sons of the northern king, Seleucus III and then Antiochus III, known as Antiochus the Great, raised huge armies and pushed south toward Egypt’s frontier fortress.

His heart shall be exalted. In 217 BC, at Raphia near Gaza, the Egyptian king Ptolemy IV defeated Antiochus III and killed thousands of his soldiers. But, proud of his victory, he did not follow it up, and “he shall not prevail”. The win did not last.

The king of the north shall again raise a multitude. Antiochus III did not accept defeat. He spent the next years campaigning in the east, and when the Egyptian king died and left a young child on the throne, he came back with a larger army than before. So God’s people should never place their hope in the defeat of one tyrant: another will rise. Our hope is in the King who has already overcome the world (John 16:33).

verseByVerse.quote: "In those times many shall rise against the king of the south, and the violent among your own people shall lift themselves up in order to fulfill the vision, but they shall fail. Then the king of the north shall come and throw up siegeworks and take a well-fortified city. And the forces of the south shall not stand, or even his best troops, for there shall be no strength to stand. But he who comes against him shall do as he wills, and none shall stand before him. And he shall stand in the glorious land, with destruction in his hand.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Judea passes from Egyptian to Syrian rule, and those among Daniel’s people who try to force the vision come true only fail.

The violent among your own people. Egypt faced enemies on every side, and some of Daniel’s own people joined in, perhaps hoping to use the wars to win independence for Judea and so to “fulfill the vision” themselves. “But they shall fail.” God’s prophecies do not come true because people try to force them. Jesus refused the same shortcut when the crowd wanted to take him by force and make him king (John 6:15).

Throw up siegeworks and take a well-fortified city. Around 200 BC Antiochus III defeated the Egyptians at Panium, in the far north of Israel, and then besieged their army in the fortified coastal city of Sidon until it surrendered.

He shall stand in the glorious land. So “the glorious land”, Judea, passed from Egyptian to Syrian control. Daniel’s people now lived under a new master, and the stage was set for the persecution to come.

verseByVerse.quote: He shall set his face to come with the strength of his whole kingdom, and he shall bring terms of an agreement and perform them. He shall give him the daughter of women to destroy the kingdom, but it shall not stand or be to his advantage. Afterward he shall turn his face to the coastlands and shall capture many of them, but a commander shall put an end to his insolence. Indeed, he shall turn his insolence back upon him. Then he shall turn his face back toward the fortresses of his own land, but he shall stumble and fall, and shall not be found.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Antiochus the Great tries to win Egypt by a marriage and the west by conquest; both schemes fail, Rome humbles him, and he dies a plunderer’s death.

He shall give him the daughter of women. Antiochus III tried to control Egypt through a marriage, giving his daughter Cleopatra to the young Egyptian king Ptolemy V in the hope that she would work for her father’s interests. Instead she took her husband’s side. The scheme “shall not stand or be to his advantage”.

A commander shall put an end to his insolence. Antiochus then pushed west into Asia Minor and Greece, and there met a new power: Rome. In 190 BC a Roman army under the commander Lucius Scipio crushed him at Magnesia and forced a humiliating treaty on him. Here Rome enters this chapter, the power that on the traditional reading became the iron kingdom of chapters 2 and 7.

He shall stumble and fall. Weighed down by the fine Rome demanded, Antiochus went looking for money, and in 187 BC he was killed while trying to plunder a temple in the east. The man once called the Great “shall stumble and fall, and shall not be found”.

Uncertain wording. “The daughter of women” is an unusual phrase, probably meaning simply a young woman, a royal bride, and it is not clear whose ruin “to destroy the kingdom” means. The ESV notes that part of verse 18 is uncertain. The general sense is plain: the marriage scheme backfires, and a foreign commander turns the king’s insolence back on him.

verseByVerse.quote: "Then shall arise in his place one who shall send an exactor of tribute for the glory of the kingdom. But within a few days he shall be broken, neither in anger nor in battle.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The next northern king is remembered for one thing, a tax collector, and he is soon struck down by a plot.

An exactor of tribute. His son, Seleucus IV, needed money to pay Rome and sent an official to collect taxes; according to Jewish tradition this official, Heliodorus, even tried to seize the treasure of the temple in Jerusalem (2 Maccabees 3). Seleucus was later murdered in a plot, “neither in anger nor in battle”. The kings of the north keep grasping, and they keep falling.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Persecution will come, but those who know God stand firm, and their suffering refines them. A contemptible man with no right to the throne takes it by flattery (v. 21). He sweeps aside armies and even the prince of the covenant, rules by deceit and bribery (vv. 22–24), defeats Egypt and lies at table with its king, and turns his heart against the holy covenant (vv. 25–28). Humiliated by the ships of Kittim, he takes his rage out on God’s people, stops the sacrifices and sets up the abomination that makes desolate (vv. 29–31). Yet while flattery wins over the covenant-breakers, the people who know their God stand firm and act; the wise teach many and suffer, and their stumbling refines them until the appointed time (vv. 32–35).
verseByVerse.theology: Persecution will come, but those who know God stand firm, and their suffering refines them.

verseByVerse.quote: In his place shall arise a contemptible person to whom royal majesty has not been given. He shall come in without warning and obtain the kingdom by flatteries. Armies shall be utterly swept away before him and broken, even the prince of the covenant. And from the time that an alliance is made with him he shall act deceitfully, and he shall become strong with a small people. Without warning he shall come into the richest parts of the province, and he shall do what neither his fathers nor his fathers' fathers have done, scattering among them plunder, spoil, and goods. He shall devise plans against strongholds, but only for a time.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now the story slows for the man who matters most to Daniel’s people: Antiochus IV, a contemptible usurper who wins power by flattery and deceit, yet whose plans run “only for a time”.

A contemptible person. This is Antiochus IV, the little horn of chapter 8. The throne was not rightfully his: the heir, his nephew, was a hostage in Rome, and Antiochus seized power by scheming and flattery.

Even the prince of the covenant. This may refer to the faithful high priest Onias III, whom Antiochus removed from office soon after he came to power and who was later murdered. The man who held the highest office among God’s covenant people was swept aside by a pagan king.

He shall act deceitfully. Antiochus made agreements and broke them, and he rose to power with only “a small people”, a small band of supporters. Tyrants rarely begin with the backing of the many; a determined, deceitful few can seize a great deal when others are careless.

Scattering among them plunder, spoil, and goods. Antiochus was known for handing out plunder lavishly to buy loyalty, as his ancestors had not done. And the chapter’s refrain returns: “but only for a time”. His plans have an expiry date set by God. For faithful Jews who lived through his persecution, this was the point of the whole prophecy: the tyrant who seemed unstoppable had been described, and his limit fixed, long before he was born.

How God sees the powerful. This king called himself Epiphanes, ‘God made manifest’, God appearing on earth, and his coins called him divine. God calls him “contemptible”. God’s verdict on the powerful is often the exact opposite of their own. And when God truly appeared on earth, in Jesus, he came the opposite way. He did not seize a throne by flattery; he emptied himself and took the form of a servant (Philippians 2:6–8).

verseByVerse.quote: And he shall stir up his power and his heart against the king of the south with a great army. And the king of the south shall wage war with an exceedingly great and mighty army, but he shall not stand, for plots shall be devised against him. Even those who eat his food shall break him. His army shall be swept away, and many shall fall down slain. And as for the two kings, their hearts shall be bent on doing evil. They shall speak lies at the same table, but to no avail, for the end is yet to be at the time appointed. And he shall return to his land with great wealth, but his heart shall be set against the holy covenant. And he shall work his will and return to his own land.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Antiochus defeats Egypt, sits at table with its king in mutual deceit, and on his way home turns his heart against God’s people and their worship.

Those who eat his food. In 170–169 BC Antiochus invaded Egypt and defeated the young Ptolemy VI, who was betrayed by his own advisers, “those who eat his food”.

They shall speak lies at the same table. Ptolemy was the son of Antiochus’s sister. Uncle and defeated nephew sat down together, pretending friendship while each planned to deceive the other. Yet even the lies of kings serve God’s timetable: “the end is yet to be at the time appointed”.

His heart shall be set against the holy covenant. On his way home, in 169 BC, Antiochus entered Jerusalem and robbed the temple of its treasures. His heart was now set against God’s people and their worship.

Another table. What a contrast with the table of the Lord. There the host does not lie: on the night he was betrayed by one who ate his bread (John 13:18), he gave himself in truth to his people (1 Corinthians 11:23–25).

verseByVerse.quote: "At the time appointed he shall return and come into the south, but it shall not be this time as it was before. For ships of Kittim shall come against him, and he shall be afraid and withdraw, and shall turn back and be enraged and take action against the holy covenant. He shall turn back and pay attention to those who forsake the holy covenant. Forces from him shall appear and profane the temple and fortress, and shall take away the regular burnt offering. And they shall set up the abomination that makes desolate.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Humiliated by Rome, Antiochus turns his rage on the Jews, finds allies among those who forsake the covenant, and desecrates the temple with “the abomination that makes desolate”.

Ships of Kittim shall come against him. In 168 BC Antiochus invaded Egypt again, but this time “ships of Kittim” arrived. Kittim first meant Cyprus and came to be used of peoples from across the western sea; here it means Rome. A Roman envoy ordered Antiochus out of Egypt, and when the king asked for time to think, drew a circle in the sand around him and told him to decide before he stepped out of it. Humiliated, Antiochus withdrew.

Those who forsake the holy covenant. He took out his rage on the Jews, and found allies among those who wanted to abandon their faith and live like Greeks. Persecution from outside is often helped by compromise inside.

The abomination that makes desolate. In December 167 BC the daily sacrifices were stopped, and an altar to the Greek god Zeus was set up in God’s temple, where unclean sacrifices were offered. This was the outrage foretold in 8:11–13. Jesus later used the same phrase for a desecration connected with the destruction of Jerusalem and the end (Matthew 24:15). What Antiochus did became a pattern for later attacks on God’s worship.

The sacrifice that ended the sacrifices. A tyrant’s violence took away “the regular burnt offering” for three years. A better sacrifice would end it for good, not by defiling the altar but by fulfilling it: Christ “offered for all time a single sacrifice for sins” and sat down at God’s right hand (Hebrews 10:12).
verseByVerse.note: Kittim (Cyprus/the West) refers to Rome, which forced Antiochus out of Egypt in 168 BC. He then set up an altar to Zeus in the temple.

verseByVerse.quote: He shall seduce with flattery those who violate the covenant, but the people who know their God shall stand firm and take action. And the wise among the people shall make many understand, though for some days they shall stumble by sword and flame, by captivity and plunder. When they stumble, they shall receive a little help. And many shall join themselves to them with flattery, and some of the wise shall stumble, so that they may be refined, purified, and made white, until the time of the end, for it still awaits the appointed time.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Under persecution God’s people divide: flattery wins over those who break the covenant, but those who know their God stand firm and act, the wise teach many, and even their suffering refines them, for a time God has fixed. Verse 32 is the key verse of the chapter.

The people who know their God. Some “violate the covenant”, won over with flattery: promises of position, safety and acceptance. Others “know their God”. The difference is not how much they know about God but whether they know him, the God who first made them his own, trusting and loving him; that is what lets believers “stand firm”. “And this is eternal life, that they know you, the only true God, and Jesus Christ whom you have sent” (John 17:3). And they “take action”. In 167 BC faithful Jews refused to sacrifice to idols, and a revolt began, led by a priestly family known as the Maccabees; many refused to eat unclean food or abandon the law, even when it cost them their lives. Such knowledge is not reserved for scholars. It grows as ordinary believers keep returning to God’s word, to prayer and to the fellowship of his people, so that when the pressure comes they can say with Paul, “I know whom I have believed” (2 Timothy 1:12).

The wise among the people. Those who understand God’s word teach others, and faithful teaching is one of the great strengths of God’s people under persecution. But the wise also suffer, “by sword and flame, by captivity and plunder”. Hebrews probably has faithful people of this period in mind when it speaks of those who were destitute, afflicted and mistreated, “of whom the world was not worthy” (Hebrews 11:37–38).

They shall receive a little help. This probably refers to the military successes of the Maccabean revolt, which brought some relief. But it was only a little: the real deliverance of God’s people would not come by the sword. And some who joined the cause did so insincerely, for their own advantage.

Why does God allow even the wise to fall? “So that they may be refined, purified, and made white.” Suffering is God’s fire for purifying his people, as a metalworker heats silver to remove its impurities: “He will sit as a refiner and purifier of silver” (Malachi 3:3). Peter says the same to Christians: faith, more precious than gold, is tested by fire so that it may be found genuine, to praise and glory at the revelation of Jesus Christ (1 Peter 1:6–7). And even this suffering is limited, “until the time of the end”, the “appointed time”.

Jesus at the Feast of Dedication. The temple Antiochus defiled was cleansed in 164 BC, and the Jews kept a yearly Feast of Dedication to remember it. John records that Jesus was in the temple at that very feast, walking in Solomon’s colonnade, when he said, “I and the Father are one” (John 10:22–30). The temple had been rescued from a contemptible king who called himself ‘God made manifest’. Now Jesus stood in it, the one in whom God truly came.

Why flattery works better than force. Antiochus had a sword, but verse 32 says his most effective weapon was flattery. Persecution makes martyrs; flattery makes collaborators. The Jews who went over to him were not dragged but invited: to the gymnasium, into the right circles, to be modern, cosmopolitan and admired rather than narrow and backward. Most of us will never face a king’s sword, but we know the invitation. The idol is approval, and it rarely asks us to deny God outright, only to keep quiet about him, laugh at the right jokes and let our convictions blur until no one important minds us. Flattery works because we are hungry, and whoever feeds our hunger to be thought well of can lead us almost anywhere. The answer is not more willpower but a fuller heart. The people who know their God are already known by him, and in Christ, who was despised and rejected so that they could be accepted (Isaiah 53:3), they already have the only approval that lasts. A person whose deepest hunger has been fed is very hard to flatter.
verseByVerse.note: Fulfilled in part in the Maccabean revolt; the temple was rededicated in 164 BC, remembered at the Feast of Dedication.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 36–45 — The King Who Exalts Himself
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The last great enemy of God will exalt himself above all, and he will come to his end. A king does as he wills, magnifies himself above every god and speaks astonishing things against the God of gods, yet prospers only until what God has decreed is done (v. 36). He despises the gods of his fathers and honours only the god of fortresses, buying loyalty with rank and land (vv. 37–39). At the time of the end he sweeps through the countries like a whirlwind, takes the riches of Egypt and pitches his tents beside the glorious holy mountain (vv. 40–45a). Then, with no battle described, he comes to his end, with none to help him (v. 45b).
verseByVerse.theology: The last great enemy of God will exalt himself above all, and he will come to his end.

verseByVerse.quote: "And the king shall do as he wills. He shall exalt himself and magnify himself above every god, and shall speak astonishing things against the God of gods. He shall prosper till the indignation is accomplished; for what is decreed shall be done. He shall pay no attention to the gods of his fathers, or to the one beloved by women. He shall not pay attention to any other god, for he shall magnify himself above all. He shall honor the god of fortresses instead of these. A god whom his fathers did not know he shall honor with gold and silver, with precious stones and costly gifts. He shall deal with the strongest fortresses with the help of a foreign god. Those who acknowledge him he shall load with honor. He shall make them rulers over many and shall divide the land for a price.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The portrait now widens to a king who makes himself god, honours nothing but power and buys loyalty, and yet goes only as far as God has decreed.

Who is this king? With verse 36 we reach one of the most debated points in Daniel. The language still fits Antiochus in part, but it begins to reach beyond him, and by verse 40, “at the time of the end”, it describes events that do not match his last years (see Where Christians differ below).

He shall exalt himself. Whoever he is, his chief mark is pride. He “shall do as he wills”, exalts himself “above every god” and speaks “astonishing things against the God of gods”. Paul seems to echo this very verse when he writes that the man of lawlessness “exalts himself against every so-called god or object of worship… proclaiming himself to be God” (2 Thessalonians 2:4). Yet even this king can go only as far as God allows: “He shall prosper till the indignation is accomplished; for what is decreed shall be done.”
