The god of fortresses. He has no loyalty to the gods of his fathers or to any other, “for he shall magnify himself above all”. The only god he truly honours is “the god of fortresses”: military power. Whatever he professes, his real trust is in force, and he buys loyalty by rewarding those who back him with rank and land. It is a portrait of every godless tyrant, and of the final one.

The god of fortresses is still worshipped. Martin Luther, explaining the first commandment in his Large Catechism, taught that whatever your heart clings to and relies on is really your god. By that test the god of fortresses has never lacked worshippers. He is the god of the secure position: the savings that mean I need no one, the reputation no one can touch, the career that makes me safe, the plan with every exit covered. He is honoured, as verse 38 says, “with gold and silver”, and for a time he rewards his followers well. What he cannot do is keep anyone. Every fortress in this chapter falls, and the king who trusted them “shall come to his end, with none to help him” (v. 45).

The God who came without walls. The gospel turns the whole thing over. The true God did not make himself safe. He came without walls, was handed over and “crucified in weakness” (2 Corinthians 13:4), and so became the one refuge no army can take. Luther spent his life singing of that God as ‘a mighty fortress’.

Where Christians differ: who is the king of verses 36–45? Some believe it is still Antiochus IV, who did make great claims for himself and slighted the gods of his fathers. But verses 40–45 do not match his last years: he did not conquer Egypt at the end of his life or die between the sea and Jerusalem, but died of illness in Persia. Most critical scholars therefore read verses 40–45 as a prediction of his end that did not come true. Many others, including many in the Reformed tradition and most dispensational interpreters, believe the prophecy here looks beyond Antiochus to the final enemy of God at the end of history, the little horn of chapter 7 and Paul’s man of lawlessness, of whom Antiochus was a small-scale preview. This commentary’s view: the last of these. The text signals that the horizon has moved (“at the time of the end”, v. 40), Paul’s echo points the same way, and the failed-prediction reading depends on the late date it is used to prove. Yet the line between Antiochus and the final enemy is not sharply drawn. The prophecy moves from the near horizon to the far one, as a traveller sees nearby hills and distant mountains as one skyline.

Uncertain wording. “The one beloved by women” is obscure. It may be a god especially popular with women, such as Tammuz, whom women mourned (Ezekiel 8:14), or it may mean the natural love of wife and family, which this king despises. “The god of fortresses”, a god “whom his fathers did not know”, may also be a particular deity; some think of the Roman Jupiter or of Zeus Olympios, whom Antiochus promoted. Most take it as power itself made into a god. The main point is clear either way: “he shall magnify himself above all.”

verseByVerse.quote: "At the time of the end, the king of the south shall attack him, but the king of the north shall rush upon him like a whirlwind, with chariots and horsemen, and with many ships. And he shall come into countries and shall overflow and pass through. He shall come into the glorious land. And tens of thousands shall fall, but these shall be delivered out of his hand: Edom and Moab and the main part of the Ammonites. He shall stretch out his hand against the countries, and the land of Egypt shall not escape. He shall become ruler of the treasures of gold and of silver, and all the precious things of Egypt, and the Libyans and the Cushites shall follow in his train. But news from the east and the north shall alarm him, and he shall go out with great fury to destroy and devote many to destruction. And he shall pitch his palatial tents between the sea and the glorious holy mountain. Yet he shall come to his end, with none to help him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
At the time of the end the last enemy sweeps through the world and camps beside God’s holy mountain, and then, in a single sentence, he is gone.

At the time of the end. The conflicts of the past now recur on a larger scale. The last enemy rushes on “like a whirlwind”, overflowing the countries.

He shall come into the glorious land. He enters the land of God’s people and conquers Egypt and its neighbours. Edom, Moab and Ammon, Israel’s ancient enemies, escape him, perhaps because they side with him, and Libya and Cush, to the west and south of Egypt, follow in his train. The names are those of Daniel’s world, but the picture is of a ruler who seems to hold all the wealth and power of the earth.

News from the east and the north shall alarm him. The scene recalls how God dealt with the Assyrian king Sennacherib long before: “he shall hear a rumor and return to his own land” (Isaiah 37:7). In fury the conqueror sets up his royal camp “between the sea and the glorious holy mountain”, close to Jerusalem, where God’s name dwells, as if for a final attack on God’s people.

Yet he shall come to his end. And then, in a single sentence, it is over. No battle is described; no army saves him. The one who rewarded his supporters (v. 39) has no one to help him. Paul says that the final enemy is the one “the Lord Jesus will kill with the breath of his mouth and bring to nothing by the appearance of his coming” (2 Thessalonians 2:8).

The message of the chapter. Kings plot, marry, betray and plunder, and God’s people suffer in the middle. But every event was known to God before it happened, every enemy is given only “a time”, and the last and greatest enemy will come to his end. “The LORD brings the counsel of the nations to nothing; he frustrates the plans of the peoples. The counsel of the LORD stands forever” (Psalm 33:10–11). Christ “must reign until he has put all his enemies under his feet” (1 Corinthians 15:25). Until then the calling of God’s people is the calling of verse 32: to know our God, to stand firm and to act, not in our own strength but in the Lord’s, praying at all times in the Spirit (Ephesians 6:10, 18).

11.title: The People Who Know Their God
11.overview:
Where we are. Chapter 11 is the heart of Daniel’s last vision (chapters 10–12). Daniel has seen a glorious man clothed in linen and heard of a war in the unseen world between the angelic princes of the nations (chapter 10); now the messenger shows him “the truth” (v. 2) of what it will mean on earth.

The message. God knows history before it happens, down to the marriages and betrayals of kings, and every tyrant runs only “for a time” that God has set. So God’s people need be neither seduced nor crushed: “the people who know their God shall stand firm and take action” (v. 32). Their suffering refines them, and their enemy “shall come to his end, with none to help him” (v. 45).

Why it was said. Daniel’s people would go home to a small land caught between empires, and one day live under a king who tried to stamp out their faith (see the introduction). They needed to know beforehand that he had been foreseen and limited, so that they would neither despair nor trust their own swords.

How the chapter makes its case. Persia gives way to a mighty Greek king whose empire is split four ways (vv. 1–4). Kings of the south (Egypt) and north (Syria) make alliances, marriages and wars that all collapse, and the glorious land changes masters (vv. 5–20). The story slows for a contemptible king, Antiochus IV, who flatters his way to power and sets up the abomination that makes desolate; yet the faithful stand firm, and the wise teach many and are refined by suffering (vv. 21–35). Then the horizon widens to a king who exalts himself above every god, overruns the world and camps beside God’s holy mountain, and comes to his end in a single sentence (vv. 36–45).

Where it leads. This chapter holds no direct promise of the Messiah; it leads to Christ by contrast and by the need it exposes. Kings who grasp at godhood, one even calling himself ‘God made manifest’, all fall, and prepare us for the one in whom God truly appeared, who did not grasp at equality with God but emptied himself (Philippians 2:6–7), and who stood in the temple rescued from Antiochus and said, “I and the Father are one” (John 10:30). The self-exalting final enemy is the one whom the Lord Jesus will “bring to nothing by the appearance of his coming” (2 Thessalonians 2:8). And to know “their God” is, for us, to know the Father through the Son (John 17:3).

For us. No tyrant outlives the time God gives him. The pressure most of us face is less the sword than flattery, the quiet invitation to keep silent about Christ in order to be accepted. The answer is to know our God, through his word, prayer and his people, so that, already accepted in Christ, we can stand firm, act and, if need be, suffer.
11.theology:
God knows the whole course of history in detail before it happens, and the plans of kings serve his purpose (vv. 2-35; Prov 19:21; Ps 33:10-11).

Human alliances, marriages and schemes cannot secure lasting peace or power (vv. 6, 17, 27).

God sees the proud as contemptible, whatever they call themselves (v. 21).

Persecution of God's people is aided by compromise within, but those who know their God stand firm and act (vv. 30, 32; John 17:3).

Faithful teachers strengthen God's people, and God uses suffering to refine and purify them for a limited, appointed time (vv. 33-35; Mal 3:3; 1 Pet 1:6-7; Heb 11:36-38).

The final enemy of God will exalt himself above every god, but he will come to his end, destroyed by the Lord Jesus at his coming (vv. 36-45; 2 Thess 2:4, 8; 1 Cor 15:25).
11.examples: A Persian king is rich enough to invade Greece, and a royal marriage meant to bring peace ends in murder. A small land is caught between two empires. A self-styled god, whom God calls contemptible, tells lies at the same table as his rival, is humiliated inside a circle drawn in the sand, and sets up an idol's altar in God's temple. And through it all, ordinary believers who know their God will not bow.

keyVerse.quote: He shall seduce with flattery those who violate the covenant, but the people who know their God shall stand firm and take action.
keyVerse.note: In the middle of a long record of kings, this verse names what decides everything for ordinary believers: not the size of the enemy but whether they know their God. Flattery wins those whose hearts are hungry for approval; those who know and are known by God stand firm and act. In Christ that knowledge is eternal life itself (John 17:3).

11.reflection:
This chapter describes centuries of wars and marriages before they happened (vv. 2–20). How does it help you to know that God knew all of it beforehand? Where in today’s news or your own life do you most need that confidence?

Antiochus called himself ‘God made manifest’, and God called him “contemptible” (v. 21). Whose approval or verdict do you find yourself living for? How does Jesus, who emptied himself instead of grasping at power, change the way we see greatness?

Verse 32 says flattery won over those who violated the covenant. What forms does that flattery take for Christians today, at work, at school or online? What helps a believer to “know their God” well enough to stand firm?

The wise “shall make many understand”, yet they suffer, and their suffering refines them (vv. 33–35). How have you seen God use hard times to purify faith, in your life or someone else’s? How can our group strengthen those who are under pressure for their faith?

12.text: <sup>1</sup>"At that time shall arise Michael, the great prince who has charge of your people. And there shall be a time of trouble, such as never has been since there was a nation till that time. But at that time your people shall be delivered, everyone whose name shall be found written in the book.<sup>2</sup>And many of those who sleep in the dust of the earth shall awake, some to everlasting life, and some to shame and everlasting contempt.<sup>3</sup>And those who are wise shall shine like the brightness of the sky above; and those who turn many to righteousness, like the stars forever and ever.<sup>4</sup>But you, Daniel, shut up the words and seal the book, until the time of the end. Many shall run to and fro, and knowledge shall increase."<sup>5</sup>Then I, Daniel, looked, and behold, two others stood, one on this bank of the stream and one on that bank of the stream.<sup>6</sup>And someone said to the man clothed in linen, who was above the waters of the stream, "How long shall it be till the end of these wonders?"<sup>7</sup>And I heard the man clothed in linen, who was above the waters of the stream; he raised his right hand and his left hand toward heaven and swore by him who lives forever that it would be for a time, times, and half a time, and that when the shattering of the power of the holy people comes to an end all these things would be finished.<sup>8</sup>I heard, but I did not understand. Then I said, "O my lord, what shall be the outcome of these things?"<sup>9</sup>He said, "Go your way, Daniel, for the words are shut up and sealed until the time of the end.<sup>10</sup>Many shall purify themselves and make themselves white and be refined, but the wicked shall act wickedly. And none of the wicked shall understand, but those who are wise shall understand.<sup>11</sup>And from the time that the regular burnt offering is taken away and the abomination that makes desolate is set up, there shall be 1,290 days.<sup>12</sup>Blessed is he who waits and arrives at the 1,335 days.<sup>13</sup>But go your way till the end. And you shall rest and shall stand in your allotted place at the end of the days."

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: History ends not in the grave but in resurrection, judgment and glory for those whose names are written in God’s book. When the final enemy makes his last attack, Michael arises, a time of trouble comes such as never has been, and every one of God’s people whose name is in the book is delivered (v. 1). The dead sleeping in the dust will awake, some to everlasting life and some to everlasting shame (v. 2). Those who were wise and turned many to righteousness, often despised and killed on earth, will shine like the stars for ever (v. 3). Daniel is to seal the book securely until the time of the end (v. 4).
verseByVerse.theology: History ends not in the grave but in resurrection, judgment and glory for those whose names are written in God's book.

verseByVerse.quote: "At that time shall arise Michael, the great prince who has charge of your people. And there shall be a time of trouble, such as never has been since there was a nation till that time. But at that time your people shall be delivered, everyone whose name shall be found written in the book.
verseByVerse.commentary:
When the final trouble comes, worse than any before, heaven acts, and God brings through it everyone whose name is written in his book.

At that time shall arise Michael. The verse continues straight on from chapter 11: “at that time” is the final enemy’s last attack, when “he shall come to his end” (11:45). Three things happen then. First Michael, the angel of 10:13 and 21, “the great prince who has charge of your people”, arises: at the decisive moment heaven acts for God’s people (compare Revelation 12:7).

A time of trouble. Second, there will be “a time of trouble, such as never has been”: the final days will bring suffering greater than any before. Jesus took up these very words when he spoke of the end: “For then there will be great tribulation, such as has not been from the beginning of the world until now, no, and never will be” (Matthew 24:21).

Your people shall be delivered. Third, and most important, “your people shall be delivered”: everyone written “in the book”, God’s book of life, the register of those who belong to him. Moses spoke of it (Exodus 32:32). Jesus told his disciples, “rejoice that your names are written in heaven” (Luke 10:20). Revelation calls it “the book of life of the Lamb who was slain” (Revelation 13:8), and the risen Christ promises the one who conquers, “I will never blot his name out of the book of life” (Revelation 3:5).

Kept by God. This is the deepest comfort in the whole of Daniel. When the worst comes, God’s people are kept not by their own strength but because God has written their names in his book, and he does not lose what is his: “I give them eternal life, and they will never perish, and no one will snatch them out of my hand” (John 10:28). The book belongs to the Lamb, and the names in it are safe because he was slain.

Where Christians differ: what is this “time of trouble”? Some, including dispensationalists, believe it describes a specific future period of great tribulation, usually seven years, just before Christ returns. Many others, including many Reformed interpreters, believe the whole age between Christ’s first and second comings is marked by tribulation for the church, rising to a final, terrible intensity before the end. This commentary’s view: the second, though faithful Christians differ. Jesus says, “In the world you will have tribulation” (John 16:33), John calls himself a “partner in the tribulation” (Revelation 1:9), and Jesus’ words in Matthew 24 speak first of Jerusalem’s fall in AD 70 and then of the end. Both views agree that believers should not be surprised by suffering, and that it will not have the last word.

verseByVerse.quote: And many of those who sleep in the dust of the earth shall awake, some to everlasting life, and some to shame and everlasting contempt.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Death is not the end: the dead will rise, bodily, some to everlasting life and some to everlasting shame. This is the clearest promise of the resurrection of the body in the whole Old Testament (Isaiah 26:19 comes close).

Those who sleep in the dust of the earth. Since the fall God’s sentence on humanity has been “you are dust, and to dust you shall return” (Genesis 3:19). But the dust is not the end. Those who sleep there “shall awake”.

Why death is called sleep. Not because the dead are unconscious (believers who die go at once to be with Christ, Philippians 1:23), nor because death is unreal: it is still an enemy, the last to be destroyed (1 Corinthians 15:26). It means that death is not permanent. Sleep is followed by waking. So Paul could tell grieving Christians, “we do not want you to be uninformed, brothers, about those who are asleep, that you may not grieve as others do who have no hope” (1 Thessalonians 4:13).

Some to everlasting life. The resurrection divides humanity into two destinies, and the same word, “everlasting”, describes both. Jesus said the same: “an hour is coming when all who are in the tombs will hear his voice and come out, those who have done good to the resurrection of life, and those who have done evil to the resurrection of judgment” (John 5:28–29); and, “these will go away into eternal punishment, but the righteous into eternal life” (Matthew 25:46).

Shame and everlasting contempt. Those raised to judgment are not put out of existence but go on, conscious, under the just and endless disgrace their rejection of God deserves. But no one should speak of this coldly. God has no pleasure in the death of the wicked (Ezekiel 33:11). If you fear for someone you love, the door is open while life lasts, and Jesus turns away no one who comes to him (John 6:37). For he himself endured the cross, despising the shame (Hebrews 12:2), and bore that shame so that everyone who believes in him “will not be put to shame” (Romans 10:11).

The martyrs will awake. This verse changes how we read the rest of Daniel. Many of the faithful were not rescued from death; the wise “stumble by sword and flame” (11:33), and if this life were all, the persecutors would have won. But the martyrs will awake to everlasting life, and their persecutors to everlasting shame. And we know how this hope is secured: Jesus Christ has already risen from the dust, “the firstfruits of those who have fallen asleep” (1 Corinthians 15:20). “I am the resurrection and the life. Whoever believes in me, though he die, yet shall he live” (John 11:25).

Why does the verse say “many” rather than all? Some believe “many” here means the great multitude of the dead, that is, everyone, as Jesus’ words suggest. Others think the verse focuses on the people of Daniel’s own story, the faithful and those who abandon the faith in the final conflict. Either way, the rest of Scripture is clear that there will be “a resurrection of both the just and the unjust” (Acts 24:15).

Where Christians differ: is the punishment of the lost everlasting? Some faithful Christians believe that the wicked are finally destroyed, and they too take Scripture seriously. This commentary’s view: with the historic church, this punishment is conscious and everlasting, as the word shared with “everlasting life” suggests, and as Jesus sets eternal punishment beside eternal life in the same sentence (Matthew 25:46).
verseByVerse.note: The clearest Old Testament statement of the resurrection of both the righteous and the wicked.

verseByVerse.quote: And those who are wise shall shine like the brightness of the sky above; and those who turn many to righteousness, like the stars forever and ever. But you, Daniel, shut up the words and seal the book, until the time of the end. Many shall run to and fro, and knowledge shall increase."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Those who lead others to God, however despised now, will shine for ever; meanwhile Daniel must seal up his book, safe and secure, until the end.

Those who are wise shall shine. They are the faithful teachers of 11:33, who “make many understand” even when it costs them their lives. Despised and killed on earth, in the resurrection they will shine. The ESV notes that “the sky above” is literally ‘the expanse’, the word used in Genesis 1:6–8 for the sky God made on the second day: their glory will be as wide and bright as the heavens. Jesus used the same picture: “Then the righteous will shine like the sun in the kingdom of their Father” (Matthew 13:43).

Those who turn many to righteousness. The brightest are not the famous or powerful but those who led others to God: a Sunday school teacher, a parent who prays with her children, a faithful pastor in a small church, a believer who quietly shares Christ with a friend at work. They will shine “like the stars forever and ever”. Even now, Paul says, believers “shine as lights in the world” (Philippians 2:15); one day the light will be complete.

The Servant behind the wise. The phrase echoes Isaiah’s suffering Servant, who would “make many to be accounted righteous” and “bear their iniquities” (Isaiah 53:11). The wise turn many to righteousness only by pointing them to the one who makes sinners righteous. Every star in that sky shines with borrowed light.

Seal the book. As in 8:26, this means to preserve it securely, like a sealed legal scroll, not to hide it. At the end of the Bible John is told the opposite: “Do not seal up the words of the prophecy of this book, for the time is near” (Revelation 22:10). With the coming of Jesus, the end has drawn near.

Uncertain wording. The sense of “many shall run to and fro, and knowledge shall increase” is debated. The verb pictures roaming about. Amos uses it of people who “shall run to and fro, to seek the word of the LORD, but they shall not find it” (Amos 8:12), so it may describe anxious, even fruitless, searching in troubled times. Read with the sealed book, it more likely means that many will search, and knowledge of Daniel’s prophecy will grow as its words come true: the Jews under Antiochus understood more than Daniel (v. 8), and we, after Christ’s coming, see further still. It is almost certainly not a prediction of modern travel and science.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God’s people are not given every date, but they are given a promise, and they wait, endure and rest in it. By the river, the question every sufferer asks, “How long?”, is answered with the most solemn of oaths: a time, times and half a time, until the power of the holy people is shattered (vv. 5–7). Daniel confesses that he does not understand, and is told gently to go his way: the coming trouble will purify the wise and harden the wicked (vv. 8–10). Two puzzling numbers stretch the waiting a little further and end in a blessing on whoever waits (vv. 11–12). Last of all, the old man is promised rest, resurrection and his own place in the inheritance (v. 13).
verseByVerse.theology: God's people are not given every date, but they are given a promise, and they wait, endure and rest in it.

verseByVerse.quote: Then I, Daniel, looked, and behold, two others stood, one on this bank of the stream and one on that bank of the stream. And someone said to the man clothed in linen, who was above the waters of the stream, "How long shall it be till the end of these wonders?" And I heard the man clothed in linen, who was above the waters of the stream; he raised his right hand and his left hand toward heaven and swore by him who lives forever that it would be for a time, times, and half a time, and that when the shattering of the power of the holy people comes to an end all these things would be finished.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Asked how long the suffering will last, the man clothed in linen swears by the eternal God that it is limited, and that it will end when the power of God’s people has been completely broken.

Two others stood. The vision returns to the river where it began (10:4). Two more heavenly figures appear, perhaps as witnesses to the oath about to be sworn, since the Law required two witnesses (Deuteronomy 19:15).

How long shall it be till the end of these wonders? The man clothed in linen of 10:5 stands above the waters, and one of the two asks the question every suffering believer asks: how long? (Psalm 13:1; Revelation 6:10).

He raised his right hand and his left hand. Raising not one hand but both, he swears “by him who lives forever”: nothing could be more certain. Revelation echoes the scene when a mighty angel “raised his right hand to heaven and swore by him who lives forever and ever” that “there would be no more delay” (Revelation 10:5–6).

A time, times, and half a time. The same limited period as in 7:25: a real time of suffering, but one God has measured and will cut short.

The shattering of the power of the holy people. The end comes not when God’s people are strongest but when their power has been completely broken. God often waits until his people have nothing left, so that the victory is plainly his: “my power is made perfect in weakness” (2 Corinthians 12:9).

The same at the cross. When Jesus hung dead and his followers were scattered, the power of God’s holy people seemed utterly shattered. Three days later, death itself was defeated. And if, as this commentary takes it, the man in linen is the Son of God before his birth (see the note on 10:5–6), then the one who swore this oath would keep it by being broken himself.

Where Christians differ: how long is “a time, times, and half a time”? Some take it as three and a half literal years at the end of history; many others as a symbol of a limited time of trouble, half of a complete seven. This commentary’s view: the symbolic reading (see the note on 7:23–25). God has fixed the length, and the enemy’s time is broken off halfway.

Uncertain wording. “Above the waters of the stream” may also mean ‘upstream’, as the ESV notes. Either way the man in linen stands apart from the two figures on the banks.

verseByVerse.quote: I heard, but I did not understand. Then I said, "O my lord, what shall be the outcome of these things?" He said, "Go your way, Daniel, for the words are shut up and sealed until the time of the end. Many shall purify themselves and make themselves white and be refined, but the wicked shall act wickedly. And none of the wicked shall understand, but those who are wise shall understand.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Even Daniel does not understand, and he is told not to strain after it but to go his way: the coming trouble will purify the wise and harden the wicked.

I heard, but I did not understand. How honest this is. After a lifetime of interpreting dreams and receiving visions, Daniel admits that he does not understand. If Daniel did not, anyone who claims to have worked out every detail of prophecy should hold his theories with humility.

Go your way, Daniel. This is not a rebuke but a gentle release. He need not understand everything, only trust God and keep living faithfully. Jesus said something similar when his disciples asked about the timing of the kingdom: “It is not for you to know times or seasons that the Father has fixed by his own authority” (Acts 1:7). God has not given us a timetable to calculate. He has given us a promise to live by.

Many shall purify themselves. The coming troubles will have opposite effects. Some will be purified by them, made “white” and “refined” like metal in the fire (11:35); others will simply go on doing evil. The same suffering that makes one person more holy makes another harder against God. Revelation says the same about the last days: “Let the evildoer still do evil, and the filthy still be filthy, and the righteous still do right, and the holy still be holy” (Revelation 22:11).

Those who are wise shall understand. Understanding God’s purposes is not a matter of intelligence but of faith. The wicked cannot understand because they will not submit to God; the wise understand because they fear him. And what was sealed to Daniel has been opened in Christ. Peter says the prophets searched and inquired carefully about the sufferings of Christ and the glories to follow, and were shown that they were serving not themselves but us (1 Peter 1:10–12). The full unveiling waits for “the revelation of Jesus Christ” (1 Peter 1:13).

verseByVerse.quote: And from the time that the regular burnt offering is taken away and the abomination that makes desolate is set up, there shall be 1,290 days. Blessed is he who waits and arrives at the 1,335 days.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Two puzzling numbers stretch the waiting a little beyond what was expected, and pronounce a blessing on whoever keeps waiting to the end.

There shall be 1,290 days. These two numbers are among the most puzzling in Daniel, and it is best to be honest: no one can be certain what they mean. Both are a little longer than three and a half years (about 1,260 days, as in Revelation 11:3). The first adds thirty days, and the second another forty-five.

Blessed is he who waits. Whatever the exact meaning, the verse puts its weight on one word: “Blessed”. The blessing does not go to the person who calculates the date but to the one who waits faithfully and endures. Jesus said, “the one who endures to the end will be saved” (Matthew 24:13), and “concerning that day and hour no one knows” (Matthew 24:36). The call of prophecy is not to predict but to persevere, and the God who wrote his people’s names in his book is the one who keeps them to the end (v. 1; Philippians 1:6).

Where Christians differ: what do the numbers mean? Some apply them to the persecution under Antiochus IV, counting from the desecration of the temple to the end of that crisis. Some, especially dispensationalists, see them as extra periods after a future seven-year tribulation, perhaps for judgment and the setting up of Christ’s kingdom. Others take them symbolically: the time of trouble may last a little longer than God’s people expect, and they must keep waiting even when the end seems overdue. This commentary’s view: the first reading is the likeliest starting point, since the taking away of the offering and the abomination are Antiochus’s acts (11:31). His persecution then becomes a pattern of the last trouble, and the same call to wait applies to both.

verseByVerse.quote: But go your way till the end. And you shall rest and shall stand in your allotted place at the end of the days."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The book ends with a personal promise to an old exile: keep going, rest in death, and rise to receive your inheritance. Daniel had been carried off as a boy, served four kings and two empires, faced lions, seen visions that left him sick and prayed for a city he would never see again. He is told three things.

Go your way till the end. Keep living faithfully for the time you have left. Daniel would not see his visions fulfilled. Like all the faithful of the Old Testament, he would die “not having received the things promised, but having seen them and greeted them from afar” (Hebrews 11:13).

And you shall rest. Daniel would die. But for the believer, death is rest from labour: “Blessed are the dead who die in the Lord from now on… that they may rest from their labors” (Revelation 14:13).

Stand in your allotted place. Daniel will rise again. He is one of “those who sleep in the dust” (v. 2), and he will awake and “stand” in his “allotted place”. When Israel entered the promised land, each family received its inheritance by lot (Joshua 14:2). Daniel had lost his home in Judah, but God had kept him an inheritance no empire could take. “The LORD is my chosen portion and my cup; you hold my lot” (Psalm 16:5).

A promise for every believer. That promise belongs to everyone in Christ. We have been born again “to a living hope through the resurrection of Jesus Christ from the dead, to an inheritance that is imperishable, undefiled, and unfading, kept in heaven for you” (1 Peter 1:3–4). Jesus said, “I go to prepare a place for you” (John 14:2).

How the book ends. The book that began with the fall of Jerusalem and a teenager carried off to Babylon ends with an old man told to rest in hope of the resurrection. In between, kings raged and beasts made war on the saints, but the Most High ruled over all of it. The stone cut out by no human hand has begun its work, the Son of Man has received the kingdom, and the Anointed One has been cut off for our sins and raised to life. And one day all who sleep in the dust will hear his voice. Until then, the word to Daniel is the word to every Christian: go your way, be faithful, and wait for him. The Lord Jesus says, “Surely I am coming soon”, and his church answers, “Amen. Come, Lord Jesus!” (Revelation 22:20).

12.title: Those Who Sleep in the Dust Shall Awake
12.overview:
Where we are. This is the last chapter of Daniel and the end of the vision that began in chapter 10. It runs straight on from 11:45, where the final enemy comes to his end. After a book of kings and empires, the angel lifts Daniel’s eyes beyond history, to the resurrection of the dead.

The message. History does not end in the grave. Through the worst trouble the world has known, God keeps everyone whose name is written in his book; the dead will rise, some to everlasting life and some to everlasting shame; and those who led others to righteousness will shine like the stars. God gives his people not a timetable but a sworn promise, a blessing on those who wait, and rest in hope.

Why it was said. Many faithful Jews under Antiochus would “stumble by sword and flame” (11:33) without seeing rescue, and Daniel himself would die in exile (see the introduction). If this life were all, the persecutors would have won. This chapter tells them that the story of the martyrs is not over.

How the chapter makes its case. At the final crisis Michael arises, and in unequalled trouble everyone written in the book is delivered (v. 1). The dead awake to two everlasting destinies, and the wise shine like the stars (vv. 2–3), while Daniel seals the book until the end (v. 4). By the river, “How long?” is answered with an oath: a time, times and half a time, until the power of the holy people is shattered (vv. 5–7). Daniel does not understand and is told to go his way (vv. 8–10). Two puzzling numbers end in a blessing on those who wait (vv. 11–12), and the old exile is promised rest and resurrection (v. 13).

Where it leads. To Christ by direct promise. Jesus took up the words of verse 2 when he said that all who are in the tombs will hear his voice and come out (John 5:28–29), and his own resurrection is the firstfruits that guarantees ours (1 Corinthians 15:20). The book in which the names are written is “the book of life of the Lamb who was slain” (Revelation 13:8). And the pattern of verse 7, the end coming only when the power of God’s people is shattered, was lived out at the cross: when Jesus lay dead and his followers were scattered, all seemed lost, and on the third day death was defeated.

For us. Do not try to calculate the end; wait for it, faithfully. If you belong to Christ, your name is written, death for you is sleep, and you too will stand in your allotted place at the end of the days. Until then, go your way: live faithfully, and help others to righteousness.
12.theology:
God delivers all whose names are written in his book, even through the greatest tribulation (v. 1; Matt 24:21; Luke 10:20; Rev 3:5; 13:8; John 10:28).

The dead will be raised bodily, some to everlasting life and some to everlasting shame, a hope secured by the resurrection of Jesus Christ (v. 2; John 5:28-29; 11:25; Matt 25:46; Acts 24:15; 1 Thess 4:13-14).

Those who are wise and turn many to righteousness will shine forever (v. 3; Matt 13:43; Phil 2:15).

God's word about the future is certain, sworn by him who lives forever, and his people's suffering is limited and ends when their own power is spent (vv. 6-7; Rev 10:5-6; 2 Cor 12:9).

Even prophets do not understand everything; God's people are called not to calculate dates but to wait, endure and be refined (vv. 8-12; Acts 1:7; Matt 24:13, 36; Rev 22:11).

Believers rest in death and will rise to receive the inheritance God has kept for them (v. 13; Heb 11:13; Rev 14:13; Ps 16:5-6; 1 Pet 1:3-4; John 14:2-3).
12.examples: God keeps a book with the names of his people written in it, and the graves are beds from which the sleepers will wake. A Sunday school teacher will shine like a star. An oath is sworn with both hands raised to heaven, and a great prophet says, "I did not understand." The blessing goes not to the one who calculates but to the one who waits, and the old exile is told to rest, promised a place of his own.

keyVerse.quote: And many of those who sleep in the dust of the earth shall awake, some to everlasting life, and some to shame and everlasting contempt.
keyVerse.note: This is the hope that makes the whole of Daniel bearable: the martyrs of 11:33 and the old exile of 12:13 are not lost, because death is a sleep from which God will wake his people. It is the clearest promise of bodily resurrection in the Old Testament, taken up by Jesus himself (John 5:28–29) and secured by his own rising from the dead.

12.reflection:
Verse 1 promises deliverance to “everyone whose name shall be found written in the book”. How does knowing that your name is written in the Lamb’s book of life (Revelation 13:8) change the way you face suffering or fear?

Verse 2 calls death sleep and promises that the dead will awake. How does the resurrection of the body shape the way Christians grieve, care for the dying and think about their own death? How does the warning of “everlasting contempt” affect the way we pray for and speak to those we love?

The brightest stars are “those who turn many to righteousness” (v. 3). Who helped turn you towards Christ? Who might God be calling you to encourage, teach or pray for?

Daniel says, “I heard, but I did not understand” (v. 8), and is told to go his way and wait (vv. 9, 12–13). Why do you think God gives us promises rather than a timetable? What does faithful waiting look like in your life this week?
